content:
Sequences are a standardized way to execute arbitrary sequences of Experiments.
The main use case is to standardize commonly repeated scripts that are too complicated for a single Experiment,
and to generate reports automatically. The exa.core.sequence module defines the framework. The main principles of sequences are: A sequence allows arbitrary control over execution nodes (experiments or subsequences) with loops and conditionals. The executions and analyses of the nodes are tracked such that the results
can be retrieved at later stage based on only the unique ID of the execution event. The end results of a sequence (plots, observations, report) are deferred and can be generated at analysis stage. The inputs to a sequence must be simple such that a sequence can be launched from e.g. command line.
While a sequence can be written to accept many options such as sweep ranges and settings,
the recommended way is to rely on the configuration file to pass the information. The data model of sequences is roughly the following: A subclass of Sequence defines a certain control flow of sequence nodes, which
are either Experiments or other (sub)sequences.
Sequences can be nested and mixed with Experiments arbitrarily.
The sequence in which the nodes are executed is defined as arbitrary Python code in the execute() method. One execution event is recorded using a context manager from Sequence.context .
The event is assigned a unique identifier.
The context manager records the execution of all nodes, their inputs and outputs.
The execution of an Experiment node means running the Experiment on hardware, analyzing the result, and saving the
resulting observations.
The results of the previous nodes are available in the context, and can be used in the control flow logic. The output of the execute() is a SequenceExecuteResult , which contains the results of
the nodes and the context information. It is equivalent to RunResult of Experiments. Sequence also defines a function to analyze the result of the whole sequence. SequenceExecuteResult.analyze calls this function
to produce a SequenceAnalyzeResult ,
which is the end result of the process. The SequenceAnalyzeResult can be used to plot the results,
generate a report, and save sequence-level observations, similar to AnalyzeResult of Experiments. Sequence execution results are stored in a structure of Pydantic models in exa.core.sequence.interface which
are serialized and stored to persistence.
Any exceptions happened during sequence execution will also be stored, and will halt further sequence execution.
Analysis results and exceptions during analysis are stored in SequenceAnalyzeResultData which will not be serialized nor saved to
persistence. Analysis results are obtained during normal sequence execution, or when loading back from persistence. Note Sequence is not yet supported when connected through IQM Server. An example sequence might look like this The default_options defines that the keyword qubit must be defined when using MySequence .
When executed, it runs SomeCalibrationSequence as a subsequence and, depending on the result,
runs the T1 experiment.
The lines with self.context() as context: and return context.to_result() are the mandatory ways to begin and
end the session. The attribute ignore_analyze_errors , set True here,
allows one to continue sequence execution regardless of any errors happening in the analyze functions of the sequence
itself or in any of its nodes. Unless overridden like this, its value is by default False . my_analysis_function could look like this: One can also provide custom analysis functions for an experiment that will then be called instead of the experiment’s
native analyze method. The custom analyze function should take an experiment instance as its first argument
(the rest of the arguments are for analyze kwargs), and return an AnalyzeResult object. The custom analyze could for example first call the experiment’s native analyze and then do additional manipulations: MySequence would be constructed to operate on QB12 and executed like this: When the result is analyzed, the my_analysis_function will be called with given arguments: Sequences can be run on an ObservationStash object instead
of accessing the DB when loading/saving observations. This happens simply by providing the (already initiated) stash in the argument observation_stash in the sequence’s constructor: What then happens internally in sequence is that all experiment execution nodes will load and save their observations
using the given stash. If the sequence contains any subsequences, they will be by default run on a copy
of the parent’s stash, and at the end of the subsequence execution, the copied stash’s new observations will be merged
to the parent (or if the parent does not have a stash, the new observations will be saved to the DB). This merging of
stashes can be controlled by the save_stash . User can also provide a custom stash for the experiments and subsequences in the Sequence’s definition: All kwargs given as the Sequences init (apart from observation_stash ) will end up in the Sequence’s attribute options (Note: these must be basic python types for serialisation reasons). It is also possible to set
the options of any execution nodes from the parent sequence’s options by specifying a corresponding option name with
a prefix that consists of the subsequence and/or experiment class names. For example, consider a sequence that contains
a subsequence (class) MySubSequence which further executes experiment of class MyExperiment . Then by providing
the option "MySubSequence_MyExperiment_some_option" in the parent sequence’s init, one can set the value of some_option in the execution of MyExperiment inside the subsequence. The function load_sequence_result() can be
used to load back results by sequence UUID. When loading, all nodes within the main sequence are loaded recursively
and analyzed with their respective analysis arguments. Sequences are saved to persistence incrementally after each experiment or subsequence execution. Execution and analysis
along with their respective results are separate data by design. Only the data necessary to reconstruct the sequence
execution results are saved. The data structure is represented by Pydantic models in exa.core.sequence.interface and versioned by exa.core.sequence.interface.SERIALIZER_VERSION . Thus, the loading code has to have matching
serializer version with the code that saved the results. ExperimentTracker classes are an advanced feature for situations where
more customization is needed than execute_experiment() allows.
A tracker wraps any Experiment such that it can be used like a normal Experiment instance while also tracking the
inputs and outputs. In the above example, the conditional execution could be written and extended as: In fact, the ExperimentTracker is always used under the hood. Finally, users are able to change the ExperimentTracker class a Sequence will use. By changing the class with their own
implementation, it is possible to further modify the behavior of the wrapped experiments.
For example, the RetryOnRunFailure tracker
retries to run any Experiment in case of a spurious error. previous Observations next EXA Configuration File By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Running Experiments
description:
Here we describe the basic workflow when working with Experiments.
This section is not about writing new experiments, or about running quantum circuits. First, we need to connect to a selected Quantum...
content:
Here we describe the basic workflow when working with Experiments.
This section is not about writing new experiments, or about running quantum circuits. First, we need to connect to a selected Quantum computer and load an Exa configuration to use. Here, iqm_server_url is the URL of the IQM Server, and quantum_computer is the name
of the quantum computer to use, since one server can host several quantum computers.
The API token can be obtained from the IQM Server frontend using a web browser. The optional command uses the "loggers.yml" file to set up logging behavior. Instead of the above, you can define the same information through environment variables.
To do that, set in the .env file and call When env_path is not given, init_from_env() reads the current process
environment and loads values from an auto-discovered .env file. If you want to load a specific env file instead of the auto-discovered .env , pass it explicitly: These two approaches can be mixed. To get meaningful results, EXA must know which calibration values to use.
Calibration is described using Observations which are stored in the server’s database. In short, you can select the observations using tags or calibration sets.
The various rules related to Observation loading are explained in more detail in Observations . To get started without diving into the details, you can load the default calibration set, which is the same
that is used by circuit execution through other client libraries: To conduct an experiment, we create an instance of the Experiment class, for example An experiment represents a recipe to conduct a certain task on the quantum computer.
The Experiment instances generate the execution instructions,
keep experimental data gathered during the session in memory,
and allow analyzing and plotting the data.
Each class has one or multiple default Sweeps
they are designed to perform, and default parameters they are designed to measure. Experiment is the base class that works also as a standalone prototyping tool.
All other experiments, like Rabi in the example, are derived from the base class. Rabi contains the standard recipe for executing a textbook Rabi experiment. Notable methods of experiments are get_settings() , run() ,
and analyze() , explained below. Basic behaviour of experiments is configured via the options attribute of the experiment instance.
It is of the type ExperimentOptions . Some options are shared by all experiments, while some are experiment-specific.
The common attributes are explained below: The number of times each circuit is executed to collect data.
It depends on the used readout_mode how the averaging is done. The readout_mode has 5 possible values. Their meanings and effects are as follows: "complex" (the default): normal complex voltage readout for each channel. The contrast and the excited state probability
are computed in post processing. The averaging is done in hardware. "threshold" : thresholded readout for each readout channel, representing the excited state probability.
The averaging is done in hardware. "single_shot" : complex single shot readout for each channel. The averaged complex readout (equivalent to the above "complex" mode) is computed in post processing, in addition to contrast and excited state probability.
The averaging is done in software, in the aforementioned post processing step. "single_shot_threshold" : thresholded single shot readout for each readout channel. The averaged complex readout
(equivalent to the above "complex" mode) is computed in post processing. The averaging is done in software,
in the aforementioned post processing step. "counter" : the correlated multi-qubit readout, counting the occurrences of bitstrings.
The data for each readout group is extracted from the full data in addition to the single-qubit excited state
probability for each qubit. The counting and averaging is done on the server. Number of active reset operations inserted at the beginning of each segment for each active qubit. Uses the default
implementation of reset . None means active reset is not used but instead reset is done by waiting (relaxation),
using the default implementation of the reset_wait operation. Integer values smaller than 1 result in neither active
nor reset by waiting (relaxation) is used, in which case any reset operations must be explicitly added in the circuit generation
function. The readout_programming_mode controls how readout operations are added to the circuit(s). "classic" (the default): Each qubit is measured at the end of the circuit. "heralding" : Each qubit is measured before and after each circuit execution. The measurement before is the
so-called “heralding” measurement that can be used to check that the qubit was initially in the ground state.
The heralding data appears in the dataset as a separate key, but data is not post-selected automatically. "reset_at_end" : Similarly to "classic" , a terminal measurement is added. However, the terminal measurement is
done with a feedback key, and a conditional prx is applied after. NOTE: this mode
overrides active_reset_cycles (forcing one conditional reset at the end of the segment)
and requires a station which supports fast feedback. "custom" : Measurements are not added automatically. Any measurement must be defined explicitly by the
experiment source code. Names of the measurement QuantumOps the various readout programming modes use when building
the circuits. The purpose of having more than one measure QuantumOps is to allow calibrating and optimizing different
implementations for different use cases. For example, for a terminal measurement of a qubit, it is not so important
that the measurement is projective, as the qubits state is just discarded after that. The value of this attribute is a dict mapping different measure-use cases to the measure operation names. By default,
it is given as: "terminal" is used for terminal measurement when readout_programming_mode is
either "classic" or heralding . "heralding" is used for the heralding measurement when readout_programming_mode is "heralding" . "reset_at_end" is used when readout_programming_mode is "reset_at_end" . Here, the terminal measurement is by default done with the measure_fidelity gate, which is meant to optimize
measurement fidelity but might not be optimally projective. The heralding measurement and the conditional feedback
providing measurements however must be projective, so they are done with the measure gate that is optimized to
be a compromise between fidelity and QNDness (this is the standard measurement best suitable for
mid-circuit-measurements) Users may change these default values in their experiment run, but note that this (e.g. making "heralding" use "measure_fidelity" ) may result in sub-optimal behavior. Specific experiments may also hard-code different default
behaviour based on their needs. Note: this attribute applies only to the measure operations added automatically by Experiment. If the experiment adds measure
operations explicitly in its circuit, you must write the logic for choosing the right operation to the circuit
generation function itself. Typically, experiments handle this also via options, in which case there is an additional
options attribute, usually named as measure_gate_name . The subscribed_components define which components are read out in the experiment. The subscribed components are given as
a list of component names. These can be different from the active components given as run arguments. The run settings
will however limit the used subscribed_components (as one cannot access the readout channel of a component that is
not in the settings). By default, the subscribed_components is set to None. This will result in the behaviour that
all active run components are read out. If the "counter" readout mode is used, the subscribed_components can also be given as a dict
of lists of component names (the so called “grouped readout”). The counter then returns correlation data
for each group, but not between the groups (the groups could be e.g. all the qubit-pairs in the QPU).
The grouped readout is only available in the "counter" readout mode, otherwise an error will be thrown. The options determine the general behavior of the Experiment.
They define how to generate the Settings and pulse playlists, which are the final truth about what will be executed
on the quantum computer. Before starting an experiment run, we might want to deviate from the baseline defined by the latest calibration.
After choosing the options and the target components for a run, the settings can be generated as, e.g. rabi.get_settings() .
The usage of settings is described in detail in Workflow with Experiment settings . By default, the experiment is executed on all qubits / qubit pairs on the QPU in parallel,
or sequentially if the pairs overlap,
whichever is applicable to the experiment. The experiment knows what settings to set, sweep and measure.
We only need to select the qubit on which we want to conduct the experiment on. To run the Rabi experiment on a selected subset of qubits we can do where "QB2" and "QB3" are named qubits of the QPU.
The names are defined in the components section in the chip_topology . The Experiment.run() method has optional arguments, explained below.
These arguments together provide a lot of flexibility and a way to improvise when conducting experiments. The locus or target of the experiment. In the example above, the experiment is performed on both qubits in parallel. The components given to the run method as an argument define the active components that will be part of the generated circuits.
The run components are propagated to the circuit generation function.
Note: the run components must be present in the settings.
By default, the settings are generated for all components even if they are not active. The run components can be given in four different forms: Flat list of component names List of tuples of component names, i.e. component groups Lists of lists of tuples of component names, i.e. colour groups. The lists of tuples then define partitions
of the QPU based on the application’s needs. (default) None . By default, this results in running the experiment as if
the user had provided a flat list of all qubits found in the QPU. Example: Passing custom settings These are the ones generated in step 4. Depending on the experiment, this allows specifying a sweep range of the default sweep(s).
For the FineSpectroscopy for example, this would change the minimum, maximum and
number of points in the frequency scan of the qubit readout signal.
If not specified, the range(s) are read from the configuration file, or hardcoded defaults of the experiment are used. Similar to the settings, the most convenient way to make modifications is to ask for the defaults using get_default_sweeps_as_dict() ,
modify the values, and feed them to run . Example: Passing custom settings Example: Add sweep over frequency Additional sweeps to perform over the default sweeps.
These can be thought as additional for loops on top of the default sweeps of the experiment.
In general, most Settings in EXA can be swept over.
For the Rabi for example, we could add a sweep over the pulse duration, or the drive frequency. Sweeps have a 3-level hierarchy. The simplest entity is a Sweep object which
defines a single parameter and the associated values to loop over.
A tuple Sweep objects defines a parallel sweep , which means several parameters are changed in tandem,
similar to the zip function in Python. The tuple can be omitted.
Finally, a list of N parallel sweeps defines an N-dimensional cartesian sweep over all the parameters.
This can be thought of as N nested for loops. Note on sweep types Singular sweeps come in 2 varieties: Software sweep : Software sweep, or soft sweep, means the looping logic is done “in software”, that is,
there is a for loop in the Station Control which goes through the range of values one by one,
passing the control to the devices after setting the current iteration of values. Hardware sweep : In contrast to software sweeps, hard sweeps perform the looping logic in a dedicated instrument.
This means that the range of values to iterate over is first gathered to a list, which is then passed to the
instrument.
The instrument then returns a list of results.
The most common use case is sweeping pulse or circuit parameters.
The list of pulse variations is generated in advance and sent to the station to be executed as a batch. The hardware sweeps are always the “innermost” loop of the N-dimensional sweep, meaning the values in hardware
sweeps change most frequently and the values in software sweeps are the slowest to change.
To the user, they appear the same. When calling Experiment.run() , a sweep request is generated and sent to the server.
The request contains the settings to
instruments, instructions to perform an N-dimensional sweep over the specified sweep parameters and to measure
data of the specified return parameters .
Station Control saves the data to a database, and the experiment instance reads it into the runtime memory. After the run, the resulting dataset can be accessed by Experiment.last_run or Experiment.run_results , which provide a RunResult object. The metadata includes the run ID, experiment options, the sweep request that was sent to the station, etc.
The measurement data is collected to a xarray datasets .
It includes the sweep parameters as coordinates and measured return parameters as data variables .
You are encouraged to get familiar with the xarray documentation . After a run, the dataset contains mostly raw data. To make sense of the data, we analyze it with Experiment.analyze() : Here, we have analyzed the latest run of the session.
Most analysis functions do some sort of fitting to the raw data according to the mathematical model defined in the
experiment, and store the resulting fitting parameters. The analyze method returns a AnalyzeResult object,
which contains plots of data, observations made, and any data arrays that were additionally calculated during analysis. Finally, we can visualize the results with AnalyzeResult.plot . See the plotting_guide notebook for an in-depth guide on the plotting functionality. We can also summarize the results in a report, which contains the plots and a list of observations: previous Installation next Workflow with Experiment settings By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Workflow with Experiment settings
description:
The quantum computer is controlled by many instruments which
typically have a large number of control knobs for different purposes.
The controls between different instrument models may differ slightly...
content:
The quantum computer is controlled by many instruments which
typically have a large number of control knobs for different purposes.
The controls between different instrument models may differ slightly in usage,
but in the end provide the same functionality. The Settings in EXA provide a way to group, change and view the huge amount of settings that need to be set to
operate the instruments. For more information, see the documentation of Parameters and Settings and SettingNode . There are two possible workflows for running individual experiments.
The first one relies on an assumption that a consistent set of observations has been loaded to update all settings.
In this case, the user does not need to change any settings.
The second workflow is getting a template for possible settings for the experiment, modifying the values in the
template, and submitting the modified settings when running the experiment. The workflows are presented in settings_workflow_figure . The arrows with large heads show the direction of Settings. Settings workflow. The arrows with large heads show the direction of Settings. # Note It is important to understand that the settings returned by get_settings are only a template.
Modifying it does not immediately change anything in the physical instruments.
Moreover, it does not reflect the current status of the instruments.
Instead, it represents the user’s intent .
The settings are only applied to the instruments when submitted to Station Control. Most Experiments can be run without modifying the instrument settings, as shown by the black
arrows in settings_workflow_figure .
This requires that the station and the configuration have been set up with sensible default values, and we have set observation loading rules
that fetch good calibration values. The workflow is roughly: Define experiment-specific default values in the EXA configuration.
Load the EXA configuration with init_experiment_configuration() . Set loading rules with set_global_default_observation_loading_rules() . Change experiment options, such as number of repetitions. Run experiment without referencing settings in any way. Note that steps 1-3 are optional.
In this workflow, the experiment merges the settings from Station Control, the configuration,
and observations, and sends them to Station Control behind the scenes. In a more experimental workflow, we might want to manually override the settings generated by the experiment. After the optional steps 1-3 above, the workflow is roughly: Get a template for settings: The method returns a SettingNode object that contains
all the suggested settings that are needed to run the experiment.
The structure and values are specific to the experiment. Make modifications to my_settings , as explained in exa.common.data.setting_node .
Typical use cases are changing an outdated value or just trying out new things.
Note that this step is optional: the settings can be passed back to the experiment as is. Run experiment as The modified settings are passed to the experiment and later to Station Control for execution. If the run is called without settings, step 4 is executed behind the scenes. The settings tree has the following main branches: controllers : These correspond to the station settings, grouped by component. gates : Gate calibration data. gate_definitions : Information about known gates and their implementations. stages : Stages of the Compiler pipeline that generates the final run definition. characterization : Other information needed by the experiment. gate_properties : Auxiliary information about gates obtained during calibration. model : Physical characteristics of the QPU. other : Namespace reserved for user-defined settings. When the get_settings method of an Experiment is called, the settings are combined from many sources and merged
with certain priorities.
A source with a higher priority overrides the value from lower-priority sources. For controller settings, the sources and their priorities are: Station Control default settings Defaults from EXA configuration, “settings” section Settings common for all components Settings specific to a component, any experiment Settings specific to experiment, any component Settings specific to a component, specific experiment Settings defined by the experiment source code Observations Runtime overrides by user For gate settings, they are: Defaults from EXA configuration, “gates” section Settings common for all loci Settings specific to a locus Settings defined by the experiment source code Observations Runtime overrides by user previous Running Experiments next Data access By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Data access
description:
When running any Experiment, Station Control stores the acquired data in its database
with a given unique identifier (UUID) called run ID. Each experiment run has a corresponding run ID, and is associ...
content:
When running any Experiment, Station Control stores the acquired data in its database
with a given unique identifier (UUID) called run ID. Each experiment run has a corresponding run ID, and is associated with a request to the station, which
has its own sweep ID. The IDs generated by a run can be seen on the plot titles and accessed in the metadata of
the dataset, experiment.run_results[-1].run_definition.run_id . The results of new runs are loaded into the memory, so using the UUID is not necessary to view latest results. To view older results, the experiment class and the data can be reconstructed using the run ID, as Experiment.get_by_run_id() constructs the dataset from persisted pieces of raw data,
applies experiment-specific post-processing to the data, and returns a new instance of the appropriate Experiment,
with the dataset inside it.
The loading works also if the run is still ongoing and raw results are being saved.
In this case, the dataset is constructed from the available data. The ExaRuntime storage has an interface that supports querying all available runs and observations,
combined with filtering by date, user, experiment, etc.
See StorageInterface for available methods. The storage interface is accessible through previous Workflow with Experiment settings next Observations By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Observations
description:
An observation is a value associated with a specific parameter or a physical observable, and a set of metadata.
Observations are generated by the analyze() method of EXA experiments.
The user of the e...
content:
An observation is a value associated with a specific parameter or a physical observable, and a set of metadata.
Observations are generated by the analyze() method of EXA experiments.
The user of the experiment can inspect the potential observations and optionally save them to the database.
Once saved, subsequent experiment runs can load the saved values to generate updated settings for the experiment.
Which observations are loaded is governed by specific observation loading rules that the user can change. Any Setting in the EXA setting tree can be saved as an observation,
and loaded back to update the corresponding Setting. However, there are also
observations that do not correspond to EXA settings. The main source of new observations is the automatic calibration service of IQM QCCSW. When an experiment needs an observation value for its computation, it retrieves the value
based on specific rules. The loaded values override default settings and will be used when running
the experiment. To see the status of the loaded values, use Each observation has a rule according to which it is loaded, as displayed by print_observations . It is possible to change the rules according to which observations are loaded with set_global_default_observation_loading_rules() where rules can be an empty list, or a list of valid rules.
For a list of available rules, see classes on observation_loading_rules .
The exa-core file contains now just backwards compatibility imports.
Note: set_global_default_observation_loading_rules() should be called before initiating any experiment instances, as the global default rules are applied in the experiment
constructor. When the global default rules are an empty list, the observation loading is turned off globally.
This is the starting behavior if no rules are set. When a list of rules is used, for example [GetLatest()] ,
all experiments will load observations based on these rules,
which effectively turns on the observation loading globally. Customized loading The loading is handled by the observation_handler attribute of the experiment instance.
The handler provides a way to manage which observations will be loaded and how.
It contains rules that are used to resolve which observations to load, and also contains the loaded values. You can manage the rules by set_load_rules() .
For example, the following lines set rules such that for 'QB2' , the latest observations will be loaded,
and for 'QB3' nothing is loaded. Most observation loading rules query their data from the database every time experiment settings need to be resolved.
To prevent unnecessary overhead and abruptly changing calibration values, it is recommended to use the ObservationStash . The stash provides a way to load observations from the database once, and after that refer to the content of
the local stash only. The stash can hold both exa.core.observation.observation.LocalObservation and ObservationData instances. Creating the stash object with a set of local and DB observations can be done by just providing the
observations mapped to their dut_fields In typical notebook use, however, what the user usually wants is to initialize the stash using a list of loading rules,
similarly to initialising an ObservationHandler . For this
purpose, one may use get_loaded_stash_from_rules() . For each observation,
it will go through the provided list of rules and try to load the observation, and once the DB returns a value,
it will stop. As a result, an ObservationStash instance
that contains a single DB observation per dut_field is initiated (in case one of the provided rules actually returned
a value for this dut_field ). Loading from the stash is done by using the observation loading rule LatestFromStash , which takes
as its arguments the stash object and optionally tags used for filtering when loading from the stash: Then observations can be saved into the stash so the next experiment loads them from there with LatestFromStash instead of accessing the database. Once you have a final set of observations you are satisfied with, you may save them into the DB in one go: See the API docs of the above functions for more info and optional arguments. As mentioned above, the main source of new observations is the automatic calibration service of IQM QCCSW.
The sections below describe how to save and manage observations manually. The analyze method of Experiments has the ability to summarize the analysis as one or more key observations, which
are returned in AnalyzeResult instance’s LocalObservations .
LocalObservations have a parameter, associated component, and a value, and some other metadata.
They can be inspected, validated, and tagged before saving: Note Saving observations to the backend is not yet supported when connected through IQM Server. example_local_storage.ipynb demonstrates how to save observations locally. validate() runs any validation rules set for the
observations. tag() attaches a list of arbitrary strings to the
observation, such that the observation can be later found by the tag or a set of tags. One way to create and save an observation manually is to create a local observation.
This is the same class that analysis outputs. Or from a Setting: Users can add their own string tags to observations to denote a specific purpose for a group of observations. Use cases for tagging include: Keeping observations personal by using a unique tag, e.g. a username, Marking checkpoints for good calibration, Jumping between two groups of observations (operating points), Reverting to an earlier calibration state. The workflow with tags begins by setting the loading rules such that only the latest observations with given
tags are loaded: And using the same tags when saving: This way, all observations are saved with my_tags and only those containing my_tags will be loaded.
Thus whatever observations are saved, effectively stay in the namespace defined by my_tags .
Other users using their own tags will be unaffected by the changes in this tag space. On the other hand, if users want to share and work with the same set of observations,
they can simply use the same set of tags (or two sets that have some intersection). It is a common situation that there is some known, good calibration set shared by many users.
A user who wants to use the known set as a starting point but not change it,
can make a copy of the known set and only change the tags with save_observations_with_new_tags() . For example, let’s say a good calibration has been tagged with known_calibration : After the command, observations identical to known_calibration have been created,
except they are now tagged with my_tags .
Then, the user can freely save and load in their own tagspace without changing the known calibration
that others use. previous Data access next Sequences By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Experiment basic usage
description:
Creating an Experiment object with no init arguments inits the class with the default options and the
default circuit generation function. The available gates are taken from configuration. By default,...
content:
Creating an Experiment object with no init arguments inits the class with the default options and the
default circuit generation function. The available gates are taken from configuration. By default, the readout_mode is “complex”.
The subscribed_components (i.e. the components that are read) default to all qubits found in the QPU. By default, this experiment generates a single circuit without gates and measures all qubits. To do something more useful, we should define circuit(s) to run.
One way is to create a new Experiment class, and define the default circuit generator in the
class, as explained later.
We can also proceed without defining an Experiment class by passing circuit generation function to the constructor. As an example, let’s create a circuit generation function that executes the T2 Ramsey experiment on all qubits.
In this case, the given pulse sequences simply consists of pi/2 - wait - pi/2 pulses.
The latter pi/2 pulse can be applied either around X or Y axis. The pulse sequence generation functions are in principle free form, but the first two parameters are fixed: components : The logical chip components, i.e. qubits and computational resonators. builder : A ScheduleBuilder object which will realize the gates. We can now use the function to execute the pulse schedule with the default circuit values. Circuit parameter values that are not part of a sweep can be set through settings.stages.circuit_generation.circuit .
If not set manually, the circuit parameters will be created from the parameter names of the circuit generation function. It is possible to sweep any of the circuit parameters.
Let’s sweep both the pulse_delay and use_XY parameters and then run the experiment. By default, the experiment does not know the units or datatypes of the circuit parameters,
so we have to add them here if we want to display them. Experiment supports five readout modes: “complex” (the default) “threshold” “single_shot” “single_shot_threshold” “counter” See the docstrings in ExperimentOptions and experiment_definitions.ReadoutMode for more
info on the readout modes. Now, let’s change the readout_mode to “single_shot” and run the same T2 Ramsey experiment: Note how the dataset now contains the “repetitions” dimension,
which corresponds to the non-averaged single shots.
The averaged results are computed as well. Let’s use Native Instructions for specifying the single qubit gates this time, and do some
CZ gates between two qubits.
Let’s run the experiment in the “counter” readout mode. Simple example of deriving a new experiment from Experiment .
The idea is not to override core functions like _run and get_settings ,
but instead just define the minimal changes needed for the experiment to function. Below, we need to only define the circuit generation function, the default sweeps and the default options. One could also add extra arguments to the circuit function and get them to the settings tree
via Experiment.get_default_circuit_settings , do additional default changes to the settings tree
via Experiment.update_settings , and modify the default observation loading rules,
or use a custom connection graph via Experiment.setup_additional_init_properties . Writing parallelized 1QB experiments in the aforementioned way is easy, but when we want to create an experiment where the parallel elements are not single components but groups of components, e.g. connected qubit-pairs, it would result in a lot of boilerplate code. For this reason, Experiment provides functionalities that allow one to write the relevant experiment functions in terms of the quantities that actually matter. Also, now that we (hopefully) understand what Experiment does, we can actually skip writing most of the typical Experiment methods and instead define them as just functions. iqm.pulse allows users to define their own gates and implementations and registering them for ad-hoc usage in a notebook/script without having to touch any of the underlying libraries. In the simplest case, this means changing some detail in one of the generic gate implementations, for example the pulse waveforms. However, it is also possible to write the gate implementation from scratch. iqm.pulse also allows for creating a completely new gate/operation in one’s notebook/script and then registering it
similarly to the GateImplementation above. The user may of course write the logic for any implementations of this new gate from the scratch, but there is also a useful base class CompositeGate, which can be used to create GateImplementations in terms of other already existing gates. By default Experiment appends each segment in a circuit with a multiplexed measurement operation that reads all the readout components simultaneously. When this behaviour is enough, the user does not need to add any measurement operations in the circuit function itself. However, in case a more complicated measurement scheme is needed, the readouts can also be included in schedule itself. There can be any number of measurements in a circuit (also different numbers between different components). Currently the number of measurements for a given component must be constant between different segments of the circuit, and the measurements must happen at same times in each segment, however. previous Example Notebooks next Local storage example By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Local storage example
description:
