implementation of StorageInterface that requires no database or server. It shows how to: run an experiment u...
content:
This notebook demonstrates exa.core.local_storage.LocalStorage , a fully local, file-backed
implementation of StorageInterface that requires no database or server. It shows how to: run an experiment using calibration loaded from a live backend, save the resulting observations both to the live backend and to a local file, load observations from local storage alongside a live calibration set, build a new observation set purely in local storage, and reload that local observation set later. This is useful for e.g. keeping scratch/exploratory observations out of the shared database, or working
fully offline against previously saved data. Connect to a station Use a matching experiment configuration file LocalStorage can be used purely in-memory ( LocalStorage() ), or pointed at a JSON file so its
contents survive across notebook/kernel restarts. We use the latter here. GetCalibrationSet("default") loads the backend’s current default calibration set (this replaces the
now-deprecated GetDefaultCalibrationSet rule). Registering the resulting stash as the global default
observation loading rules makes it the calibration source for the experiments run below. The simplest way to execute and analyze an experiment, relying on the calibration loaded above. We do this as an easy way to generate some observations. Each save() call independently persists the tagged observations: the first call writes to the live
backend (the ambient storage configured above), the second writes the same observations into local_storage instead, via the storage_interface override. These end up as two separate sets of
observations, one per backend, sharing the same tag. Loading rules can mix storages freely: here GetCalibrationSet("default") still reads from the live
backend, while GetLatestForTags(tags, storage=local_storage) reads only from local_storage , in the same call. exa.core.observation_set_utils.create_observation_set only targets the ambient storage, so to create
an observation set in local_storage specifically, we call its create_observation_set method
directly with a hand-built ObservationSetDefinition . Note that all observations you add to the set must already exist in local_storage Finally, reload the observation set we just created, entirely from local storage. previous Experiment basic usage next API reference By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Sweep generation
description:
While discussing the prototyping of Exa Experiment s, we
learnt that any experimental setting can be swept, and we saw a simple sweep generation function in the subclassing chapter. Here, we will talk...
content:
While discussing the prototyping of Exa Experiment s, we
learnt that any experimental setting can be swept, and we saw a simple sweep generation function in the subclassing chapter. Here, we will talk about the default sweeps in more detail and explore ways
to design your experiments effectively. When you sweep a setting, Exa executes multiple experiments, one per each value, and returns the results back to you
aggregated into a xarray.Dataset , where the sweep name becomes a coordinate, and most of the time, also
a dimension of the measured data xarray.DataArray . Just like we saw with our Bell state experiment, where phase became such a coordinate. Note Q: Wait a second, you just said that every setting can be swept! What is happening? A: You can create a Sweep from any Setting ,
that much is absolutely true. It is done through the sweep() method, like
demonstrated before, and you can add that sweep to your experiment. However, not every sweep will affect execution
of your experiment directly, or at all. Some settings are given as information, which can be used and referenced,
and so is valuable, but does not do anything or cannot be set at the instrument level. Some settings have an
explicit read_only property, which prevents them from being changed or swept. This is what this section
is about. In Exa, the setting tree is a SettingNode object, containing 5 separate sections: Controllers. This section contains all the settings that directly affect some instrument participating in experiment
execution. This is the only section which is actually submitted to the station. Modifying most of the settings here,
via a sweep or otherwise, will turn some knob or change a value somewhere in the laboratory. Some of the settings
are just references and cannot be changed, however. They are still included in the setting tree, because knowing them
is necessary. For example, controllers.QB1.drive.awg.sampling_rate cannot be changed from the settings
(on some devices it can only be changed at the hardware level). It is useful to know it, though, because when
sweeping a duration of anything, it has to be
a multiple of one time sample. Gates. Here, all the gate calibration data is stored. These settings populate the ScheduleBuilder we learnt about in the section concerning circuit design.
If sweeping a setting from this section, each time the circuit generation function is called during compilation,
the builder will contain modified calibration data, adjusted by the sweep. Gate definitions. Here, the definitions of operations are stored, as well as which implementations are default for
which loci. Sweeping those is definitely unusual, but possible, for example to evaluate the performance of
different implementations within one experiment run. Note that most of these settings are anyway read-only. Exceptions
include exactly the gate_definitions.<gate>.default_implementation setting. Characterization. This section is entirely for your convenience, it contains the characterization information,
such as relaxation times or couplings that were measured, and does not affect anything when swept. Stages. This section sets the behaviour of the compiler , specifically the compilation stages and
passes within them. One of the first passes is to resolve the circuit , so this is where all the
arguments to the circuit generation function end up. These arguments are one of the most important settings to sweep,
so we will talk about them separately. Note that every setting affecting the compiler can be swept, and it will
alter the compilation process producing the schedule for that specific sweep spot. In summary, section 1 settings affect the instruments themselves, while sections 2 and 5 affect the instructions we give the instruments. This is an important distinction. All the sweeps from sections 2 and 5, collectively known as
hardware sweeps, are combined into one very long Playlist before being sent to be
executed. This means the time needed to switch from one value to the next is only limited by the sampling time of those
instruments (in practice you might want to reset your qubits, but you don’t have to). On the other hand, the controllers
settings need to be modified between executing subsequent playlists. As a result, the hardware sweep spots, or sweeps
of gates and stages settings, are always done in the inner loop, while the software sweeps, or sweeps of
controllers settings, are always done in the outer loop. We have seen so far how to make a single sweep, and what kinds of sweeps are possible. Often the design of the
experiment requires multiple settings to be swept. How to combine different sweeps together? In Exa, there are two ways of doing that: Cartesian sweep, or “nested loop” sweep: one circuit per each possible N-tuple of values from N sweeps. Pointwise sweep, or “zipped” sweep: one circuit per a corresponding pair of values. Also known as “parallel sweep”
across the codebase. To produce a Cartesian sweep, put two sweeps together in a list, and to produce a pointwise sweep, put them in a tuple: The type annotation Sweeps is list[ Sweep | tuple[ Sweep , …]],
which is as far as those can be nested. The output of the sweep generation function needs to be a list of either tuples
of sweeps, or individual sweeps. The sweeps are then, as much as possible, executed from left to right. The first sweep
becomes the innermost loop, changing the fastest, and the last sweep becomes the outermost loop, changing the slowest. In the example above, the first 21 executed schedules have the coupler pulse amplitude and width set to 0.0 and 20 ns,
while the qubit pulse amplitude is increasing from 0.0 to 0.1. Then, the schedules 22 to 42 have coupler pulse amplitude
increased to 0.01 and the width to 21 ns, while the qubit pulse amplitude again starts at 0.0, increasing to 0.1. Note The gates and compiler (hardware) sweeps cannot be combined with the controllers (software) sweeps to form a single
pointwise / zipped / tuple sweep right now. In some situations we would really like to do that, but there are ways
around it - for example using a modulated drive pulse to change the drive frequency (hardware sweep) instead of directly changing the drive frequency (software sweep). Any of the above sweeps can be added to any type of experiment discussed in the conceptualization chapter. However, there are certain strong correlations. When we calibrate gates, we typically sweep the calibration settings of those gates. Sometimes, certain gate
implementations will have parameters others don’t. It is OK, and probably necessary, to write experiments
sweeping those parameters – they need calibration too. It is good to have informative error messages show as early
as possible, informing the user that the experiment cannot go through if the default gate implementation does not
have this parameter. When characterizing the chip or calibrating the general frequency landscape, we often sweep the controllers settings,
most commonly centre AWG frequencies and flux voltages. But we might also use certain kinds of auxiliary gates,
such as flux_pulse or chirp . Sometimes, we want to actually characterize the instrument or the whole
classical transfer line between the instrument and the QPU, and the controllers settings’ sweeps are necessary then. Circuit settings are swept in almost any type of experiment, because often we simply need more than one point
to determine some property of a gate or the chip. The most common sweeps have names like wait or phase , but
there are some taking discrete values, like add_initial_pi_pulse . Some of these could be achieved with adding
a new compiler pass and sweeping its settings instead, but there is a lot of freedom in the framework for you to
choose which way you prefer. The first argument to the sweep generation functions always is, like in the case of the circuit
generation function, either components or group . The other arguments can be any default context arguments.
Two commonly used ones are chip_topology , which the framework will
populate with a ChipTopology corresponding to the QPU the experiment is
executed on, and settings , populated with the full setting tree. The other context arguments are discussed in
the next chapter . You may add additional arguments, which can be anything, and their
values will be supplied from experiment options, as long as the names match up. We will discuss parallelization later,
for now let’s focus on the other arguments. The chip topology is supplied for the sweep generation function for a simple reason. The components given are only the
active, computational components, but in many experiments we would like to sweep a setting which is not associated with
any of those, but with a component connected to them. The simplest example is the coupler: Sweeping the DC voltage on the coupler flux line is needed in experiments measuring the ZZ interaction between
the qubits, which are used to calibrate such a coupler frequency that the effective ZZ coupling is zero. Another example is the probe line: Note Q: Wouldn’t it be easier to just have the coupler or probe line included in the components to begin with? A: You can absolutely do that. In our collection of experiment classes, we have mostly adopted the convention of
only using computational elements (qubits and occasionally computational resonators) as “active” components which
are given to the run() method. But whatever you provide there will
end up in the components argument for the circuit and sweep generation functions. So you can absolutely just
use the coupler. The chip topology is there for your convenience. In practice, it is much cleaner to always think
of qubits as active, and supplying both the connected qubits and their connecting coupler each time is redundant. Keep in mind also the expectations and assumptions other users will make when using your experiment. In 99%
of cases, the experiments concerning pairs of qubits and couplers connecting them will accept pairs of qubits
as run arguments, and users will expect that and be confused if it is not the case. However, if your QPU happens to
have driveable and directly measurable couplers, they will expect an experiment calibrating a single qubit gate to
work when a coupler is provided as a run argument – because now it is an active component! When using the parallel execution framework, the first argument to the sweep generation function needs to be group ,
which is a sequence of the components involved in one particular slice of the experiment, like in case of the
circuit generation function. When writing the default sweep function, you can almost just think about a single qubit or pair that the experiment
is affecting, and write your sweeps just like these were all the components. The only thing you need to remember is to use the same number of points in each sweep for each component group . If the first default sweep has 10 points, and
the second has 5 points, this has to be uniform for all the involved groups. Under the hood, the sweeps returned by this function will be combined into pointwise sweeps by the framework, following
the same order. The sweeps affecting the same parameters will not be duplicated. If the same parameter is swept for two
different groups, only one of the sweeps is maintained. For that reason, this common parameter needs to always get the
same sweep values. For example, in a two-qubit gate calibration experiment, you might sweep a gate parameter like gates.cz.crf_crf.QB1__QB2.coupler.amplitude and also a circuit parameter phase , determining a phase of the used
Z rotation in a Ramsey sequence. At least, this is what the parameters are for the group ("QB1", "QB2") . For
another locus, e.g. ("QB3", "QB4") , we would like gates.cz.crf_crf.QB3__QB4.coupler.amplitude and phase . In such a scenario, the QB3__QB4 sweep has to have the same number of points as the QB1__QB2 sweep, but the
values of these points can be anything. The phase sweep however needs to be the same for both loci. One simple way of achieving this is to have one of the options in the ExperimentOptions be something like amplitude_sweep_points , setting the number of points in the amplitude sweep for all involved
pairs. This may look something like this: And yes, the sweeps returned by this function can already be pointwise – they will just be combined into a larger
pointwise sweep. Here we ensure not only that amp_sweep and width_sweep have the same number of points, but also
that the analogous sweeps for other pairs have the same number of points. Note Q: Why is this so complicated, why can’t I just define everything independently? A: Ultimately it is because the “parallel execution framework” is not performing multiple different
experiments on different parts of the chip completely in parallel. It is still just one big job which is executed
as one big job on the hardware. Completely parallelizing the execution on disconnected parts of the chip by
running separate experiment instances at the same exact time is not supported now. This means we need to conform
to limitations imposed by xarray for example. This is not really about writing new experiments, but it is useful to know regardless. Having hundreds of default sweeps
attached to the experiment, all with different values, might make it problematic to allow users to change their values.
Typically, it is good to use options to provide maximum flexibility, so the users never have to do this. This may
result in options like amplitude_sweep_frequency_range , width_sweep_start or width_sweep_end_per_pair ,
but you should aim to do all the frequently needed adjustments via options, and not by passing
the default_sweep_ranges run argument. However, it can still be done. A useful method here is get_default_sweeps_as_dict() ,
which returns a dictionary where the keys are full sweep parameters and the values are numpy arrays representing the
sweep data. To update one sweep out of many, you can pass an update dictionary, containing only the keys you would like
to modify, to the default_sweep_ranges run argument. This will just modify the range of the sweep for the first pair, keeping the default sweep for the second pair. Note Be careful when adding soft sweeps in the parallel framework! If two of the component groups share components,
their circuits cannot be executed simultaneously, and they will be downgraded to a sequential execution.
However, software sweeps are just added to the entire experiment. If you modify the voltage on a coupler, this
voltage will be modified for all the component groups. Changing the voltage on TC-1-2 might be intended when
measuring the pair ("QB1", "QB2") , but it will also affect results on the pair ("QB1", "QB4") by virtue of
hybridizing the coupler differently with QB1 . In such cases it is better to throw warnings or prevent the
user from running sequential experiments. They are not even the fastest way of accomplishing the task in practice. The term “design-of-experiments” (DoE) in general refers to everything we may do ahead of time to help the experiment
estimate the required information faster, more accurately or precisely. The general area is vast, but this is a
chapter specifically about how to generate sweeps that follow certain rules which improve our efficiency in terms of
extracting information from an experiment. There are adaptive experiment designs , in which one would perform some
measurements and use them to inform the sweeps used in the next experiments, targeting the volume of the space where
measuring provides the most information, for example using Bayesian inference. Here, we will not be talking about adaptive experiment designs, because they break the abstraction of a single
experiment run, as understood within the Experiment framework. They might
be implemented on a higher level of abstraction, such as using Sequence or
optimization frameworks outside of EXA. Instead, we will focus on static designs . There is a plethora of static designs, but the overall target for them
is to answer a question that can be roughly defined as “How to best fill a multidimensional space with points to
learn the most information”. Different types of designs aim to answer this question in different ways, such as
minimizing the mathematical “discrepancy” between the multidimensional hypercube and the experiment design, or
maximizing some property of the Fisher information matrix. The actual extraction of the information from the measured
data will be then described in the analysis chapter. Our implementation uses the emukit toolkit, and you are invited to read its documentation
as a supplement to this guide. Sometimes, we already have some constraints on our space. For example, we know that the readout pulse that is both very
long and high amplitude will excite our qubits too much. However, both weak but long pulses and short but high amplitude
pulses might be fine. In other words, we might want to not sample from a hypercube, but for example from a hypersphere. This can be achieved by adding constraints directly to the design space. A constraint here needs to be a function, which
takes a mapping from parameter names to their values (produced later by the space sampler) and returns either True ,
if the point is OK, or False if it is not. For example, here we might want to do: You can add multiple constraints, which uses only points satisfying all of them. The constraints are enforced
by rejection sampling, so it might increase the sampling time. Also beware that certain constraints might make it
impossible to find points due to being infeasible, so it is important to define them carefully. Now, a significant area in the sampling space is empty after applying the constraint. # To close off this chapter, let’s talk about some additional sweep-related tips and tricks. Often times, one wants to add a sweep that just does nothing in a safe way. Usually it is to collect statistics, or
statistics over time. This sweep is also a good way of checking if your analysis supports extra
sweeps. It is doing literally nothing, so it should be the easiest sweep to support on the level of handling data. This sweep should be added in the following way: Do not add any extra settings, or sweep settings which “seem unrelated” and “probably won’t do anything”. This section belongs somewhere between this chapter and the previous one about circuits . When designing
your experiment, you might want to execute multiple circuits which differ by more than a simple phase or duration, but
in a more fundamental way. Executing multiple circuits is a type of a sweep, and the easiest way to implement it is
as a sweep of an argument to the circuit generation function: Then, the state argument becomes a circuit setting under settings.stages.circuit_generation.circuit.state and
can be swept: There are some settings which are not single numbers, but sequences of numbers, for example the IIR filter amplitudes,
or the measurement integration weights. Unfortunately, sweeping entire sequences at once is not allowed due to limitations
of xarray , which is used to store and handle data after execution. Instead, we might extract single values at certain
indices of these sequences and sweep just those. This is especially useful for calibration of the precompensation filters. This sweep can then be executed and added to the dataset. After consulting this chapter, you should be able to write arbitrary sweep generation functions and design your
experiments properly. Since sweeps often involve circuit generation and compilation pass arguments, making an experiment
can be an iterative process. previous Circuit generation functions next Configuring compiler passes By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Producing observations
description:
You should now know how to write the majority of the analysis function and add plots to the AnalyzeResult object.
The other important output of the experiment run are observations. You should make sur...
content:
You should now know how to write the majority of the analysis function and add plots to the AnalyzeResult object.
The other important output of the experiment run are observations. You should make sure you understand how they work
by reading the relevant sections of the basic guide first: Observations .
Note that similarly to analysis, observations are also not entirely mature right now, and some changes might be made in near future. Just like plots are a means of communication with humans, observations are a means of communication
with the software around the quantum computer. Think of an observation as a “unit of knowledge” about the system.
Most observations closely map to settings, with their different kinds explained earlier in the sweeping chapter. The name “observation” is therefore a little bit of a misnomer - you cannot really observe that the flux
voltage on the coupler line is -0.034, if you are the one setting this value. Yet the way to set the value is to save
a LocalObservation for it. You need to get used to this nomenclature
to write good experiments. There are also observations which do not map to settings. An important kind are the quality metrics observations.
Those observations are actually “observations” in the common sense, as they tell us something about the quality of the
system, e.g the \(T_1\) time or the fidelity of a specific implementation of the CZ gate. Quality metrics observations
need to follow specific syntax to be picked up by the automated tooling which then creates visualizations of how certain
metrics change over space and time. Finally, you can just save anything you want as an observation. Simply insert any string satisfying certain regex
rules into the dut_field attribute. It is good practice
to nevertheless apply some logic here and do it for a good reason. Those observations are accessible from the analysis
result - maybe you want them to change the execution logic of a larger sequence of experiments. The experiment analysis needs to create specifically LocalObservation objects, and this may be done directly, but is heavily discouraged. You should generally never need to just initialize
this class yourself. Instead, use the appropriate AnalyzeResult methods introduced later. Let’s however have a look at what are the different fields of the class. The DUT field is the name of the observation. For setting observations, it needs to exactly map to a setting using the
dot syntax, e.g "controllers.QB1.drive.frequency" . For quality metrics, it needs to start with "metrics" . The DUT
field decides what the observation is. An observation with the same DUT field, which was created later, will override
any earlier observation with the same DUT field, if it is fetched together or put into the same observation set. When
fetching observations from the DB or stash, only the latest observation for a given DUT field, satisfying certain
loading rules (like specific tags) will be fetched. The DUT field needs to have a format of a dot separated string, where each segment needs to start with a letter or
the underscore "_" , and the segments cannot include dots "." or double underscores "__" , unless they represent locus
strings. A value of the observation can be anything. However, it has to be of the same type as any other observation
with the same DUT field. For setting observations, the value needs to be of the same type as the setting, with an
exception for the settings which are lists - the observation needs to be saved as a numpy array. The setting units are important, because in iqm.pulse , certain logic exists which converts time-like and
frequency-like settings into dimensionless reduced quantities, and the units are used for this purpose. This only matters
for gates settings – for everything else, just make sure the unit is the same as the previous saved observation and
makes physical sense. Always use the SI unit, and not its derived version, e.g use “s” and not “ns”, “Hz” and not “MHz”. Tags are not to be populated by experiments, they can be set by the user later. Unless you have a very good reason, do
not attach any tags to the observations. This value is the experiment run ID, which will be populated automatically as long as you use the correct method of
adding observations to your AnalyzeResult . You can add here an object of the class RangeValidationRule ,
representing a range in which the observation value should realistically be. This helps prevent saving e.g negative \(T_1\) times, or single Hz qubit frequencies. It is recommended to do so, but only if the range is actually strictly
limited, e.g do not add an upper limit for \(T_1\) - they might indeed reach more than 1s one day! Finally, we learn how to do it correctly! This depends on the observation type. For the setting observations, use add_setting_observation() ,
providing the actual setting object for which to save the observation, its value and uncertainty, and optionally
validation rules. Everything else will be automatically created from the settings. For the metrics observations, use add_observation_with_qon() ,
where QON stands for “Qualified Observation Name” and should be first created using either the class QONMetric or one of its subclasses. For example, to save gate fidelity, you can
use: You can also specify the DUT field yourself, by using add_observation() . Now you should know how to add observations to your analysis result. This becomes more important when you start integrating
the experiments together. For now, the main purpose of the observations will be modifying the calibration. previous Plotting the analysed data next Integrating your experiment into a sequence or graph By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Plotting the analysed data
description: We have learnt how to write analysis functions in the analysis chapter, and we have seen simple PlotDefinition examples in the prototyping chapter. It is time to explore the topic more! There are two ...
content:
We have learnt how to write analysis functions in the analysis chapter, and we have seen simple PlotDefinition examples in the prototyping chapter. It is time to explore the topic more! There are two main reasons: Plots are a means of communication between humans. We acquire information through our senses, like in this case,
our eyes via looking at the plot. The automated calibration procedure running on a large QPU does not need to
make plots, because it does not need to look at them. All the information is already there in the data. Making plots might be a lot more computationally expensive than analysing the raw data. Making a bar plot of all the
result bitstring counts from a 10 qubit experiment takes significantly longer than calculating the fidelity, XORing,
or fitting the data. It is just expensive to do that. In short, plotting is separate because most often we do not have to and we do not want to do it. When writing a plotting function, you should all the time think of the users of the experiment class. This includes
yourself, your colleagues and whoever would run the experiment in the future. This makes this plotting more art than
science – it is a lot more subjective. What is attached to your AnalyzeResult is a PlotDefinition object. This object contains the plotting function
and a dictionary of default keyword arguments. The plotting function is only required to have one argument, and that is run_result , which takes the whole RunResult object generated by your run, and returns a plot. Additional arguments can
be added, and they generally should be provided in the dictionary to the plot definition. To decide, what those arguments should be, consider how they can be used. After analysing your experiment run, you
get an AnalyzeResult object. Then, you can call: And this replaces the default values of those two arguments. Combine this with the fact that plots are used to
communicate between humans, and it becomes clear that these arguments should be something that humans can be realistically expected to change . For example, an entire 3D data array is a bad keyword argument - no one will
be plugging their own data there. The plotting function is attached to this specific experiment. Maybe your experiment sweeps two settings in a pointwise sweep, and it is a bit of an arbitrary choice which one of
them should be the X-axis? Include a kwarg to select for that! Maybe there are multiple data arrays being generated,
and the plot could be cleaner if some of them are not included, but then they are not included? Include a kwarg that
controls that. Additionally, the plotting functions do not automatically work with parallel experiments. So if your experiment is
meant to be run on multiple qubits, or pairs of qubits, you should include an argument group , which lets the
function know which data to plot. Everything else, all raw data, options, all analyzed data variables, is already included in the RunResult .
Your plotting function should just extract it from there. If you’re using matplotlib to make your plots, remember to wrap the function with wrap_mpl_plot() . Let’s now have another look at our old plotting function from the Bell experiment: We can see that: It only has one extra argument: target_qubit . It extracts the required data and the fit from run_result.dataset . It is wrapped to return the correct object. The function itself returns a Matplotlib Figure, but that is wrapped
to return an EXA Figure. The figure will look the same, but the framework needs some additional functionality, which
the EXA Figure has. The title includes the experiment label (to let other users know what experiment created the plot) and the run_id
(to let other users know what specific data, available for them in the database, has been used to create this
plot) in the figure title. Other users tend to share plots with little context, and having the run id allows
access to the data, as long as you’re connected to the same database. It is however not perfect, as for example 'excited_state_probability' variable is referred to via a string,
instead of the global constant. As a reminder, this is how the plot definition is then attached to the analyze result: Keeping all the above in mind, we should be able to create some plots. The most common library to make plots in Python
is Matplotlib, and it is generally recommended to use it here as well. This is not a guide to use Matplotlib, however.
Fortunately, there is a well maintained Matplotlib user guide you
can reference instead. Let’s now go through some general good practices when making plots. Sometimes, it might be tempting to do some additional analysis in the plotting function, to generate an auxiliary
data variable to plot. If this is something on the level of binning the data for a histogram plot, it is fine to do.
However, doing any “serious” analysis in the plotting function is heavily discouraged . Running an experiment,
plotting the results, and then finding out that the plotted variables are missing from the dataset is extremely
annoying! If something is a good representation of the experiment result, it should be in the dataset .
As a baseline, try to only extract already analyzed variables from the dataset, and just create the plots in the
plotting function, breaking this rule only for a very good reason. As plots are created at the end of analysis, and testing analysis is quite difficult, you should make sure to manually
test your plotting functions as much as possible. Keeping the data variables in the dataset also means you need a mock
dataset to unit test your plots, which makes testing them not really straightforward. A long time ago, we wanted to make plotting fully generic. This isn’t really possible. But it resulted in the
existence of the generic_plot_definition() . This function
only takes the data variable name you want plotted, and does the rest, including finding the fits in the dataset,
labelling the axes and adding an informative legend with all the fit parameters. It may be useful when prototyping
a new experiment or supporting a rarely used functionality. As explained in the analysis chapter, Model Selection Fitter makes good default plots, which have
a bit more information in them. The plot always contains the data, the fit, initial guess and a confidence interval.
Here is an example from the \(T_2\) experiment fitting described in the previous chapter: As you can see, this plot is perfectly enough in prototypes but also in mature experiments which do not
use extra sweeps. Be careful when analysing over extra dimensions - you get a plot per sweep spot!
That may be too many plots and you will need to make another, custom plot anyway. # I am just going to list some basic scientific good practices here, which I am sure you’re well aware of. These also
apply to default experiment plots – they are scientific plots! Put informative labels on all axes of the plot, and use a unit every time. The unit should be the actual unit
corresponding to the data. E.g. if you multiply the X axis by 1 billion to convert from seconds to nanoseconds,
you should also change the unit from [s] to [ns]. Do not connect raw data points with lines / segments. The lines are for the fits and theoretical models. Add informative and clear legends to your plots. If a particular data variable is associated with a number, for
example fits typically have parameters, include the most important ones in the legend, especially if there are more
than one different fits. If possible, and it does not make the figure too crowded, plot uncertainty and error. For data points, add errorbars,
which can be done with Matplotlib errorbar function, and for fits, use fill, which can be done with the fill_between function. Different people view colours in different ways. Those, whose ability to distinguish between different colours
is significantly decreased compared to a typical one, are referred to as colour blind. There are at least 10 different
kinds of colour blindness. The default Matplotlib colour cycle is pretty colour-blind-friendly, but different users might have different
preferences. For that reason, avoid hard-coding colours in your plots . Let users individually override their
global Matplotlib colour cycle, so that it fits their individual wants and needs. This can be done through
a modification to rcParams['axes.prop_cycle'] . Avoid using too many colours: if plotting too many variables,
consider if a 2D plot is not more appropriate. For plotting many different raw data sets, consider using different marker
shapes. Note Q: What if I want multiple things to be the same colour? I have to pick one! A: Not really! Instead of specifying a colour, you can use the “CN” colour spec where “C” precedes a number acting
as an index into the colour property cycle. This allows you to make the data points, the fit, and the uncertainty
band the same colour, with possibly different transparency settings, without actually fixing what the colour is. The default colour maps for the 2D plots are not so easy to change globally. You may decide to include a plotting function
keyword argument like cmap to allow different colour maps. Keep in mind that some people might find it hard to read very small font. Again, the default Matplotlib font size is
pretty fine for most uses. Sometimes however you might find yourself making the plot bigger, and then that large
plot is rescaled to fit on someone’s smaller screen, making the font smaller than intended. The dataset is an xarray.Dataset object, and xarray supports Matplotlib-based plotting directly through
the plot() method, like demonstrated in the example plotting function for the Bell experiment. This can be useful,
as the X and Y plot labels are automatically filled with data variable labels, and colour bars are generated on the
2D plots. See the Xarray user plotting guide for more
details. You can add any number of plots to your AnalyzeResult . The user can
use the plot_all() method to plot all the plots or render_report() method to see all the plots and
observations, but these do not allow changing arguments. If your experiment needs two or more different visual representations, think if they are fundamentally independent or
not. If they should be viewed together, and you cannot imagine talking about one without seeing the other,
consider making them subplots of the same figure. If they are however representing different aspects of the experiment,
maybe having separate plotting functions and separate plot definitions is better. The latter is also more friendly
for code reuse , as these same plotting functions might be attached to multiple experiments. Typically, a presence of an extra sweep makes your hand-crafted default plot not work. The data has an additional
dimension, after all! There are things you can still do. First, if your experiment produces some observations, which are typically single numbers, with extra sweeps those
observations are now arrays. Those can be plotted. Consider adding an extra plotting function for when there is one
(or more, but it is harder to support more) extra sweep. Additionally, you might want to add an argument like selection_dict to your plotting function, which is then used
inside it to select a slice of data such that the original plot can still be made. This can be done using the sel() method of xarray Datasets and DataArrays. This is the most meaningful if a single “best slice” in your experiment
can be somehow identified. As mentioned before, the experiment run in parallel will produce a plot for each of the included component groups.
This implies the component group should be an argument to the function, so that they can be actually different. The
name of the plot in the plots dictionary should also be
unique – best practice is to just include the qubit group in there. If using the sequential feature of the framework, we might sometimes find ourselves in a pickle: we need to plot
a raw data variable, like QB1_excited_state_probability , but it contains meaningful data for two or more parallel
layers, for example one for qubit pair ('QB1', 'QB2') and one for ('QB1', 'QB4') . We don’t want these mixed up. The solution is to first add a context argument circuit_index: int to the analyze function signature, and then
modify the creation of plot definition as follows: The wrapper will automatically select the correct data for your plotting function to plot. You can’t really know if your plots are good, because people don’t talk about good plots really. They just get used to
them. You can know if your plots are bad . Some of the signs are: No one is actually using the default plots from the experiment. Instead, your colleagues are sharing notebook
code snippets to make a different plot out of your experiment. In such a situation, try to understand what is it
that their plots achieve and your default plot does not. Then, try to implement it in the experiment itself. The plot takes very long to generate. This typically means you’re trying to show too much. Maybe not all the
information is necessary? You should now know how to make plotting functions and attach them to your analyze results. You should understand that
plots are means of communication between humans, and thinking about those humans and their needs is the most important
component to making good plots. You also should understand little intricacies of EXA and which specific things to do to
make best use of them. previous Automated data analysis next Producing observations By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Prototyping your experiment
description:
The Experiment framework
allows one easy prototyping of almost any experiment idea. Open your favourite Python IDE or a Jupyter notebook and
let’s get started! Make sure you’re connected to a station ...
content:
The Experiment framework
allows one easy prototyping of almost any experiment idea. Open your favourite Python IDE or a Jupyter notebook and
let’s get started! Make sure you’re connected to a station - it is always better to prototype with a real QPU, but a
simulated or a mock station will allow you to execute most of the code successfully. We are going to need some imports: These are only the classes we will actually need to use – for the purpose of typing we would need more, but since
we are prototyping, this will not be necessary. We will start by defining our circuit generation function . We will learn more about those later, but
for now let’s explore the simplest version of it. We will write an experiment that is not too simple, but also not too
complicated – we will prepare a Bell state, apply a Z rotation and then uncompute the state to measure its coherence.
It will need to sweep a phase , or the angle of applied Z rotation, but otherwise the circuit will not change. Let’s unpack this. First, the argument components will be populated with the components we later pass when we run
the experiment. In this case, we will use two qubits. The argument builder is ScheduleBuilder , which Experiment will populate automatically with the correct gate calibration.
Then, any remaining arguments will be turned into circuit settings for us to change or sweep, with the default
value given in the signature. Inside the function we first create all the gates, and then add them to the circuit in order. This is of course a
matter of preference. Some gates, like u or rz admit arguments, others, like cz , don’t. What the get_implementation() call is returning is a gate factory , a class
containing the calibration for a specific locus, which is then called to produce the gate implementations. The locus
can be any sequence, for example tuple or list, of computational components. You may observe that the circuit does not contain any measurements. This is because by default, Experiment appends measurements
to the circuit automatically during the compilation. I will explain how to modify this behaviour shortly. Notice that the final output of this function is a list, and it is a list of these TimeBox objects. When the function is called, the builder will know all the calibration and thus the output of the
function will contain unscheduled pulses, which are later scheduled into a full playlist. This means what is output
isn’t really an abstract circuit, but a very specific series of pulses implementing a circuit. Nevertheless, the
circuit generation function is called that because it can be created while thinking only in an abstract way. Next, let’s initialize an Experiment instance with this circuit: We also create a SettingNode object that contains all the experimental settings,
including instrument settings, gate calibrations and circuit parameters. Let’s create a sweep over the
phase: Experiment can be run with two connected qubits (called QB3 and QB4 in our example). Before executing the experiment,
we may want to look if the final schedule (after Experiment compilation) makes sense and corresponds to
what we wanted to achieve. To do so, we call: We will see an interactive window containing the full schedule: Each channel corresponds to a specific instrument line, a drive, flux or readout. Each element can be clicked and
inspected further. We see that the schedule we had in mind is correctly represented. # Now, we can run our experiment. We now wait until the experiment has run. Afterwards, we may access the run result under bell_exp.last_run . This is
a RunResult object, which contains two main attributes: run_definition and dataset . The former is a collection of metadata and additional properties
that characterize the experimental run before the execution, and the latter is an xarray.Dataset object
containing the collected and post-processed experimental data. A good practice is to take note of the experiment run id, a UUID under which the collected data are stored in the
database you are connected to. It is stored in bell_exp.last_run.run_definition.run_id . Next, let’s have a look at the dataset. We used the default readout post-processing mode, complex , but regardless
of that mode any Experiment dataset will always have a data variable called QB3_excited_state_probability , which
corresponds to readout-post-processed estimate of the probability of measuring QB3 in the excited state. We can use the xarray plotting functionality to visualize the data: Resulting in the following figure: The in-built xarray plotting lets us quickly visualize the data. The x label is not that descriptive,
because we are prototyping and did not provide any information about what “phase” is. We see the
Z rotation applied to QB4 has been successfully transferred to QB3 through the uncomputation of the Bell state. # Most of the time when prototyping, one would analyze the data in the notebook directly. However, Experiment provides an analysis framework which should be used when writing a new experiment, and can also be used while
prototyping, so we will take this opportunity to introduce it. Exa contains several fitting and analysis helpers, we will use one of them to generate a fit to the experimental data.
Measuring qubit phase through a combination of an RZ, Hadamard and a Z measurement is a common trick, so fast and
efficient methods for its extraction exist. The analysis function has two arguments – components and run_result . It also supports additional arguments,
which contain more information about the experiment – but we will learn about that later. Unlike the circuit
generation function, the first argument is not automatically populated, and its purpose is to limit the analysis to
certain components, a feature important for large, parallel experiments. For that reason, we first find all the
components in the run_result in case they were not provided. In this case, we are only interested in the state of
the first qubit. We use the phase fitting function to obtain a fit, then add all the calculated quantities to the
result. After writing this function, we may analyze our experimental data: We can render the analysis report, but it is currently empty. We can populate it by adding plots and observations . Let’s add a simple plot showing the data with a fit and some observations. What we just wrote is a plot function – a function that takes the run result and plots the data. This function,
together with some default arguments, creates a plot definition , which is attached to the analyze result. The
reason to do plotting like this is to only create the plots if they are needed – the function is only executed if
you ask for the plot to be generated. An experiment can be included in a calibration procedure that runs autonomously,
when there is nobody to look at these plots. You should never just create plots directly in the analyze function! Let’s attach this plot to the analysis result: Now, running yields this: The exa.core.analyze_result.analyze_result.AnalyzeResult.render_report() allows visualization of plots and observations from the experiment. Here,
we see that our coherence might be too good to be true… Probably the readout error has been over-mitigated. # All in all, our analyze function first retrieves the correct target qubit, finds data in the dataset, fits it, creates
a plot and adds an observation for the “coherence” of the Bell state. Here, the error is actually dominated by the
readout and its mitigation, but in general this coherence could be a way to bound the state fidelity from above. Note Q: I understand why the circuit generation function needs to be a function – Experiment supplies all the calibration
information, and the output of the function is then compiled into physical schedule on the chip, which seems very
difficult to do manually. But I do not see the point of writing an analyze function – I can do all of that just
in the notebook! I have the resulting dataset, I can visualize the data, fit them, all in the notebook – I am just
prototyping. What is the reason to package it into an analyze function? A: Good observation. Analysis is currently the least mature part of exa, some call it just a “collection of random
scripts”. Nevertheless, there still are specific guidelines to follow, regarding plots and observations for example.
There are two reasons to write these functions when prototyping. First, you are forcing yourself to think a bit more
abstractly; use a generic target_qubit instead of 'QB3' , as you might have done in the notebook. This makes
it easier to then use the same code to analyze the experiment run on a different subset of the chip, and the
function you write while prototyping can be later directly attached to the Experiment subclass you create. The second
reason has to do with the convenience analyze functions provide when using the parallel framework, which is what
we are going to cover next. One useful method of Experiment is Experiment.process_run_components() . This method converts the run
components Experiment receives – typically a list of qubits – into a more structured object, which can then be passed into
the circuit, sweeps and analyze functions. While prototyping, you will most likely not override this method, but you can
control its behaviour by setting a Experiment.parallel_group attribute. The main purpose of the
processing is to split all the run components into smaller sets, such that the experiment can be executed in parallel on
multiple of these sets at the same time. If your experiment is primarily two-qubit experiment, you may want to execute
it on many pairs of qubits simultaneously. Here’s how the components are processed if you specify that your experiment is a two-qubit parallel experiment: All the possible connected pairs of qubits within the submitted list of components are found from the chip
topology. Then, the pairs are colored – or split into the minimum number of sets such that no two pairs in one set
share a qubit. That would be impossible to run simultaneously! Mathematicians call these sets matchings . The experiment is then performed the number of times equal to the number of colors, each time on all the pairs
included in that color/matching. All we need to do to utilize the power of the parallel framework for the Bell coherence experiment, is slightly modify
the circuit and the analyze functions: We changed the argument components to group everywhere and we removed the line which was getting all the
components from the run result – it is not necessary, because the parallel framework will now feed the pairs to the
analyze function as well. We also used additional arguments: data_color , which only contains the data for the
parallel layer we are interested in, and circuit_index which is the index of the colored set our pair belongs to.
This index is used to wrap the plotting function to correctly only plot the data collected when executing that circuit. We still need to tell Experiment that we want the execution to be parallelized over connected pairs,
but after we do so, each of these functions will just receive a tuple of two qubits, which are guaranteed to be
connected on the chip – and thus have a CZ gate defined between them. Each of these functions will therefore be
executed multiple times, which now justifies writing an analyze function a bit better! To initialize the experiment, we now call: And we can run the experiment, for example like this: I am using a 5-qubit chip, where QB3 is connected to the other 4 qubits, so the automatic coloring will
select the pairs QB2-QB3 and QB3-QB4 for me. These cannot be run in parallel, so the experiment will execute first
on the first pair, and then on the second pair. On a bigger chip, the results would be slightly more impressive. Now the report shows data for two pairs. The observations could be called something better, but for the
prototyping stages this is fine – we are not saving them! # There are more options for the parallel framework, using one qubit, disconnected pairs, qubits on the same probeline –
that will be covered later. We hope you now feel more confident prototyping and running experiments using Experiment. Remember, you can also use Experiment subclasses to prototype, if they are already implementing some of the behaviour you want.
Any Experiment subclass can be initialized with an overridden circuit generation function, and most can also have their
analysis function replaced. In the future, it will also be easier to replace the default sweeps. This means you
can pick and choose which implemented properties of another subclass you’d like to use for a quick prototype. Speaking of Experiment subclasses, let’s now learn how to write one. We already know about circuits, sweeps and analysis, but
there is more that goes into a mature Experiment subclass ! previous Conceptualization: What is my experiment? next Making an Experiment subclass By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Conceptualization: What is my experiment?
description:
Any creative process starts from an idea. The idea for a new experiment may come from a paper, conference talk,
a corridor discussion or it might strike from nowhere. This section will help you catego...
content:
Any creative process starts from an idea. The idea for a new experiment may come from a paper, conference talk,
a corridor discussion or it might strike from nowhere. This section will help you categorize the idea and understand
how it fits into the framework, so you can use appropriate tools when implementing it. The section is structured into
a series of questions – it is recommended to answer each and simply keep the answers in mind (or write them down)
for now. In this guide, we consider an experiment any protocol executed on a quantum chip to extract information. As such,
a resonator spectroscopy is an experiment, but so is a collection of QAOA quantum circuits
equipped with automatic post-processing. The extracted information might be anything, and what it is defines a purpose of the experiment. Most experiments
will fall into one (or more) of the following categories: Characterization experiment - extracts information about the quantum chip or the entire system. Examples include
relaxation experiments ( \(T_1\) ), experiments measuring the coupling between qubits and couplers, measurements
of the microwave transfer function etc. The numbers measured can later be used to inform the calibration, but are not
used to modify the calibration or any instrument settings directly. Typically they measure some intrinsic quality
of the quantum device. Calibration experiment - used to find best parameters for instrument settings or quantum gates, which improve the
quality of the quantum computer. Examples include Rabi experiment, Ramsey
experiment, experiments setting the appropriate idling voltage for the coupler etc. Benchmarking experiment - used to measure the quality of the calibration. Examples include Randomized Benchmarking,
Floquet benchmarking, Gate Set Tomography, Cycle Benchmarking, Quantum Volume, etc. The information extracted
depends mostly on the calibration. It is good to keep in mind the purpose of the experiment, but it does not translate directly into specific practices,
other than the kind of observations the experiment produces. Think about why you need this experiment to exist. Finally, it is possible that your idea is not a suitable candidate for an experiment at all. If you require multiple
sequential steps of measurements to be performed, with data processing and logic in between, it is recommended to use the Sequence instead. The experiment classes are building blocks which you will need
to create a Sequence, so continue reading this guide even if that is what you want to do. In exa, the experiments are defined by circuits and sweeps . The circuit is not necessarily the abstract
quantum circuit, only containing gates and measurements – it is a broader term including low-level pulse schedules.
The sweeps define which experimental parameters need to be varied by default and in what way. Those may be just circuit
parameters, angles of rotation gates, or number of certain “blocks” included in the circuit. Alternatively, they might
be specific instrument parameters, such as DC flux voltage applied to a certain component, or the time AWG waits after
it is triggered. For example, in the Rabi experiment, the circuit consists of a single X gate followed by a measurement,
and there is one default sweep, varying the amplitude of the pulse implementing the X gate. Think about the main building blocks of your experiment. What does the circuit or schedule look like? Do you need
multiple different circuits, or is one, static circuit, enough as long as it is parametrized? How would you generate
those multiple circuits (this logic will need to be implemented as a sweep!)? What are the main parameters you want to vary in the experiment? How do you want to vary them: independently, or
in a complicated, dependent fashion, e.g. following a space-filling curve? Conversely, what are the parameters that
should not be varied in your experiment? Exa allows adding arbitrary sweeps to every experiment, but not every sweep
is a good idea! The experiments might be defined to operate directly on the level of different instrument settings, continuous wave
microwaves, and voltages; or they may be defined by abstract quantum circuits. Generally speaking, characterization
experiments tend to be more low-level, less abstract, and benchmarking experiments tend to be more abstract, but it is
not a strict rule. Pulse-level experiment uses pulses and continuous waves directly, has direct access to all the instrument settings and
makes use of that. Typically you would think of an experiment schedule or playlist describing the used pulses,
instead of a quantum circuit . Measurements of the TWPA electrical delay or flux pulse distortions are pulse-level
experiments. Semi-abstract experiment primarily uses quantum gates as building blocks, but it might involve some pulses
acting on the level of the QPU physics as well as some waiting in the “circuit”, left there for the free Hamiltonian
evolution. Those experiments do not generally measure classical system parameters, and can be modelled using cQEC
Hamiltonians. Measurement of the ZZ-coupling or Floquet benchmarking are semi-abstract. Circuit-level experiment only concerns itself with quantum gates arranged in circuits. The experiment is modelled
using abstract unitary operators in computational frame and maybe some physical error models. A good criterion
to distinguish a circuit-level from a semi-abstract experiment is the role of waiting in the schedule - in a
circuit-level experiment, the waiting is expected to act as identity. Gate Set Tomography is circuit-level. Experiment can handle all the abstraction levels, but it is currently most optimized for the semi-abstract ones.
The abstraction mostly matters when designing the circuit generation function , which is the main engine generating
subsequent schedules. Note Q: I only know about circuits! I thought all quantum protocols use them. Will I be able to effectively use exa, which is a pulse-level access tool first? I am not an experimentalist. A: Right now, most of the really pulse-accessy things were abstracted away, and you need to use them only if you
actually need to use them. This means, you can write your experiment fully thinking in an abstract way, and
it would work. You may need to dig a bit deeper into IQM packages to find automatic circuit transpilation, if
that’s what you want to do, but for example sampling of random circuits and their inversion based on their unitary
operators was implemented for randomized benchmarking. Some experiment classes are written to do one specific task, and perform it automatically and quickly. Others are
primarily tools used to explore physics. The first need to be more mature as pieces of code, but humans do not really
need to look at the generated data. The latter might be less mature, because their primary function is flexibility. An example of the former could be an error amplification experiment used to calibrate the virtual Z rotations in the CZ
gate. An example of the latter could be Floquet benchmarking of the coupler leakage during the CZ gate. Think about how you want your experiment to be used. This will inform how you write your code. An experiment designed
to do one specific thing does not need to be flexible and implement all the possible tricks, but it needs to break
as rarely as possible. previous Creating your own EXA experiments next Prototyping your experiment By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Automated data analysis
description:
You have your circuit and sweeps, and you have run the experiment. Now it is time to analyze the data. We have seen a
simple analysis function in the prototyping chapter. Here we will explore analysis...
content:
You have your circuit and sweeps, and you have run the experiment. Now it is time to analyze the data. We have seen a
simple analysis function in the prototyping chapter. Here we will explore analysis in more detail. By the time the analysis function is called, automatic post-processing has happened and produced the RunResult object for us to use. The post-processing can be adjusted via post-processing
passes, which belong to the compiler chapter, but we will here assume the default post-processing has
run. The division between post-processing and analysis is not clear-cut, and it is possible to arbitrarily process
data during the analysis. If possible, using compiler passes is preferred, but the analysis is the most flexible
part of the framework for a reason. In this chapter, we will learn about how to approach analysing data produced by the Experiment class, different fitting methods, some basics of operating on xarray , as well as some additional tricks to making
your analysis fast and reliable. Automatic analysis is where your experiment finally produces the information it was designed to produce. This is done by
calculation of one or multiple derived quantities . It may proceed in phases, deriving further quantities from ones
derived earlier. Remember, analysis is a communication tool! It is important to strike the balance between communicating to the experimentalist using the
experiment class, and enabling further automation. For an experimentalist, keeping all the derived quantities making
the experiment visualization easy is important. It enables flexible use of the experiment class, as a starting point
for further research. For an automated process, speed, reliability, and keeping just enough data to explain why
something went wrong, are crucial. Each raw dataset is stored in the database, but the analysis needs
to run every time it is recovered. Thus the speed requirement for analysis should be stricter than for the execution,
as it could be performed multiple times for the same raw data. Note Think about the purpose of the experiment class. Sometimes, producing a single number at the end is not the
goal, but instead visualizing some 2D quantity. This is commonly true for experiments where the circuit may be
complicated, and the measured quantity is highly sensitive to small variations in the input parameters. The analysis is allowed to create observations and plots. However, plots should never be built in the main body of the
analysis, because they can be pretty expensive, both in time and memory, even on relatively small datasets, and the
automated routines consisting of many experiments typically do not need to make them at all. Instead, make all the
actual plotting in a separate plotting function . Observations are described in a later chapter of this guide. Each observation is either a quantity
metric, or it should map to somewhere in the setting tree. For this reason, think about if producing observations
makes sense with arbitrary extra sweeps. Maybe it does with some sweeps, but not others? As mentioned before, the analysis framework is not very mature, but it is very flexible. Still, organizing it internally
into multiple stages using separate functions that can be then reused is a good practice, even if not enforced by
a structure of some compiler. A good way of starting the analysis is to create the AnalyzeResult ,
and extract the dataset and settings from it. Then, try to work as much as possible with the result variable, adding arrays, observations and plots to it. You
can use these methods: A useful function is iqm.cpc.core.dataset.annotate() , which attaches Parameter to a xarray.DataArray : It modifies the array in place, but also returns it, which makes it easier to use it on views into some bigger array.
The parameter label is automatically used as a plot label when plotting from xarray , and the prefix argument, typically the name of the qubit or a pair, is appended to both the parameter name and label by the annotate() function. Note Q: What quantities should I add to the dataset? I would like to avoid from it becoming too large. A: Come back to the purpose of your experiment. If it is meant to be a flexible research tool, generally any
quantity carrying useful information should be added to the dataset. Such a flexible tool could be run with extra
sweeps added by the user. For this reason, even the zero-dimensional quantities , like the final observations
produced along with their uncertainties, should be added to the dataset, making sure any extra sweeps become a new
dimension on this variable. Stashing information, for example fit parameters, in the attributes of the array is not
recommended for this reason, as it makes it harder to plot them. However, some of the fit parameters are not really interesting on their own, so skipping adding them to the dataset is OK. As a reminder, the analysis function needs to return the AnalyzeResult object, if it created a new one. Similarly to the compiler passes, the analysis functions can take some extra context arguments. Arguments chip_topology ( ChipTopology ), chip_properties and gate_definitions (mapping of names of QuantumOp s) are always available. Additionally, when the first argument is group and you’re using the parallel execution framework, the arguments data_color ( Dataset , reduced to only contain data pertaining to this group), and circuit_index (index of the circuit that contains this color group, relevant for sequential execution of overlapping groups)
are available. In the parallel framework, analyze_result could also be given as an argument, in which case a new AnalyzeResult needs not be created or returned. The function should
instead modify the received object. The dataset will contain some raw and post-processed data, depending on the readout_mode option. Each of these DataArray s
name is of the format f"{label}_{name}" , where the label is by default a qubit name, such as 'QB1' . If the
measure operations were performed with custom keys (which can be added through the key argument when creating the
timebox), the labels are f"{qubit}__{key}" . This helps separate data collected with different kinds of readouts.
For example, the default heralding key is "__HERALD" , resulting in data variable labels like "QB1____HERALD" . The default readout variables are: The variable readout contains averaged raw measurement results, either the averaged complex or averaged
raw counts, depending on the readout mode - complex in complex and single_shot modes, averaged counts
otherwise. The variable readout_single_shot contains single shot complex data, individual in-phase and quadrature
amplitudes of the integrated signal. This variable always has a repetitions dimension, corresponding to shots.
It is only present if the readout mode is single_shot . The variable state_single_shot contains single shot thresholded data, each being either 0 or 1. It also has a repetitions dimension. If the readout mode is single_shot_threshold , it is what is returned from the readout
instrument. In the single_shot (complex) readout mode, the post-processing passes produce this variable by
thresholding in software, if the readout calibration information is already available. In the counter mode,
it is calculated from the counts. The variables contrast and phase_optimal_quad are calculated in complex and single_shot modes
by performing a principal component analysis of the averaged complex data along the first dimension. They correspond
to the amplitude and phase of the first principal component. These are useful variables before the readout is
calibrated. The variable excited_state_probability is the readout-error-mitigated best estimate for the probability
of the qubit collapsing to the excited state when measured. In complex and single_shot modes, it is
calculated from the averaged complex data using the average complex response of the ground and excited state
measured with a readout calibration experiment. In the other modes, it is calculated from the averaged counts by
inverting the readout assignment matrix. This mitigation is necessary so the variable is unbiasedly the same in all
readout modes, assuming no higher states are present. The counter.result variable does not have a label, because it corresponds to all the qubits. It is the default
variable when the readout mode is counter , but also calculated in single_shot and single_shot_threshold modes. These are the raw, unmitigated frequencies of different bitstrings (like “110”, “010”) measured across all
qubits. Only when using counter mode, if the subscribed_components are a mapping from names to subsets of qubits,
there will be additional variables f"{group_name}_counter_readout" , containing counts only for those subsets.
The ordering of the qubits within this subset is inside run_result.additional_run_properties["readout_groups"] ,
and will need to be extracted if the ordering of the bits inside the bitstring is important. This is the default
behaviour when using the counter mode while parallel_group is CONNECTED_PAIRS , in which case the names of
the groups are the names of couplers connecting the qubits and the groups each have two qubits. The general principle behind the post-processing is to always give the user all the available information, so all the
variables which are possible to be calculated, are calculated. You could always remove or add more post-processing
passes, if that is what you require! Analysis functions are allowed to have extra arguments, which can be populated when calling analyze() . Make sure that the analyze call without any
arguments works almost all, or ideally, all the time. Each experimental data are different, and a parameter default that works
on one station might not work on another. It is good practice to make the arguments dimensionless and derive as much
as possible from the chip and component properties stored in the settings. Note For example, flux pulse amplitude modifies the qubit frequency, but this relationship is non-linear. The qubit
frequency itself has some maximum and minimum. In an appropriate context, “max relative qubit frequency shift” might
be a better argument than “max qubit flux pulse amplitude”. Those analysis knobs can be turned instead of rewriting
the analysis. Including arguments with defaults in your function signature is better than using magic numbers, but
an automated routine will at least need an automated way of adjusting them. All the data in analysis are represented as an xarray DataArray s. Those structures generally
behave similarly to numpy arrays, and can be manipulated directly, using already implemented “utility functions”
or “ufuncs”. Those operations will generally always return a DataArray and maintain all the dimension
structure, including extra sweeps, and so using them should be your first priority. Let’s have a look at some examples. The arrays in analysis will have dimensions and coordinates corresponding to sweeps. Additionally, single shot arrays
will have a repetitions dimension and coordinate. Instead of indexing with integers, use sel , isel or loc to ensure the correct slice is selected. This allows the original phase array to have any extra coordinates. Here we used sel which selects based on the value of the coordinate. This is generally the correct approach, but you might also want to use isel , which
selects based on the index – you need to know what is the correct index, but you don’t need to
know the value, which is helpful if it was generated automatically. This is one of consequences of the analysis not being entirely mature. In the chapter about sweeping we discussed pointwise sweeps, or sweeps where multiple settings are swept in parallel. The way those are handled in xarray is that all swept settings become coordinates of the dataset, but only the first one becomes
a dimension, and the dimensions are the same for all arrays. For example, let’s say we ran an experiment on many qubits, and swept the amplitude of a PRX gate on all of them as
a pointwise sweep. Then we want to do some analysis on it. Using the actual setting name, not the dimension name, will sometimes work, but it is generally safer to use the
dimension name. In the above scenario, both of these names are quite convoluted, and will generally only differ by the
name of the qubit and optionally, the PRX gate implementation. Sometimes there is a need to change the coordinate of the data. For example, the swept quantity was voltage on the
flux line of the coupler, but the analysis needs the coupler frequency to derive meaningful results. We can use
some xarray functionality to address this problem. First, we can use assign_coords() to assign new coordinates to our array. Now, this will add a new coordinate, but this coordinate is not a dimension of the array. Maybe this is fine, but if
it is not, you should follow it up with: The method swap_dims() returns a new DataArray with swapped dims. Note Be careful with swapping dims on the arrays already in the dataset. This might prevent the analysis from being
re-runnable, as the dataset is modified in-place, and the swap_dims() method will expect
the old dimension to still be a dimension. If you invoke it twice, it will break on the second call. Other useful methods of DataArray and xarray functionalities include: Concatenation of multiple arrays along a new or existing coordinate: concat() . Merging multiple Dataset objects (you need to be careful in analysis): merge() or merge() . Renaming the variables, rename() . Additionally, you can make coordinate arrays directly from Parameter . Which populates attributes like standard_name , long_name correctly. Those arrays are useful when combined with
concatenation of multiple arrays. This produces a new array with a new coordinate and dimension given by coord_array_1 . Many numpy utility functions have been ported to xarray , but not all. Some will still work on xarray objects,
but produce a numpy array. In such a scenario, first try using apply_ufunc() . A good example is unwrap() , since it is commonly used in quantum experiment analysis: Check the documentation for apply_ufunc() to learn more tricks. Most importantly, input_core_dims and output_core_dims are always lists of lists of dimension names, corresponding to the dimensions along which not to vectorize,
or in other words, the dimensions the original utility function expects the data to have. In the unwrapping example, it
is the dimension along which to unwrap. Because the unwrapping function takes one array, there is only one list of
dimensions. Each list corresponds to a separate array. Because the unwrapping function returns one array, the
argument output_core_dims also has only one element. Finally, the argument vectorize is set to False , because
the unwrapping function is already vectorized. Note Q: What functions can I use inside apply_ufunc? A: Any function which takes and returns some numpy arrays will work. If some of the arguments the original
function needs should be fixed, or are not DataArray s, you might consider writing a small wrapper which fixes
them. Otherwise, you may write your own function, which takes some arrays and returns some arrays, and then setting vectorize = True will make apply_ufunc() work with xarray arrays of any dimensions, albeit
the implementation of that is no more efficient than a for loop. Before going down this rabbit hole, please consider if
the functions apply_along_coordinate() or multifit_along_coordinates() are not better suited to the task. Often, you would like to specifically fit some model to the data, in order to extract some fitted parameters. These
tasks form a subset of “manipulating xarray arrays”, and can in principle be done using apply_ufunc() and
