arbitrary fitting tools. However, there already exist more specific helpers for fitting, which will also produce
properly annotated arrays and sometimes even plots. The basic tools are written on top of scipy.optimize.curve_fit() , and should be used if the problem is quite
simple, there is not much variability, and performance is important. Then, exa.core.model_selection_fitter.fitter.Fitter is built on top of lmfit and supports more advanced statistics and automatic selection of the best model. Both
work fully with xarray and allow arbitrary extra dimensions. First, let’s have a look at apply_along_coordinate() . This helper function is made mostly
for fitting, but it might be used for other purposes. Let’s have a look at the syntax: The most important mechanics to understand here is the interplay of the outputs of fitting_function , the returns argument and the returned arrays. The fitting_function must take only two 1D numpy arrays, understood to be
x-values and y-values representing some data to be fitted, and return two things: first, a dictionary mapping arbitrary
names of fit parameters to their values, and second - a numpy array representing the fit. The names given to returns are keys in that dictionary. The function will package these values into data arrays.
The first returned array is the fit , which will have the same dimensions and coordinates as the input array. All
the other arrays are fit parameters, and they will be missing the dimension corresponding to the given coordinate along
which the fit is performed. Exa contains several typical fitting functions, and it is not difficult to write your own. The fitting_function is
allowed to do anything, as long as the output is correctly formatted. These examples are in model_functions . Typically, you’d write a function that takes some meta-parameters, or guesses,
and that returns the fitting function proper, eg: To generate these fitting functions we can use the iqm.cpc.core.dataset.compute_1d_fit() function. This function
takes the x and y data, as well as a model function and some guesses, and wraps scipy.optimize.curve_fit() to
produce output in the correct format. The keys in the returned dict are the names of the arguments of the model
function plus those same names with a _stddev suffix, which is the standard deviation calculated from the output
covariance matrix for each parameter. Note Q: The limitation to only 1D models is quite severe, why wouldn’t I just use apply_ufunc? A: Realistically this is what you need most of the time, and all you need to define is the model function and
some guessing logic, for which there are many examples. With raw apply_ufunc() , you need to do the same calls
to scipy.optimize.curve_fit() every time, extract the uncertainties yourself etc, which generates a lot of
bloat. If you need something more powerful, be sure to check the next section though. Alternatively to using apply_along_coordinate() , you may want to consider a solution built
on top of lmfit called the Model Selection Fitter (MSF). Please check the lmfit documentation to learn more about making your own models, since
it is something you will need. This section only covers the usage of MSF. What MSF does for you: Fit multiple lmfit.Model s to the data. Parallelize over extra dimensions. Select the best model, separately for each sweep spot, based on the Akaike Information Criterion. Wrap everything into DataArray s. Generate informative plot definitions. Let’s look at an example. A common reason to select from multiple models arises in a \(T_2\) Ramsey experiment,
where the signal not only oscillates, but also decays. This decay might be a simple exponential decay, a Gaussian decay,
or a combination of both. That is, we need three different models. Here we construct different models by simply taking the same model and setting some of the parameters to not vary.
As you can see, Model Selection Fitter produces many extra arrays, such as \(R^2\) or standard errors of each
fit parameter. It also produces a plot definition, which can be immediately attached to the analyze result. More about
those in the plotting chapter. Note Q: Why are you annotating? I thought that is done automatically… A: Apply along coordinates does annotate the data arrays, but MSF doesn’t, so you need to do it yourself to the
output. Model Selection Fitter uses the model’s lmfit.Model.guess() method, so it should always be defined. Additionally,
it is good practice to make sure each of the used models has the same fit parameters, even if they are fixed or
quantities derived from other parameters via an expression. This will ensure proper error propagation, which lmfit
will perform for you, using the full covariance matrix – sometimes, the uncertainty in some derived quantity can be lower than either of the uncertainties of the “original” parameters, if those parameters are strongly correlated. The lmfit library supports models with an arbitrary number of independent variables, and MSF will correctly
package them into DataArray s. Check the collection of models in Exa and in the lmfit library proper
for examples. In most analysis protocols fitting only a single dimension of the data at the time is sufficient. Additionally,
collecting data along only a single dimension is much faster, and reducing the number of dimensions your experiment
needs is one of the most effective ways of making it quicker to execute. But what if your problem is fundamentally larger? As mentioned above, the lmfit library and by extension MSF support two-dimensional models. Simply define a
model with two independent coordinates and some parameters and proceed like described in the previous section. You might
even assume the shape of one of the dimensions, e.g. always using two frequencies for a Ramsey experiment. There is a variation of this problem which would require substantial modifications to lmfit Models to solve, and there
is a solution to it in Exa. This is where you have multiple 1-D datasets which generally follow the same kind of model,
but some parameters vary between them. For example, multiple exponential decays which are expected to have the same
decay rate, but different amplitudes. Or \(T_2\) traces where the Gaussian part is considered the same for all
traces, but the \(T_1\) contribution varies quickly. To fit such a dataset, we need to treat some parameters as global , affecting all traces, and some as local , affecting just one. If all parameters are global, the problem
reduces to a 2-D fit; if all are local, it reduces to multiple 1-D fits. There is a tool called multifit_along_coordinates() which allows you to fit your data like that.
Let’s go through its usage. The function itself is mostly an xarray wrapper that works similarly to apply_along_coordinate() with slightly different arguments: In the above example, the main_coord is the independent coordinate along which regular 1-D fitting would take place.
In the example with multiple decaying exponentials, this would be e.g. the time variable. The supp_coord is the
other coordinate. This coordinate could be an index of measurement, initial state, or something else that modifies the main experiment, which is measuring the exponential decay in time. The cloned_arguments is a list of arguments to fitting_function which will be cloned along supp_coord . The
number of times it is cloned depends on the number of points in supp_coord . If there are 5 points in supp_coord ,
there will be 5 parameters in the model, independently fitted to the data, all representing the variable param_0 ,
but for different values of supp_coord . The returned arrays will have different shapes and dimensions depending on which arguments were cloned. The param_0_array will have a dimension supp_coordinate_name , which param_1_array will not have. Of course fit is the total
2-D array which has the same dimensions as the input data array. For this to work, the fitting_function has to be quite specific. It should still return a dict of fitted parameters
and a fit, but the values in the dict need to be themselves either numbers or 1-D numpy arrays, depending on which
arguments have been “cloned”. This means this function needs to take a kwarg cloned_arguments too, to know what to do. Thus the fitting_function has 3 positional arguments: x, y and z, corresponding to the main coord, supp coord and data,
as well as the 4th, keyword argument cloned_arguments . Note that if anything is cloned, x and y are not equivalent,
as the cloning is done along y. The simplest way to make such a function is to use compute_2d_fit() : Inside this function all the heavy lifting associated with upgrading the simple model to a model with some arguments
cloned is done for you. This enables changing which arguments are cloned without rewriting the fitting function. The actual model function should be written to work with parameters param_0 , param_1 being numbers or 1-D numpy
arrays with the same shape as y. If the model only uses simple arithmetic, numpy will generally do it automatically.
Note that y itself does not need to be used in the model and often is not - the
functional relationship between y and the data is captured through the cloned arguments. This means the actual values
of y could be anything, e.g. strings, and setting only_index_y=True is essentially saying that the value of y is not
important. If your model does explicitly depend on y and you’re not cloning any arguments, it is most likely easier to just use
the model selection fitter instead. You should now know how to write a good analysis function that works with Experiment .
Now let’s learn more about observations and plotting. previous Configuring compiler passes next Plotting the analysed data By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Is your experiment mature?
description:
We have reached the end of this guide! Congratulations. You should now have all the information needed to design
great Exa experiments, which future generations of physicists will enjoy. Before we clo...
content:
We have reached the end of this guide! Congratulations. You should now have all the information needed to design
great Exa experiments, which future generations of physicists will enjoy. Before we close off, let’s talk about maturity of your experiment class. When we are born, we require full attention of an adult, typically a parent. Then we grow up and become gradually
more independent and responsible for our choices. Our guardians begin to trust us, giving us more freedom, and
eventually we begin our own independent lives. We continue to grow, learn and make mistakes, but on our own. Maturity of an experiment class is achieved when the experiment is able to function with no involvement from its
original creator. When you first add the experiment, or any code, to the shared codebase, you might assign yourself
as an owner of that code. You continue teaching colleagues how to use it and fixing bugs. Eventually, no one
needs you to run, fix bugs and add features to the experiment and then it becomes mature. Let’s go through some obvious signs of immaturity. If your colleagues need you, your presence, your replies to their messages or your involvement to: Be able to run the code – for example, because the code is not part of a common codebase, but lives in some notebook,
which you have to send out – your experiment is still a baby. Be able to understand what the code is doing – typically, because the physics behind the experiment is complicated
and it is not clearly explained in training materials – your experiment is a teenager. Be able to fix bugs in the code – usually because the amount and quality of documentation is lacking, or the code
itself is too complicated – your experiment is not mature. Ideally, you as the original designer, are never needed at all and you don’t even know if the experiment is run.
Getting there, will however require work. Experimental physics is tricky. There is no foolproof way to automatically test an experiment, because it is a piece
of code which runs physics experiments and attempts to understand the results. Sometimes, accidentally,
an experimental run will run into physics which may not be entirely new (don’t get your hopes up for a Nobel Prize!),
but may have been unexpected in this context. Often the analysis might be improved to handle these additional cases. This might only occur after you
start measuring a new device or something fundamental changes – about the current device or the rest of the software stack.
You might not necessarily be the person making these changes, but you do hold certain implied responsibility over them,
like a parent of a kid who is misbehaving at school. When using a mature, independent, well-scoped experiment class, you should generally only ever need three lines of code: If you notice that your colleagues are sharing among them “code snippets” which are any longer than the above,
regarding the standalone use of your experiment, it has still not graduated high school. Of course, options, settings,
analyze arguments exist for a reason - they should be changed for non-standard use. Anything that is shared as
a useful snippet, where the same options, settings and analyze arguments are changed in the exact same way every single
time eventually becomes a standard and as such, should be integrated into an existing or a new
experiment class. Releasing a toddler into the world on their own is probably not the smartest idea, but you can and should let a high
schooler have their freedom. When merging/pulling your experiment into a common codebase, do not wait until it is
perfectly mature and ready. For sure, introducing bugs you know about is not good, but rarely does the experiment need
to cover all the experimental bases and be entirely self-contained to be useful. Keeping an experiment in a feature
branch until it is perfect will prevent your coworkers from gaining any real value from it, and will prevent you from
learning what the real issues are. Aim for a piece of code which: Does what it is designed to do in several useful cases. Is well documented and tested. Can be reviewed in 15-20 minutes by someone of the same level of knowledge as you. Is easy to extend/improve upon. Initially, you might need to still “parent” that code for a while. Maybe your coworkers discover that the default options
should be different, or make better plots than you - integrate them in using a follow-up MR/PR. Because of the modular nature of the Experiment class, where circuit generation,
sweeps and analysis are attached as static methods, and compiler passes can be freely modified, it is generally strongly
recommended to inherit each subclass directly from Experiment . This has very few exceptions, usually having to do
with large frameworks of several methods being added to a new base class, which takes place of the parent Experiment.
Sometimes you will need to copy a small amount of code from a different source, or define a function. This is ok.
Making a chain of 10 experiments all deriving from each other leads to much bigger problems. When writing automatic tests, aim to “break” the experiment, aim for things that are actually important for it to get right.
We can generally trust that numpy will work correctly, but if your experiment involves really tricky physics,
and that physics might be misunderstood by a coworker who didn’t study this area in detail and changed accidentally,
cover that part in well-designed automatic tests. The tests can take time to run, so adding multiple tests that just
check trivial things is typically a waste of compute. When writing documentation, it is possible to use Sphinx :cite: to include citations to scientific articles. If
your experiment is derived from such an article, consider adding a citation to the docstring. Running physics experiments, even on a fast platform like superconducting qubits, can take time. But constructions
of run definitions and analysis should not be just a little bit faster, it should be a lot faster. As chips grow,
the number of involved qubits will grow, but the execution time may remain the same or very similar. It is important
to keep the classical part also fast. You may use tools such as snakeviz , cProfile or timeit to
check how performant are different parts of the experiment. In crucial applications, accelerating the execution by
writing parts of it in a lower-level, compiled language, such as Rust or C++, could be the solution. Python is a language commonly used by physicists in academia to create useful frameworks. You might want to use some of
them in your experiments. When writing production-quality code, consider if a package you’re introducing is well and actively supported.
This can be judged for example by the activity on the project on GitHub, number of releases last year, support of latest
Python etc. Oftentimes the person driving the package development leaves the academic group and the package becomes
effectively abandoned. Depending on abandoned work will introduce issues to your codebase down the line. In such situations,
try to find an alternative solution. Depending on the license, you might be able to simply copy the code from an
abandoned open-source project to your codebase. Remember to follow the license in such cases, sometimes simply attributing
the original contributors is sufficient. Now, you should have everything you need to design and take care of an Exa experiment subclass until it reaches
its full potential. Good luck and farewell! previous Integrating your experiment into a sequence or graph next Example Notebooks By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Configuring compiler passes
description:
Under the hood, the Experiment uses the Circuit-to-Pulse-Compiler
(CPC, Compiler ) to produce the final Playlist and RunDefinition which are sent to the station for execution. You might even view
the ...
content:
Under the hood, the Experiment uses the Circuit-to-Pulse-Compiler
(CPC, Compiler ) to produce the final Playlist and RunDefinition which are sent to the station for execution. You might even view
the Experiment as a thin layer on top of the
Compiler, or a convenience class which simply lets you define the circuits and analysis, but all the “heavy lifting”
is done elsewhere. In this chapter we will learn more about how the Compiler works and how to modify it to best serve the specific
experiment we are writing. It is heavily recommended to also consult the compiler documentation ,
specifically the compilation stages . In CPC, the compilation pass is simply a function that takes some data , which could be an abstract circuit of some
kind, a list of TimeBox es, or even Schedule ,
and also some context arguments, and produces a different kind of data, potentially modifying the context. It could be visualized as a generic “process”, in the style of Bob Coecke and Aleks Kissinger, with time flowing left to
right: The pass consumes the circuit, produces the timebox and modifies the context. # In fact, we have actually seen a compilation pass already, although not a typical one! The circuit generation
function is functionally equivalent to a pass that only takes context as input: The pass produces the timebox based on the context and modifies the context. # Ok, let’s be explicit. What is this context? Context is simply a dictionary of objects and variables which can be helpful in compilation. The default context contains: The full settings tree under key “settings”. The calibrated ScheduleBuilder under the key “builder”. The ChipTopology under the key “chip_topology”. All the components given to the run and properly processed, under the key “components”. And also some other things. If a pass function has an argument matching the name of one of the default context variables
or the context itself,
during the compilation that context variable is simply given to the pass. All the other arguments become compiler settings ,
which are fetched from settings.stages.stage_name.pass_name.argument_name . You may recognize that this is how
the circuit generation arguments work, as described in the circuit generation functions chapter. This makes writing them extremely convenient, as long as you know what is in the context. Since the compiler passes are
pure functions and thus there is no way to do self references within them, the context is the designed method for adding
arbitrary stateful effects to your compiler pass functions. As such there’s no limitation to what you can write to context,
so any stateful effects should be achievable. The first argument to the pass function should always be the circuit payload - circuits, timeboxes, schedules,
etc – the actual thing being compiled. Any further arguments other than context or the aforementioned default variables
need to be typed and conform to the supported Setting data types. The passes are arranged into CompilationStage s, although this arrangement is
mostly for convenience and to arrange the passes according to abstraction layers they operate on – in the end, all the
passes are executed in order. The entire experiment execution can be visualized like so: The default compiler used in EXA. The presence of the “circuit stage” is dependent on the InputType . Also included are the execution (which is not a compiler stage,
but also a process in the Coecke-Kissinger sense) and post processing. # We have talked about ExperimentOptions , and how it is a general rule that the
options are allowed to affect the settings, but in case of conflict, the settings are the final source of truth. This
is also true for options which are designed to influence the compilation. Those are included by default, because they
are often changed. The option readout_programming_mode takes values from ReadoutProgrammingMode . This option affects settings of the passes: Heralding pass prepend_heralding() - if set to 'heralding' , adds a
readout before the circuit execution. You can use it in analysis to post-select the data, keeping only those where the
heralding readouts found the qubits in the ground state. Terminal measurement pass add_terminal_measurement() - if set to 'classic' ,
adds a terminal measurement to all qubits. If set to 'reset_at_end' , uses the bit from that measurement to
conditionally reset the qubits with X gates. Classic is the default option for experiments, and it should be kept
that way for experiments that do not explicitly need to benchmark or calibrate the readout, and are just using
one readout. This is especially true if using the parallel execution framework, which does not work very well with
measurements added explicitly. If the readout programming mode is set to 'custom' , no readout-related passes will do anything, no additional
measurements will be added on top of the one explicitly defined in the circuit. You should use this option if writing
experiments that use repeated or otherwise non-trivial readout operations. The option active_reset_cycles specifies how many active resets
are performed on each qubit before each shot. The active reset refers to a measurement followed by a conditional bit
flip using the X gate. If this option is not None , the passive wait of the “reset_wait” between two subsequent realizations of the
circuit is removed, so setting it to 0 will result in a “restless” experiment. This option affects the prepend_reset() pass. The option used_measure_operations is a mapping from the keys “terminal”, “heralding” and “reset_at_end” onto names of measure operations
used for each one. Unless you decide to use this option for something else, it only affects the measurements added by
the passes already mentioned above and no other measurements. The option subscribed_components is a list of components which
have readout, and will receive some measurement operations, whose measurement results will end up in the final dataset.
Note that if you include components that have no readout capability here, they will be ignored. Note Q: So not all data from the measured qubits is in the dataset? A: No. The final measurement is calibrated to be performed in parallel on multiple qubits. The compilation stage
adds the readout pulses to all components, not just the ones the circuit is run on. Most of the time, you are
only interested in the qubits you are doing something to, so to not clutter the dataset, only the results
from those qubits are included. You can, however, change that behaviour by including some additional qubits in
this option. By default, the option value is None , which results in subscribing the components included in the components variable, which is what you give when running the experiment. It does not affect any pre-processing stage, but the
actual execution, the setting is still in the stages settings subtree: settings.stages.additionally_subscribed_components . Finally, the options data_size_safety_switch and force_ragged_data affect the create_run_definition() pass, which is by default the last pass executed by
the Compiler , building the final RunDefinition sent to the station for execution. They affect the size and shape of the dataset. The data size safety switch should generally be never False by default in your experiment, but the users can switch
it to run a longer version of experiment. You should force ragged data if the number of readouts on qubits may change
as a result of an extra sweep (most likely of some circuit argument), but you are not doing that sweep by default, as
then writing analysis which is robust to that sweep is easier. The default input type for Experiment is TimeBox, and unless you change it,
none of the circuit passes will be added. Currently, the only other available InputType is Circuit. If you wish to write an experiment, where the circuit generation function returns an
abstract circuit, you should change the input_type attribute on your
class. The input type affects the default passes added to the compiler when initializing your experiment class. With
circuit input type, the compiler will also receive some default circuit level passes. Those passes assume the input is
an iterable of Circuit , which contain CircuitOperation s
and some metadata. Unless that is what you want your circuit generation function to output, you will need to create your
own passes that convert the abstract circuit you create into either an iterable of Circuit or an iterable of TimeBox (where you would delete the default circuit passes). This behaviour is to ensure that when the circuit generation function is added as the first pass , and it will always
be first because it does not take any data input, the output produced by it will actually match the input of the first
default pass. The default stages and passes are detailed in the CPC documentation . The
Experiment does one additional pass on the pulse level, the aforementioned add_terminal_measurement() pass, which is not in the default compiler used for circuit execution. At the moment, the post-processing passes work a bit differently in Experiment ,
compared to the standalone use of the Compiler . When running experiments, the
raw data is saved in the database as a binary, and only then sent to the user. It is also possible to extract the data
from the database long after the experiment has been run, using the experiment run_id and the class method get_by_run_id() . In that situation, the originally used context is lost. The first pass, iqm.cpc.compiler.post_process.construct_run_result() produces a iqm.cpc.core.run_result.RunResult object,
which contains not just data, but also all the settings used when preparing the run, and many additional run properties,
which you can also affect by adding passes to the job_stage which stash relevant objects into the RunDefinition ,
to be accessible later. The original context used to compile the run definition is lost, and the post-processing
passes start with an empty context dictionary. They may freely add objects to the context and then later reference
them. You should not modify the first post-processing stage, which just makes the iqm.cpc.core.run_result.RunResult .
The second post-processing stage converts all the raw data into convenient derived variables. Which variables are
calculated depends on the readout_mode option. We will discuss it
more in the analysis chapter, as this information is needed there to understand what variables are
available for you to use. The second post-processing stage could in principle be completely replaced for your experiment, however doing it is
definitely quite advanced and only recommended if necessary. Remember that the passes attach to the experiment object,
but recovering the data from the DB via get_experiment() creates a new object ,
so the modified post-processing passes need to be defaults set in the experiment class. In contrast, the pre-processing
passes could be simply modified by the user when running and prototyping the experiment. Addition of new passes is also detailed in the CPC documentation , but let’s take
a second on how to do it when writing an Experiment subclass. The Compiler is attached as an attribute compiler ,
and created at initialization. The Experiment also has attributes circuit_stages , pulse_stages , and final_stages ,
which are deepcopied into the Compiler at initialization. You can override those attributes, so that during the
initialization your custom passes are automatically added to the compiler. Alternatively, you can also modify the passes and stages inside the compiler after the initialization. Simply
override the setup_additional_init_properties() : The Compiler abstraction allows you to write experiments which take your favourite
quantum language and compile it into IQM data formats. As mentioned above, all you need to do is define additional
circuit-level passes, which will finally result in either a list of Circuit s or
directly a list of TimeBox es. Note Q: Why would I want to use TimeBoxes? A: The IQM Circuit class is simply a flat list of circuit operations,
assuming the circuit abstraction, i.e. only the order of the gates matters. If your abstract language has a concept
of otherwise commuting operations happening simultaneously or non-simultaneously, this concept will be entirely
dropped when converting to Circuit . Such languages are for example
Cirq or Stim. To maintain this abstraction, you need to not only compile to Circuit differently, but skip the
class altogether. To illustrate, consider this abstract draft of a pass converting Cirq Circuit to TimeBox while maintaining the Moment
structure: Because the function (not shown here) _map_moment_to_timebox returns TimeBox , the
later resolution and scheduling passes will respect that each of those boxes is a hard-boundary time-space region,
and the gates included in that moment are indeed happening simultaneously, while gates included in different moments are
forbidden to overlap in time. Then, we would define a compilation stage: And include this stage in our experiment: Of course, this one pass is not enough. In earlier passes, you could for example transpile the circuit to IQM
native gates (which you can reference via the builder), or make other logical passes. They will work as long as they
conform to the general structure of a pass function. In this chapter, we learnt how to affect the default compilation behaviour, control what kind of experiment we are
performing (circuit or pulse-level) and even add our own arbitrary passes. Adding passes at the beginning of
the compilation is equivalent to just making the circuit generation function do more heavy lifting, but it is preferred
if you are designing a whole suite of experiments and want to reuse code. previous Sweep generation next Automated data analysis By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Creating your own EXA experiments
description:
EXA is a software created by experimentalists for experimentalists — but you can also use it effectively if you’re
a theorist! In this guide we will learn how to create your own automated experiment, ...
content:
EXA is a software created by experimentalists for experimentalists — but you can also use it effectively if you’re
a theorist! In this guide we will learn how to create your own automated experiment, beginning at conceptualization
and ending with a fully integrated procedure. Familiarity with using EXA to run experiments will be useful, but
it is only assumed that you know how operating and calibrating superconducting quantum computers works, and ideally
have some experimental experience, not necessarily with this software. Note This guide is written in a conversational, casual style, as this is what works best in communication.
EXA is a flexible and casual but powerful tool, and this guide should reflect that! I will include questions and answers from the reader to the author in the following way: Q: This sounds a lot like pulse level access (Pulla) in IQM Client.
Why are there two similar frameworks and which one should I use? A: You can think of EXA as being built on top of the circuit-to-pulse compiler,
to which IQM Client is just another access point – you need to
define everything yourself every time you want to run some quantum circuits. An EXA Experiment is a way
to combine multiple notebook cells into a single object, which later can just be run, and produce all the
required output. We will begin with conceptualizing the experiment, or answering the question What does my
experiment do? You should always start any development by asking yourself this question – it helps ground the work
you’re doing. An experiment on two connected qubits, executable in parallel, using the full power of pulse level access
may need to be written differently than an experiment acting on the whole QPU and defined in terms of abstract quantum
circuits. Next, we will explore prototyping the experiment. The Experiment class is
designed to make prototyping easy and fun using a Jupyter notebook or your favourite Python IDE. The code you produce
while prototyping can be easily reused when creating a mature experiment. You should always prototype with a real
system if possible - this is quantum physics we are talking about, and you may discover something unexpected! After you’re happy with your prototype, it’s time to write an Experiment subclass . Here we will
put the code together into something that does not require setup - just initialize, run and analyze! This section is
self-contained, and you may decide to stop reading the guide there – but all the building blocks are described later
in more detail. The first topic to discuss in depth is the circuit generation functions , which are the
main engine of the experiment, producing pulse schedules or abstract circuits which together define it.
We will talk about different kinds of “circuits” that can be generated, from the most abstract to the bare pulse
schedules, discuss tips and tricks and even dive into iqm.pulse . Next, we will discuss adding default sweeps to the experiment, and how to make them work
in different scenarios, especially with experiments meant to run in parallel. We will look into different types of
sweeps and how to think about them - those modifying or selecting a circuit, those affecting the gates in the circuit
and those affecting global calibration settings. We will briefly talk about compiler passes next. EXA is built on top of the circuit-to-pulse compiler
(CPC), with fully adjustable compilation passes from abstract circuit definitions all the way to the low level
description of the quantum job. We will learn how to adjust, add and remove the passes as necessary for the experiment
you’re writing. After the experiment is run, it is time to analyze the collected data. We will learn about
proper post-processing, data handling and using xarray effectively – especially when it comes to supporting extra
sweeps and maintaining the flexibility of the Experiment framework. Even though the plots and observations are generated in the
analysis, they deserve their own sections describing how to use them and discussing best practices. Both plots and
observations are communication tools – plots are used to communicate with humans, other experimentalists looking at
your data, and observations are used to communicate between parts of the series of experiments. After the experiment subclass is ready, it is time to integrate it in a larger context.
In this section, we discuss what features the experiment needs to be properly integrable, and explore
sequences Sequence , leaving the documentation of the Graph-Based Calibration to the
appropriate place. Finally, we will create a checklist of how mature the experiment is, and provide rules
of thumb to decide if making the experiment more mature is worth it. Welcome to EXA and remember to have fun! Contents previous EXA Configuration File next Conceptualization: What is my experiment? By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Circuit generation functions
description:
This is the first detailed section of the guide. By now, you should already know how to write a simple experiment. In
this section, we will explore the generation of circuits in more detail. This sect...
content:
This is the first detailed section of the guide. By now, you should already know how to write a simple experiment. In
this section, we will explore the generation of circuits in more detail. This section will have a lot of overlap with
the iqm.pulse documentation , so it is recommended to check it too for full understanding. The circuit is a heart of the experiment. It defines what is executed on the device. The circuit will look differently
depending on the abstraction level of the experiment. As mentioned in the conceptualization part of
the guide, we have broadly three abstraction levels: pulse, circuit and semi-abstract, mixing the two. The circuit generation function always needs to take arguments components (or group for parallel experiments)
and builder and output a TimeBox , so what defines the abstraction level are the tools you can
use to create it. Roughly speaking: In pulse-level circuit generation, you’d work directly with Schedule , defining the final
time-resolved experiment schedule, and then wrap it into an atomic TimeBox. This is not really recommended outside
of very specific cases that require it, but I will describe how to do it. In most cases however, it is recommended
to create a custom QuantumOp and GateImplementation and work on a semi-abstract level, if possible. In semi-abstract circuit generation, which is the default one, you’d create TimeBoxes directly by asking the ScheduleBuilder for gate implementations. You may want to create your own gates, or use custom
calibration, which replaces some of the calibrated parameters of the gate, but you’d let the compilation resolve
the scheduling and timing, and handle which parts of which gate are executed on which physical instrument. In circuit-level generation, you’d create an abstract quantum circuit, and then only at the very end ask the
ScheduleBuilder to convert it into a TimeBox while mapping logical qubits to physical qubits that come from the components variable. For very complicated experiments it is often necessary to convert or transpile the abstract
quantum circuits before they can be run, and that is not possible to be done with TimeBoxes that already implement
those operations. As each of these ultimately yield a TimeBox, they can also be combined, immediately in the circuit generation. I will
start from the default, semi-abstract approach, and cover tips and tricks to building good circuit generation
functions. I will talk about the other two levels at the end. In IQM Pulse there are several gates defined. You can always check which gates are currently available to you by viewing
the QuantumOpTable attached to ScheduleBuilder as ScheduleBuilder.op_table . The most standard single qubit gate is called prx , standing for phased x rotation. QASM calls this gate r .
Calling get_implementation() returns a special object known as a gate factory. This object
is populated with the calibration for the gate and implementation selected, and calling it produces TimeBoxes
implementing different variants of the gate. Some gates, like prx , have arguments. This gate has two arguments,
rotation angle and phase. Phase 0 corresponds to an X rotation, phase \(\pi/2\) to Y rotation. We can generate some
TimeBoxes like so: Each of the default gates, such as prx also generates a builder shortcut method, which you can use if you prefer it.
They are generated when the ScheduleBuilder instance is initialized, so any gates you add
afterwards will not have one. There is also a u gate, which corresponds to a single qubit unitary. This gate is by default implemented using
a single prx gate and virtual Z rotations that happen at the beginning and end of the gate, without increasing the
execution time. It may be useful specifically for complicated circuits using Hadamard gates, which cannot be
exactly described with a single prx . The syntax for the u gate arguments is (theta, phi, lambda) , where: Here are some examples: Sometimes, you would like to use a specific implementation of a given gate. This does move your experiment
in the direction of full pulse abstraction level – for example, requiring specifically a flattop flux pulse suggests
you are more interested in the physics of the fluxline and using the qubit only as a probe. Fixing an implementation
in the circuit generation function is also a useful tool when prototyping. A good example here is the rz gate, or a Z rotation by a certain angle. By default, it is implemented with a zero
duration virtual Z, which only adjusts the microwave phase for the next prx . However, this is not really a quantum
gate and it does not interact with operations that involve the physical couplings between the qubits and are implemented
with flux pulses. You can specify you’d like to use the physical rz implementation, which uses 3 prx gates,
in the following way: There are other possible rz implementations, for example with AC Stark or flux pulses, they are not calibrated
by default. Hint If your experiment requires a specific implementation to work, put it in the circuit generation function. It makes
the experiment less flexible, and narrows its focus, but sometimes it is exactly what you want. Each of the outputs of a factory is a TimeBox . In most cases, they will be atomic boxes,
or boxes that do not contain other TimeBoxes, and instead define a full time-resolved Schedule .
This schedule might include instructions on one or multiple channels. It also has a well defined duration, and blocks
all the involved channels for the duration (see the definitions of all the concepts in iqm.pulse documentation ). Another type of TimeBox is a composite one. This box contains other TimeBoxes, and is not scheduled, which means it is
not yet decided when exactly would the specific pulses and other instructions be executed. If two atomic boxes are
included in a composite box in a certain order, and they contain the same channels, only then we can say that the later
one will be scheduled later. Composite TimeBoxes have an attribute scheduling_strategy , which can be
either ASAP (as soon as possible) or ALAP (as late as possible). Together with barriers and
nesting TimeBoxes, this is enough to specify the order and timing of instructions at the level of the entire schedule. Speaking of nesting, composite TimeBoxes are infinitely nestable, which means that you can make a composite box out of
multiple composite boxes. Hint Read carefully the iqm.pulse documentation regarding working with TimeBoxes,
they are powerful tools offering both flexibility and precision! After going through the iqm-pulse documentation regarding TimeBoxes, let’s have a look at a slightly non-trivial example
of how to use different ways of combining the boxes and scheduling them to our advantage. We’re going to extend our
Bell experiment to 3 qubits, and create a Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) state: and then apply some Z rotations and unprepare it. We will need to use 2 CZ gates on each side, and some Hadamards to
convert them into CX gates. We want the Hadamards on both sides to “hug” the CZ gates, because that maximizes the time
their qubits are expected to be in the ground state. How to do this? We split the circuit into three natural parts: preparation, application of the phase and uncomputation. The first part
is scheduled ALAP, the last part is scheduled ASAP. Here’s how to do it: We initialize a new experiment with this circuit and inspect the scheduled segment using three qubits. Note the first and the last pulse on the QB2__drive channel. If we scheduled the entire circuit ASAP,
the first pulse would happen immediately at the beginning. If we scheduled it ALAP, the last pulse would
be executed immediately before the readout. # Another way to affect the scheduling is by using Barriers. They were not actually necessary here, and the splitting and
different scheduling would be needed anyway. Note Q: Isn’t the pipe operator essentially a Barrier? A: It acts effectively like a Barrier, but there is no actual Barrier box added anywhere. Unlike | , the Barrier
can specify the components it affects, and it does not allow one to schedule the two sides of it independently. It can
however be passed down from more abstract circuit definitions, where it exists as a concept, and ASAP/ALAP scheduling
does not. The pipe operator | has a large functional overlap with the Barrier, but it is not the same thing. The scheduling algorithm can be trusted to schedule your entire circuit correctly. However, sometimes you really need
to know the duration of a specific part of your schedule before the circuit is fully completed. The TimeBoxes do not
have durations, because the duration depends on the scheduling. Not all hope is lost, though, because we may preschedule a part of the circuit to learn about its duration. In the example above, we are calculating what is the extra time during which the qubits 1 and 2 are idling while the
qubit 0 is being measured. The measure operation can only be repeated with certain frequency, so calculating this extra
time is quite complicated manually, as it depends on whether the minimum waiting time or the circuit duration is longer.
The circuit duration is not simply the sum of durations of individual gates – that would be wasteful. For more information about the pulse timing, check the iqm.pulse documentation . As mentioned before, the default readout programming mode in Exa adds a measurement operation to all qubits at the end
of the circuit. You can, however, also add measurements to the circuit explicitly in the generation function. The programming mode is controlled by experiment options. More specifically, the option options.readout_programming_mode accepts the values of the Enum ReadoutProgrammingMode .
Generally if adding measurements explicitly, you should set that to custom in your experiment. Note Q: Why not always add measurements explicitly? It seems to be cleaner that way. A: If you call the builder for an implementation of a measure operation for multiple
qubits, it will most of the time create a “multiplexed” pulse, where multiple qubits are measured together by sending
a single, complicated pulse down the probeline connected to all of them via individual readout structures. This logic
is implemented on the schedule level, and measuring qubits 1 and 2 together is generally different than measuring
qubit 1, and then afterwards qubit 2. If using parallel framework, the scheduling will separate all the measurements
for different groups of components, such as qubit pairs. This will slow the experiment down unnecessarily. The general rule of thumb is to use the explicit measurement if you’re investigating the measurement operation itself,
usually either calibrating or benchmarking it, or you need to add a mid-circuit measurement into a more complicated
benchmark. This might however necessitate writing the circuit generation function
without using the parallel framework. Ok, but if you know you need to add more measurements, how do you do it? If multiple measurements of the same component exist in the circuit, additional dimension will be created in the Dataset , named {qubit}__{key}_readout_slot . If each sweep spot has a different number of readouts
per label ( {qubit}__{key} ), the results are ragged into a pandas.MultiIndex named {qubit}__{key}_ragged_data_index . This index might be difficult to work with and generally requires special treatment in analysis. It is however the best
way to interpret the measurement results using xarray without creating arrays full of NaNs or giving up
functionality. You might trigger this behaviour on purpose by setting the option force_ragged_data to True . You should consider it strongly
if you expect users to add extra sweeps to the experiment – it will make it easier to write analysis. We will revisit
this topic in the compilation chapter. When creating a circuit generation function where the number of measurements is an argument, for example: Be aware that even though you might not be adding a default sweep over n_measures , it is perfectly possible for a user
to add an extra sweep over this circuit parameter, which will then create a ragged DataArray for
the user. It is up to you whether that is something that would be supported in analysis. I will come back to these issues when discussing sweeps and analysis . Exa is an experimentalist’s tool. Using it means you would like at least a little bit of control over the pulse level.
However, sometimes it is useful to start from a large, abstract circuit and modify it a little bit. In IQM QCCSW there
are compiling tools for languages such as Qrisp, Qiskit and Cirq, which when applied would yield circuits in the “IQM
format”. What is that format? At the bottom, it is a sequence of objects of type CircuitOperation . These operations may or may not be mapped to physical qubits, but they do contain names of placeholder / logical qubits, in
their locus attribute. These are tuples of one or more computational elements (qubits or
resonators). Different names should be mapped to different physical elements. In circuit generation function, you are given the list of physical components to act on, so if you want to use this
abstract circuit, you need to map the loci of all operations onto your physical components and create corresponding
TimeBoxes. This can be done using the circuit_to_timebox() method: If the above is all you’d like to do, it is recommended to use the compiler directly. Remember however
that TimeBoxes can be combined arbitrarily, so it is possible to add further pulse-level modifications to the resulting
TimeBox by converting it yourself. If you would like, it is also possible to create such an abstract circuit from scratch in the generation function. To
do that, use the CircuitOperationList , which extends the inbuilt list with
additional functionality. The syntax here is similar to one used in the major quantum programming languages. Note Q: This seems pretty pointless, you’re not achieving anything beyond using the ScheduleBuilder, are you? A: Usage of this class in experiments is mostly convenience and preference. Using the Builder directly, you need to supply
the components / locus first, and then the arguments. Here, you supply the arguments first and then the locus only at
the end. It is genuinely useful when the circuits are long and difficult to compute, but we want to
execute them on many qubits or qubit groups in parallel. We don’t want to recalculate the circuits multiple times,
so we cache the function that prepares the CircuitOperationList , making the
overall process slightly shorter. They are used in this exact way in the implementation of randomized benchmarking, as each unitary operation has
a defined unitary matrix, which are then combined to calculate
the overall circuit unitary via get_unitary() . Let’s now move on to more pulse-level topics. In the iqm.pulse documentation there is an example on how to modify the calibration stored in the builder: You should not do this in a circuit generation function. The builder object is attached to the experiment instance
and is not recreated between sweep spots, the swept values are just updated. Updating the calibration in this way in
the context of Experiment may cause some “leakage”. Instead, you may use an argument to get_implementation() called priority_calibration . This updates the calibration only for the wanted GateImplementation and locus. What is more, you can use both the default calibration and the priority one in one circuit, which is useful
for some experiments. For example, we want to write a single qubit error amplification experiment to fine tune the amplitude of the \(\pi\) rotation gate. The circuit we would like to have starts from preparing an equal superposition state with a \(\pi/2\) rotation, followed by repeated \(\pi\) rotations. In order to calibrate the amplitude, we need to sweep it, but we
trust that our initial guess for the amplitude was quite close, so we do not want to modify the amplitude of the first
pulse. Thus, we may introduce the parameter scale which enters the circuit via priority calibration. The priority_calibration is a dictionary which updates the existing calibration. It does not need to have all the
keys and values, but it does need to have the same nesting structure. Another good use case for the priority calibration is to achieve a finer control over timing. The timing resolution of wait() operations is limited by the granularity of the channel, typically
to around 4ns. If for any reason you need to introduce a timing control finer than that, it is possible using priority
calibrations of the center_offset parameter most of the implemented Waveform classes have. Typically we would follow these steps: Obtain the granularity of the channel from the builder. Split the required wait into a multiple of the granularity and the remainder. Add a coarse wait. Add one granularity to the gate duration via priority calibration. Move the gate waveform by the fine wait using the center_offset priority calibration. The circuit by itself does not do anything useful, but you may include it as a building block in a more complicated
experiment. Note Q: I would assume this fine control over timing would be implemented by some kind of automatic pass, which I would not need to care about. Why isn’t it? A: This is not that easy to do, and this functionality is rarely needed. The fine control is implemented where it is
needed the most. For example, trigger timing granularity is only 1 sample, achieved with similar tricks. Nevertheless,
it is good to know this trick, because fine timing can unlock marvelous physics by allowing us to look into high
frequency effects. Sometimes, you would need to make a specific gate just for the experiment you’re writing. Maybe it is a prototype, or
some very specific physics experiment that needs this gate. Hint If developing a new gate, it is generally recommended to add it to the set of gates that are registered
automatically everywhere. The general guidance on making custom gates can be found in the iqm.pulse documentation .
Following that, I will show how to add the gates to your experiment. The ScheduleBuilder is only created by the
experiment class just before the run. Therefore, the gate needs to be registered with the experiment itself, not just the
builder. This can be done through the method setup_additional_init_properties() : It is also worth to set some defaults. Typically you would anyway override them somehow in update_settings() , but having a default allows one to run the experiment before
all work is done. This gate can then be used by calling: The entire TimeBox paradigm has been invented so that no one has to schedule things manually anymore. However, sometimes
it is still necessary. Typically in those situations it is recommended to make a new gate implementation instead.
This guide would nevertheless be incomplete if I didn’t explain how to play with schedules directly. Even though TimeBox is a single class, it has two variants: composite and atomic. The
composite TimeBox would have an attribute children populated with other TimeBoxes, and the atomic TimeBox has its
attribute atom populated with a Schedule instance. This TimeBox is essentially
a wrapper around the Schedule, so that it can be combined with other TimeBoxes seamlessly. We can access the atom in the circuit generation function and make some changes to it. Each Schedule is a dictionary,
where keys are specific channels, and values are iterables of instructions ( Instruction ).
Generally any Schedule which results from some kind of compilation or scheduling algorithm will have the same duration
on all the channels, but ones made by hand do not need to. In such a case, they are typically padded to “hard box”
( pad_to_hard_box() ), or Wait instructions are appended to the ends of all
the channels to make their durations all equal. One case in which one might want to modify the Schedule by hand is to bypass restrictions put in place by gate implementations.
For example, the prx implementations typically only use the drive channel for one qubit. However, they block all
the channels associated with that qubit. This is to prevent executing flux pulses during the microwave pulses. You may be interested in writing a very specific physics experiment where the flux pulse must occur during the
microwave pulse, though. What then? Well, you can just force it to behave this way! Have a look at the example below: Other genuine uses of this functionality might include directly assessing probe pulses, their timing, integration and
multiplexing. Now you should have all the information necessary to write good and useful circuit generation functions! Remember,
keep it simple! Try not to use advanced tricks if simple do job. previous Making an Experiment subclass next Sweep generation By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Making an Experiment subclass
description:
After making a successful prototype that allows you to run the experiment you want to create, it is
time to actually create it! We will inherit from Experiment ,
but most of the time there is no need ...
content:
After making a successful prototype that allows you to run the experiment you want to create, it is
time to actually create it! We will inherit from Experiment ,
but most of the time there is no need to override many or any methods, just the ones we will need. The code in exa
is written to follow the principle of composition, not inheritance, as often as possible. This is why circuit, sweep and
analyze functions are functions, and are just attached to the experiment as static methods. We already have those from
the prototyping stage! We will use the Bell coherence example here as well, but build it up to something more interesting. For now, let’s just
define a new class: The Experiment.name and Experiment.default_label attributes should be added as
soon as possible, especially the first one. This is because the function get_experiment() ,
which is used to retrieve experimental data from previous runs from the database, uses the name attribute
to decide which class to initialize. The latter attribute will be displayed in all the reports, so it should be more descriptive. We also specify the Experiment.parallel_group and attach the parallel versions of the functions written before as static
methods. This experiment can now be initialized, run and analyzed to produce results identical to our notebook
prototype… If we attach the sweeps manually. The default sweeps are clearly missing, so let’s add them next! Note What do you think will happen if we do not add any default sweeps? The Experiment subclasses use
the ExperimentOptions , which are a
pydantic model, to specify the behaviour of the experiment object. The options become an attribute Experiment.options and can be modified after initializing. When creating a subclass, we need to
specify the default values of the options, if different from the base class, and we can also add our own, new options,
if they are needed. Options are used for many things at the moment, but can be thought of as variables that affect many
settings needed to work in tandem, and too complicated to modify separately. Options are also commonly used to control
the behaviour of sweeps, especially in parallel experiments used for calibration. There, each used gate needs a sweep,
but all sweeps happening in parallel need the same number of points. To add new options we create a subclass of ExperimentOptions : To modify the values of the default options we modify them at init: Here, we added a new option which will control the behaviour of our default sweep, as well as modified the existing
default values for repetitions and readout_mode . Now each point will be averaged 128 times, and the readout
instrument will decide if the measured voltage corresponds to 0 or 1, and only then they will be averaged all together
during postprocessing. Let’s write the sweep generation function now: The first argument to a sweep generation function must be group or components , depending on whether one wishes
to use the parallel framework or not. Here, it does not actually matter since the sweep does not affect any
locus-specific settings, but we will use group for consistency. The second and third arguments must be chip_topology and settings . The setting tree is a source of the swept parameters, and chip topology is used for
example for finding the relevant coupler connecting a qubit pair. The remaining arguments should be a subset of the
options, with the same name and type, because they will be automatically populated from options where the function is
called. We can now attach it to the experiment: This class now captures our prototype exactly. We can modify the number of points in the phase sweep very easily: We see: We see that we were able to easily modify the number of points in the sweep using options. Note that the label we
set is also displayed instead of “Multi Qubit Experiment”. # We will discuss sweeps and how to generate them more in the appropriate section. Now, let’s explore what
other class methods and attributes can be useful to override. The circuit argument defaults may be provided using the method: Experiment.get_default_circuit_settings() .
The most common use of this method is to set the circuit defaults based on experiment options, which allows specifying
how the circuit is to behave per experiment instance. If your circuit defaults are static, you can just provide them in
the signature of your circuit generation function, and there is no need to override this method. Our circuit only has one argument, phase (the first two don’t count), so let us provide some default for that. We added a label to the phase parameter, which will now display automatically as a plot label if we plot against
this quantity. Other than that, this experiment is a bit too simple for this to be particularly useful, so I will revisit
the circuit settings later. In the Experiment framework, a setting tree may be generated by calling exp.get_settings() . The setting tree is mutable,
and may be modified and passed back to the experiment run through the settings key argument. You should never
override the Experiment.get_settings() method, but you are allowed and encouraged to override Experiment.update_settings() which is called inside of it. We may decide some
experiment needs the settings modified in some way systematically, and we would like that to be automatic. Common
reasons include: A more complicated calculation is needed to obtain correct circuit settings. The experiment needs additional post-processing information, for example for multi-state readout. Certain gate implementations should do something different than in general (for example, not use Virtual Z rotations). All of these can be added in the Experiment.update_settings() . This method is called at the end of
the creation of the setting tree and receives the setting tree already updated with the full calibration and all the
other information needed. previous Prototyping your experiment next Circuit generation functions By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

content:
Generates a fitter function for exponentially decaying sinusoidal oscillation. The fitter will do a least-squares fit to the model \(y(x) = A \exp(-x / T) \cos(2\pi f x + \phi) + B\) ,
where \(A>0\) is amplitude, \(f>0\) is frequency, \(T>0\) is exponential decay constant,
and \(B\) si offset.
The ESPRIT method will be used to get initial guesses for the least-squares fit, see esprit() .
The arguments can be used to override the guesses from ESPRIT method. amp_guess ( float | None ) – Initial guess for \(A\) . t2_guess ( float | None ) – Initial guess for \(T\) . Typical use case is the T2 Ramsey time. freq_guess ( float | None ) – Initial guess for \(f\) . phase_guess ( float | None ) – Initial guess for \(phi\) . offset_guess ( float | None ) – Initial guess for \(B\) , defaults to mean of the data. title: exa.core.experiment.utils.analysis_utils.analyze_singles
description:
A helper tool to analyze data of independent qubits. This function repeats the function analyzer on all single qubits in the experiment defined by run_result .
The purpose of the analyzer is to modify...
content:
A helper tool to analyze data of independent qubits. This function repeats the function analyzer on all single qubits in the experiment defined by run_result .
The purpose of the analyzer is to modify the AnalyzeResult instance that is passed to it. This assumes that the run_result.definition.additional_run_properties has the keys "qubits" and "readout_components" , and the analysis is applied to qubits that appear in both lists. analyzer will be called with arguments that match the signature in the following way: The first argument result is a template AnalyzeResult which should be modified by analyzer .
Most notably, it contains the full dataset of the run, where more data arrays can be added. It also contains the run_result so that the analysis function can access all the metadata. The second argument is always qubit (str) which specifies the qubit. target_name (str) is the key to the “target data” for that qubit, as defined by Experiment.
This is to access the target array as result.run_result.dataset[target_name] .
It is passed to analyzer only if target_name" is in the signature.
Assumes that “target_data_parameters” come in the same order as flattened “subscribed components”.
If “target_data_parameters” is not defined, uses “default_data_parameters” instead. Other arguments can be passed with analysis_kwargs . run_result ( RunResult ) – The run result containing the full dataset and run data. analyzer ( Callable [ [ ... ] , None ] ) – Function that analyzes a single qubit. qubits ( Sequence [ str ] | None ) – Optionally run analysis only for these qubits. By default, runs on all qubits. analysis_kwargs – Additional arguments for analyzer . A new instance of AnalyzeResult, where repeated calls to analyzer have added content. content:
Generates a fitter function for sinusoidal oscillation. The fitter will do a least-squares fit to the model \(y(x) = A * \sin(1 / p * 2\pi * x + \phi) + B\) ,
where \(A>0\) is amplitude, \(p>0\) is period, \(B\) is offset, \(\phi\) is phase.
The phase can be fixed or a free parameter.
The ESPRIT method will be used to get initial guesses for the least-squares fit, see esprit() .
The arguments can be used to override the guesses from ESPRIT method. period_estimate ( float | None ) – Initial guess for \(p\) . By default given by esprit() . amplitude_estimate ( float | None ) – Initial guess for \(A\) . By default given by esprit() . offset_estimate ( float | None ) – Initial guess for \(B\) , defaults to mean of the data. phase_value ( float | None ) – Fixed value for \(\phi\) . If None, the phase will be a free parameter in the model. Function for fitting data to an oscillation model. description: Utility for loading observations resolved by the given rules and mapping them to their dut field paths. Unlike get_loaded_stash_with() , this does not scan every dut field ever recorded for the DUT. I...
content:
Utility for loading observations resolved by the given rules and mapping them to their dut field paths. Unlike get_loaded_stash_with() , this does not scan every dut field ever recorded for the DUT. It only
touches the dut fields that load_rules themselves surface from the DB (see load_observations_by_rules() ), so it needs no prior knowledge of which dut fields exist. NOTE: This may slightly alter how the settings tree is built. In particular, its possible that certain
branches are not initially created, if they do no exist in the observations the stash was initialized with.
Such observations can however still be added to the stash. load_rules ( list [ RuleType ] ) – The load rules for loading the observations. dut_label ( str | None ) – The dut label to use. If not provided, will use the dut label from the ExaRuntime experiment
configuration. default_storage ( StorageInterface | None ) – The default storage to use when no storage is pinned by the loading rule. If not provided,
will use the ExaRuntime storage. compare_db_and_local_time ( bool | None ) – Allow comparing local and database timestamps when fetching latest observations.
If disabled, local observations will always have priority to database observations, and a warning will be
shown in case a database observation may be more recent. Setting the flag explicitly to ´False´ Suppresses
the warning. Disabled by default. content:
Akaike information criterion for small sample size. From wikipedia ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akaike_information_criterion ):
The formula for AICc depends upon the statistical model.
Assuming that the model is univariate, is linear in its parameters,
and has normally-distributed residuals (conditional upon regressors),
then the formula for AICc is \(AICc = AIC + \frac{2k^{2}+2k}{n-k-1}\) aic ( float ) – Akaike information n ( int ) – sample size k ( int ) – number of free parameters extra_parameter_penalty_factor ( float ) – extra factor penalizing additional parameters AIC corrected for small sample sizes if condition n-k-1 is met, else returns np.nan . float previous exa.core.model_selection_fitter.utils.auto_rotate next exa.core.model_selection_fitter.utils.calculate_model_probability By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. title: exa.core.observation_set_utils.copy_station_specific_observations
description: Make copies of existing station-specific observations in an existing observation set, linking them to a new QPU. Currently all observations and most observation sets are linked to a specific QPU via t...
content:
Make copies of existing station-specific observations in an existing observation set, linking them to a new QPU. Currently all observations and most observation sets are linked to a specific QPU via the dut_label attribute.
However, some observations are more correctly associated with other parts of the station,
e.g. the instrumentation and wiring. Their values do not change (much) when the QPU is changed.
These include e.g. instrument trigger delays, pulse precompensation settings, and TWPA settings. This function takes an existing observation set, and makes copies of all station-specific observations
in it in the DB, linking them with a new dut_label . It then groups them in a new observation set,
which can e.g. be used as the starting point of a new calibration run for the station after the QPU
has been changed. Note The station-specific observations are determined using a fixed whitelist which must be updated
when new observations are introduced. set_id ( UUID ) – ID of an existing observation set. dut_label ( str ) – DUT label of the new QPU. set_type ( ObservationSetType | None ) – Observation set type for the new set. If None, use the type of the existing set. dry_run ( bool ) – Iff True, only log the observations that would be copied, do not make actual copies. ID of the new observation set, containing of copies of all the station-specific observations
in the existing observation set but linked to dut_label , or None on a dry run. title: exa.core.util.fft_helper.get_frequency_estimate_via_fft
description: Function to estimate the frequency of an oscillation via FFT. The following assumptions of the data must hold: Data has already been rotated to the real part (therefore, complex part is neglected). Th...
content:
Function to estimate the frequency of an oscillation via FFT. The following assumptions of the data must hold: Data has already been rotated to the real part (therefore, complex part is neglected). The following steps are taken to extract the dominant oscillation frequency of the raw data: First, we subtract the DC component (mean of the raw data along the delay axis). The data along the delay axis is padded with zeros at the end. This has the effect of smoothening the FFT
frequency spectrum. Find the integer corresponding to the highest peak in the frequency spectrum. With this index, we find the frequency corresponding to the dominant oscillation frequency. raw_data ( DataArray ) – Data containing the dimensions corresponding to the delay sweep and some additional sweep, usually
detuning sweep. delay_array_name ( str ) – The name of the array corresponding to the delay sweep. zero_padding ( int ) – Amount of zeros to be added along the delay sweep dimension to smoothen the FFT spectrum. Data array containing the dominant oscillation frequency for each extra sweep point. ndarray previous fft_helper next formatting By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. (The full one which includes the component name). Duplicates are removed. db_observations ( Mapping [ str , Sequence [ ObservationData ] ] ) – Dictionary mapping lists of db observations to their dut field path
(The full one which includes the component name). Duplicates are removed. The DB observations will be
returned by get_latest_observation() in case there is no local observation for that dut_field found. compare_db_and_local_time ( bool | None ) – Allow comparing local and database timestamps when fetching latest observations.
If disabled, local observations will always have priority to database observations, and a warning will be
shown in case a database observation may be more recent. Setting the flag explicitly to ´False´ Suppresses
the warning. Disabled by default. Methods copy Copies the observation stash. from_observation_set Create an observation stash containing latest observations from the DB filtered using set_id . from_tags Create an observation stash containing latest observations from the DB filtered using tags . get_db_observations Get the DB observations stored in the stash. get_latest_observation Gives the latest observation for the specified name (i.e. DUT field path). get_latest_observations Get the latest local or DB observations stored in the stash. get_local_observations Get the local observations stored in the stash. merge_to Merge the local observations from self to another stash. modify_tags Tag observations in the stash. save Saves the local observations to the DB. set_observation_value Change the value of an observation in the stash by adding a new LocalObservation. stash Adds local observations to the stash. Create an observation stash containing latest observations from the DB filtered using tags . Only contains observations for the dut_id of the station. tags ( Iterable [ Iterable [ str ] ] ) – Observation tags to choose which observations to load. Outer iterable is a short-circuit OR, inner is
AND. Example: [['awesome', 'monday'], ['base']] means “For every observation (dut_field) we need,
first try to load the latest such observation that is tagged with both 'awesome' AND 'monday' .
If one with these tags cannot be found, try finding one tagged with 'base' ” instead. If tags is
empty, no observations will be loaded. observation stash containing the requested observations ObservationStash Create an observation stash containing latest observations from the DB filtered using set_id . Only contains observations for the dut_id of the station. set_id ( UUID ) – The observation set ID for which to load observations. observation stash containing the requested observations ObservationStash Copies the observation stash. ObservationStash Adds local observations to the stash. Only observations not yet found in self are added. observations ( LocalObservation | list [ LocalObservation ] ) – A list of observations or a singular observation to be added. stored in the stash when initialising it. This can be altered using the compare_local_and_db_time flag when

title: exa.core.sequence.util.update_options
description:
Updates the options of an experiment or a sequence from the sequence-level options. The relevant sequence level options are chosen and their values applied to the node’s options.
For the usage of this...
content:
Updates the options of an experiment or a sequence from the sequence-level options. The relevant sequence level options are chosen and their values applied to the node’s options.
For the usage of this function, the sequence options should be named f"{experiment_class_name}_{experiment_option_name}" .
For example, to set the repetitions of CPhaseDiag one should have the sequence level option named as CPhaseDiag_repetitions . The convenience prefix GLOBAL can be used in place of an experiment class name to set the option for any
Experiment or ExperimentTracker regardless or class name. In case node is a Sequence the option is set for all
contained experiments. Class name options take precedence over GLOBAL options if both are specified for the same
option. Options can also be preceded with RECURSIVE , which will cause the option to be recursively applied
also to all subsequences in case node is a Sequence. For example, RECURSIVE_CPhaseDiag_repetitions or RECURSIVE_GLOBAL_repetitions . Omitting RECURSIVE sets the option only on the top level sequence.
The RECURSIVE prefix has no effect on Experiment or ExperimentTracker node objects.
Non-recursive options take precedence over recursive ones if both are specified for the same option.
The order of prefixes has no effect on execution. node ( Experiment | ExperimentTracker | _Sequence ) – The experiment instance or an experiment tracker or a subsequence. options ( dict [ str , Any ] ) – The sequence-level options dict. ValueError – if both GLOBAL and node name prefix name are specified; e.g GLOBAL_CPhaseDiag_repetitions None previous util next wrap_analyze By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0.
