title: exa.core.experiment.edge_coloring.color_qubit_pairs
description:
Create an edge-coloring of the given graph with minimum number of colors:
any edges connected with a vertex do not share the same color. If graph is bipartite, we use a simple edge-coloring algorithm ...
content:
Create an edge-coloring of the given graph with minimum number of colors:
any edges connected with a vertex do not share the same color. If graph is bipartite, we use a simple edge-coloring algorithm which gives a coloring using d number of colors,
where d = maximum degree of a vertex in the graph.
If graph is not bipartite, we use the Misra-Gries algorithm, which gives a coloring with d+1 number of colors. Works for both simple and multi-graphs (parallel edges), for connected and disconnected graphs,
for bipartite and non-bipartite graphs. qubit_pairs ( list [ tuple [ str , str ] ] ) – list of tuples of two qubits List of sublists of tuples of two qubits. title: ExponentialDecayWithOffset
description: Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.models.exponential_offset_model Bases: BaseModel Lmfit model for single-exponential decay with constant offset. This model describes data that decays exponentia...
content:
Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.models.exponential_offset_model Bases: BaseModel Lmfit model for single-exponential decay with constant offset. This model describes data that decays exponentially from an initial value toward a constant baseline offset. The model function is: A : Initial guess 1.0 (no bounds). \\tau : Initial guess 30e-6 (30 μs), lower bound 1e-9. y_0 : Initial guess 0.0 (no bounds). Initializes the ExponentialDecayWithOffset model. args – Passed to parent __init__. independent_vars ( list [ str ] | None ) – Independent variable names. kwargs – Passed to parent __init__. Attributes Methods guess Estimate initial parameters for exponential decay with offset. Estimate initial parameters for exponential decay with offset. For non-trivial data, it estimates the amplitude as the difference between the first and last data points,
and the offset as the last data point. If the amplitude is close to zero, it uses the range of the data as the amplitude and the
minimum value as the offset. The decay constant (tau) is estimated by finding the point where the data falls
to 1/e of its initial amplitude above the offsets. If this estimation fails, a default value is used. The method ensures tau is positive and not too small data ( ndarray ) – Dependent variable data. x ( ndarray ) – Independent variable data. kws – Values for the model parameters. Estimated parameters for fitting. Parameters Inheritance previous BiexponentialDecayWithOffset next gaussian_model By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. title: exa.core.util.phase_helper.get_phase_fitter
description: Generates a fitter function for cosine oscillation with frequency 1, used to determine the phase of the data. The fitter uses numpy.linalg.lstsq() to calculate the phase of the cosine oscillation. Its...
content:
Generates a fitter function for cosine oscillation with frequency 1, used to determine the phase of the data. The fitter uses numpy.linalg.lstsq() to calculate the phase of the cosine oscillation. Its behaviour depends
on the number of phases in the phase sweep. With 2 phases, the fitter will calculate the amplitude and phase
corresponding to the model: \(y(x) = A * \cos(x+phi) + 0.5\) where \(A>0\) is amplitude, \(phi>0\) is phase. Thus, this should only be used if excited state probability
is calibrated correctly, and thus the model’s assumption is satisfied.
With 3 phases or more, the fitter will do a least-squares fit to the model \(y(x) = A * \cos(x+phi) + B\) ,
where \(B\) is offset. This three-parameter model cannot be used if there are only 2 phases, and
if there are exactly 3, it is fully determined, so the resulting fit will be equal to the provided data. n_phases ( int ) – size of the phases array Function for fitting data to a cosine oscillation with frequency 1 model. title: BiexponentialDecayWithOffset
description: Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.models.exponential_offset_model Bases: BaseModel Lmfit model for biexponential decay with constant offset. This model describes data that decays biexponentially...
content:
Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.models.exponential_offset_model Bases: BaseModel Lmfit model for biexponential decay with constant offset. This model describes data that decays biexponentially from an initial value toward a constant baseline
offset. This happens when, for example, there is a TLS changing frequency on a timescale shorter than
a T1 experiment, or there is hybridisation in the presence of dephasing. The model function is: A_bi : Initial guess 1.0 (no bounds). \\alpha : Initial guess 0.7, bounded between 0 and 1. \\tau_a : Initial guess 30e-6 (30 μs), lower bound 1e-9. \\tau_b : Initial guess 5e-6 (5 μs), lower bound 1e-9. y_0_bi : Initial guess 0.0 (no bounds). Initializes the BixponentialDecayWithOffset model. args – Passed to parent __init__. independent_vars ( list [ str ] | None ) – Independent variable names. kwargs – Passed to parent __init__. Attributes Methods guess Estimate initial parameters for the decay. Estimate initial parameters for the decay. For non-trivial data, it estimates the amplitude as the difference between the first and last data points,
and the offset as the last data point. If the amplitude is close to zero, it uses the range of the data as the amplitude and the
minimum value as the offset. Alpha is taken as default. The ‘major’ decay constant (tau_a) is estimated by finding the point where the data falls
to 1/e of its initial amplitude above the offsets. The ‘minor’ decay constant (tau_b) is taken to be tau_a/5. If this estimation fails, a default value is used. The method ensures tau is positive and not too small data ( ndarray ) – Dependent variable data. x ( ndarray ) – Independent variable data. kws – Values for the model parameters. Estimated parameters for fitting. title: Experiment
description:
Module: exa.core.experiment.experiment Bases: object Base class for multi-qubit experiments. This class is designed to run arbitrary control sequences on multiple qubits.
Sequences can be provided eit...
content:
Module: exa.core.experiment.experiment Bases: object Base class for multi-qubit experiments. This class is designed to run arbitrary control sequences on multiple qubits.
Sequences can be provided either as time-ordered Timeboxes ,
or in the circuit-level, represented as quantum operations (i.e. gates),
or even above the gate-level if the necessary compilation stages to
go from that abstraction to the circuit-level is included. __init__() should not be overridden in the subclasses. Instead, one should override
the non-final methods below and/or default_options in order to achieve the desired behaviour. label ( str | None ) – Human-readable label for this experiment. circuit_generation_function ( CircuitGenerationFunction | None ) – The circuit generation function.
Define when using Experiment without inheritance.
The function should take at least 2 arguments: components and builder and return a list of
TimeBoxes. Any other arguments are treated as extra circuit parameters.
See get_default_circuit_generation_function() for more details on the signature.
By default, returns an empty TimeBox, so no pulses are played. Attributes allowed_component_grouping_modes Only for backwards compatibility, does not actually do anything anymore. allowed_qpu_types Defines if the experiment supports only star or normal QPUs. chad The CHAD data this experiment will use when running. chip_layout  chip_topology  circuit_stages Circuit-level (above TimeBox) sweepable compilation stages. coupler_mapping  default_label The default label for the experiment. default_options Default experiment options. executor The instance implementing the ExecutorInterface that this experiment will use when running. final_stages The final stages for creating the SC RunDefinition. gate_definitions  gates  input_type Input type of the Experiment class. last_run Get the results from the latest run. name Unique identifier for the experiment class. observation_handler  parallel_group Unit of parallelization for the experiment. pp_stages The return data post-processing stages. pulse_stages TimeBox and below sweepable compilation stages. storage The instance implementing the StorageInterface that this experiment will use when running. Methods analyze Analyzes an experiment run and returns the result. chip_properties Get a selected properties of chip components. create Create a complete RunDefinition for a new run. default_analyze_function The sweep generation function is a Callable that returns an AnalyzeResult object. default_circuit_generation_function The circuit generation function is a Callable that returns either a TimeBox or a list[TimeBox] object. default_sweep_generation_function The sweep generation function is a Callable that returns the type Sweeps . default_sweep_parameters Returns default sweep parameters. from_dut_label Construct an Experiment instance for loading and re-analyzing old run data. get_by_job_id Get an instance of the Experiment that produced job_id , holding its run result. get_by_run_id Get an instance of the Experiment that produced run_id , holding its run result. get_default_analyze_function Returns default analyze function. get_default_circuit_generation_function Circuit generation function for this experiment. get_default_circuit_settings Override to define default circuit parameters. get_default_sweep_generation_function Return the sweep generation function. get_default_sweeps Default sweep definition for the experiment. get_default_sweeps_as_dict Returns the default sweeps from get_default_sweeps() as a dict that can be fed to run() . get_settings Retrieves and modifies settings for Experiment. has_required_gates Check whether the station provides all gates required by the circuit generation function. inspect_segment Visualise the segments of a playlist. make_final_mutations Make any experiment-specific changes to the final run definition. print_default_sweeps Prints the default sweeps from get_default_sweeps() in a human-readable format. process_run_components Process components and ExperimentOptions.subscribed_components inputs given by the user into parallelly runnable component groups. register_gate_implementation Register new gate implementation for this experiment instance. remove_operations Removes the given operations from the settings tree under the given component or group. run Run the experiment to get results. set_calibration_data_for_gate_implementation Set calibration data for a gate implementation in this experiment instance. set_gate_implementation_as_default Set this gate implementation as default for this experiment instance. setup_additional_init_properties Override to e.g. change the observation loading rules or register new gate implementations for this experiment instance. submit_run Submit an experiment for execution on Station Control, wait for the results and post-process them. update_compilation_context Additional updates for the compilation context. update_settings Additional updates for the settings. Unique identifier for the experiment class. Used to differentiate between different datasets in the database. Circuit-level (above TimeBox) sweepable compilation stages. TimeBox and below sweepable compilation stages. The final stages for creating the SC RunDefinition. The return data post-processing stages. The circuit generation function is a Callable that returns either a TimeBox or a list[TimeBox] object. For more information see get_default_circuit_generation_function() components ( list [ str ] ) builder ( ScheduleBuilder ) list [ TimeBox ] The sweep generation function is a Callable that returns the type Sweeps .
For more information see get_default_sweep_generation_function() components ( ComponentGrouping ) chip_topology ( ChipTopology ) settings ( SettingNode ) list [ Sweep | tuple [ Sweep , …]] The sweep generation function is a Callable that returns an AnalyzeResult object. For more
information see get_default_analyze_function() components ( ComponentGrouping ) run_result ( RunResult ) AnalyzeResult Default experiment options. Inheriting classes may override this attribute to suit their use case. The default label for the experiment. Inheriting classes may override this attribute. Defines if the experiment supports only star or normal QPUs. By default all QPU types are supported.
Inheriting classes can override this attribute. Only for backwards compatibility, does not actually do anything anymore. Unit of parallelization for the experiment. Determines the
logic for processing and validation of the experiment’s run components (see process_run_components() ).
Certain commonly encountered parallel groups are defined in ParallelGroup , but a custom
string may also be used and the process_run_components() may be overridden to process these appropriately. Input type of the Experiment class. See InputType . Construct an Experiment instance for loading and re-analyzing old run data. Gets the station properties from ExaRuntime.storage .
Cannot be used for executing new runs. dut_label ( str ) – Constructed Experiment instance will refer to this QPU/station instead of the the
one you’re connected to. label ( str ) – Human-readable label for this experiment. Experiment instance for loading and re-analyzing old data. Self The instance implementing the ExecutorInterface that this experiment will use when running. The active executor instance. The instance implementing the StorageInterface that this experiment will use when running. The active storage instance. The CHAD data this experiment will use when running. Check whether the station provides all gates required by the circuit generation function. Subclasses should override this method to verify availability of any non-default gates they depend on. Note Currently overridden only by experiment classes that require the MOVE operation. bool Circuit generation function for this experiment. By default, the function stored (as a static method) in the attribute default_circuit_generation_function is returned, but in case more complex logic
(including any number of self calls)
is needed for determining the function, the default method can be fully overridden in inheriting classes. The circuit generation function (CGF) is a Callable that produces the control schedule
the experiment wants to execute. There are two kinds of CGFs, which are identified by inspecting
their signature: Subcircuit CGF:
Has group: tuple[str, ...] and builder: ScheduleBuilder as its first two parameters.
Returns a TimeBox that contains the control schedule for the parallelisable
unit of QPU component names given in group . parallel_group determines how the different groups of simultaneously parallelizable
units (also called color groups since determining them is a graph coloring problem)
are derived from the components given to create() .
All the subcircuit TimeBoxes corresponding to the same parallel group are automatically
wrapped into the full circuit Timebox, which runs them in parallel. Full circuit CGF:
Has components: ComponentGrouping and builder: ScheduleBuilder as its first two parameters.
Returns a list[TimeBox] that represents the full circuit control schedule. In addition to the above required parameters, a CGF may have any number of additional args
which may have default values. The default values will be added as Settings in the settings tree unless they are defined as default circuit settings (see get_default_circuit_settings() ). Note that couplers are not given as default arguments to the CGF. They are accessible via
the builder argument (mostly implicitly, as the user does not have to usually adress the couplers;
the builder will do that under the hood). If the user explicitly includes the couplers in the run components,
they will be accessible in the components argument. The CGF gets the values for its extra parameters from the following sources in this order of precedence: Sweeps that are defined for a parameter with the same name as the argument. These can come from either get_default_sweeps() or given by the user in the run() argument sweeps . Circuit settings values given by the user after if they have defined a parameter of the same name in get_default_circuit_settings() (or by inserting a parameter manually to circuit_settings ).
These values can be inserted in several places: manually in the notebook/runtime, in get_settings() by overriding update_settings() or in the actual setting definitions in get_default_circuit_settings() (as the default value of the Setting). The default values provided for the parameters in the definition of the CGF that
do not have a circuit setting in circuit_settings (these will still be added to the settings tree
but without any labels or units). Circuit generation function. SubTGF | FullTGF Override to define default circuit parameters. Enables specifying default values and units for circuit generation function parameters. This method should
return a list of Settings that will be added in the settings tree (including their units).
Then if their name coincides with an argument of the circuit_generation_function, their value will be used
to generate a circuit (you can add circuit settings which do not coincide with an argument of the circuit
generation function). The default circuit settings. These will be added in the Settings tree alongside with their units. list [ Setting ] Override to e.g. change the observation loading rules or register new gate implementations
for this experiment instance. Here you may add new components to self.observation_handler , or new observation to be loaded for a given
component and change the default observations rules associated with any component and observation. Note that
any active global observation rules will override whatever defaults you add here (including the defaults added
to new observations you yourself added in this method). You can also register here a specific gate implementation needed only in this experiment. None Default sweep definition for the experiment. Calls get_default_sweep_generation_function() , and then calls the returned function
to generate the sweeps, applying automatic parallelization logic for group-wise sweep
generation functions. Sweeps defined as the input argument of the run() method take precedence.
The default sweeps are assumed to be done in the innermost loop. The default sweeps can be defined for any parameter in settings tree (including pulse
parameters and circuit parameters), or for a parameter whose name coincides with a circuit_generation_function argument. Hint For a parallel Rabi experiment, this method could return Sweep(parameter=<parameter for the I amplitude of a PRX gate>, data=[...]) for all the qubits. Note Overriding this method is allowed for backwards compatibility, but should be done anymore.
Define default_sweep_generation_function instead. components ( ComponentGrouping ) – Qubits and couplers for which the sweeps are defined. settings ( SettingNode ) – Full settings object for the experiment. Default sweeps. list [ Sweep | tuple [ Sweep , …]] Return the sweep generation function. Returns the static method default_sweep_generation_function , with all its
non-standard parameters bound to the values of similarly named attributes in :attr`options`,
if they exist. default_sweep_generation_function can be either a full function or a group-wise function,
acting on the defined parallelisable unit of the experiment (see parallel_group ),
in which case it is automatically wrapped into the full sweep function.
In each case it has three standard positional parameters: Group-wise functions have the standard parameters [group: tuple[str, ...], chip_topology: ChipTopology, settings: SettingNode] , with group containing the QPU component names of the parallelisable group. Full sweep functions have the standard parameters [components: ComponentGrouping, chip_topology: ChipTopology, settings: SettingNode] ,
where components contains the full component grouping. Note If more complex logic (including any number of self calls) is needed for determining the
function, this method can be fully overridden in inheriting classes, but this
should be avoided. Callable [[…], list [ Sweep | tuple [ Sweep , …]]] Additional updates for the settings. Inheriting classes should override this function instead of overriding the whole get_settings.
Here, you can for example: Add/remove operations or settings or setting nodes. Override values in the settings tree (including any values for the circuit parameters). Add more validation for options. What you should not try to do here: Change get_settings() behaviour related to readout_mode . qubits ( list [ str ] ) – qubits for the settings. couplers ( list [ str ] ) – couplers for the settings. settings ( SettingNode ) – the settings tree. None Process components and ExperimentOptions.subscribed_components inputs given by the user
into parallelly runnable component groups. The behaviour of this method is determined by parallel_group such that commonly encountered parallel
groups are processed automatically. In addition, this method can be overridden in the inheriting classes for
a specific behaviour needed in that class and not achieved by one of the default ParallelGroup cases. Note that this method should never return None or empty dict which are valid values for both run
argument components and options.subscribed_components . These cases must be dealt in one way or
another so that a non-empty ComponentGrouping and a non-empty subscribed_components are returned. components ( ComponentGrouping ) – The components given as the run argument by the user. settings ( SettingNode | None ) – Settings to set before sweeping. Defaults to None if settings are not needed to process run
components. Parallelization for components , subscribed_components. tuple [ ComponentGrouping , list [ str ] | dict [ str , list [ str ]]] Additional updates for the compilation context. Inheriting classes should override this function instead of subclassing Compiler just to override what is in the context. What should be done here: Add additional context objects needed for compilation, eg. a Backend. What you should not try to do here: Override any existing default context object, eg. components, builder. The context dictionary at input contains any additional keyword arguments added by the user when calling create() , and by default it is empty. The modified dictionary is then used to update the Compiler’s
context. context ( dict [ str , Any ] ) – Additional context provided by the user. components ( ComponentGrouping ) – Component groups given to the compiler. settings ( SettingNode ) – Full settings tree to use as reference. None Make any experiment-specific changes to the final run definition. The RunDefinition contains the complete information of the run, including both the request to be
sent to Station Control, and experiment-specific details. This method can be overridden in inheriting experiments to make any kind of last-minute mutations to the
definition before it is executed. The base implementation does nothing. The method will be called as the
very last step of create() . For example, this can be used to change metadata, such as the target data variables, which is needed by
analysis. This method should be used only as the last resort if the desired logic cannot be expressed using the other

The analyze function can be either a full analyze function, in which case it should have the arguments [components, run_result, **kwargs] , and it should perform the whole analysis for the experiment. content:
Basis matrix for the four linear parameters of the two-tone Ramsey response. With \(\Theta_j = 2\pi(f_q - f_{d,j})(t - t_0 + \tau)\) , the shared oscillation expands as so the first two columns are the sine and the cosine of that angle under the decay envelope, and the
last two the offset of each tone. t ( ndarray ) – The time coordinate values. f_d ( ndarray ) – Frequencies of the two drive tones. f_q ( float ) – Frequency of the qubit. tau ( float ) – Constant time offset, accounting for phase the time coordinate does not carry. T_exp ( float ) – Exponential decay time, shared by both tones. Array of shape (len(t) * len(f_d), 4) , rows in np.ravel order of the (len(t), len(f_d)) response, so basis @ [c_cos, c_sin, offset_1, offset_2] is the flattened
response. ndarray previous ramsey2f_separable_model next exa.core.model_selection_fitter.models.ramsey2f_separable_model.ramsey_2f_separable_response By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

Full path: exa.core.local_storage A fully local, in-memory or file-system implementation of StorageInterface . This module provides LocalStorage , which keeps all data in plain Python objects
in the current process, with no database or server required. It only implements the
observation and observation set related methods of StorageInterface ; everything
else raises NotImplementedError . It is meant for small-scale local use (notebooks,
scripts, tests), not for production workloads with large amounts of data. Optionally, an instance can be pointed at a JSON file on disk: existing state is loaded
from it on construction, and every create/update operation transparently persists the
new state back to it. Classes LocalStorage Local, in-memory implementation of StorageInterface . Inheritance previous X_EF_GateImplementation next LocalStorage By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: ExperimentOptions
description: Module: exa.core.experiment_options Bases: BaseModel Options for controlling experiment behavior. Options change the behavior of the experiment execution in a way that is specific to the experiment ty...
content:
Module: exa.core.experiment_options Bases: BaseModel Options for controlling experiment behavior. Options change the behavior of the experiment execution in a way that is specific to the experiment type.
Unlike instrument settings, these are not propagated to the instruments. Create a new model by parsing and validating input data from keyword arguments. Raises [ ValidationError ][pydantic_core.ValidationError] if the input data cannot be
validated to form a valid model. self is explicitly positional-only to allow self as a field name. Attributes model_config Configuration for the model, should be a dictionary conforming to [ ConfigDict ][pydantic.config.ConfigDict]. readout_mode Defines what type of final readout the experiment uses, see ReadoutMode for the possible values. readout_programming_mode How the experiment handles final readout, heralding and reset, see ReadoutProgrammingMode for the possible values. active_reset_cycles Number of active reset operations inserted at the beginning of each segment for each active qubit, in their own TimeBox . used_measure_operations Names of the measurement QuantumOp the various readout_programming_mode s use when building the circuits. repetitions Averaging used in the experiment. subscribed_components Components that are read out in the experiment. exclude_operations_for Dictionary containing operations that are excluded from the experiment for given components. data_size_safety_switch If True does not allow runs that would result in excessive amounts of data, possibly straining the DB. force_ragged_data If False the result datasets will be reshaped to an N-dimensional box based on the segment (hard sweeps) dimensions, whenever that is possible. Methods from_dict Construct an ExperimentOptions instance from specified state provided as a dictionary. to_dict Extract state of the current experiment options as a dictionary. readout_mode ( str ) readout_programming_mode ( str ) active_reset_cycles ( int | None ) used_measure_operations ( dict [ str , str ] ) repetitions ( int ) subscribed_components ( list [ str ] | dict [ str , list [ str ] ] | None ) exclude_operations_for ( dict [ str , list [ str ] | str ] | None ) data_size_safety_switch ( bool ) force_ragged_data ( bool ) extra_data ( Any ) Defines what type of final readout the experiment uses, see ReadoutMode for the
possible values. How the experiment handles final readout, heralding and reset, see ReadoutProgrammingMode for the possible values. Number of active reset operations inserted at the beginning of each segment for each active qubit, in their
own TimeBox . Uses the default implementation of reset . None means active reset is not used
but instead reset is done by waiting (relaxation), using the default implementation of the reset_wait operation.
Integer values smaller than 1 result in neither active nor reset by wait being used, in which case any reset
operations must be explicitly added in the circuit generation function. Names of the measurement QuantumOp the various readout_programming_mode s use when building
the circuits. Changing the defaults (e.g. making "heralding" use "measure_fidelity" ) may result in
sub-optimal behavior. "terminal" is used for terminal measurement when readout_programming_mode is
either "classic" or heralding . "heralding" is used for the heralding measurement when readout_programming_mode is "heralding" . "reset_at_end" is used when readout_programming_mode is "reset_at_end" . Note: this attribute applies only to the measure operations added automatically by Experiment.
If the experiment adds measure operations explicitly in its circuit,
you must write the logic for choosing the right operation to the circuit generation function itself. Averaging used in the experiment. This value will be used for controllers.options.playlist_repeats ,
and possibly for controllers.options.averaging_bins , depending on readout_mode . Components that are read out in the experiment. Can be a list of component names, or a dict
of lists of component names where the keys are the readout group names (this option is only available
with readout_mode == "counter" ). Dictionary containing operations that are excluded from the experiment for given components. Operations
are given as keys and component or components as values e.g. exclude_operations_for = {“readout”: [QB1, QB2]}.
The operations are removed as part of get_settings() . If True does not allow runs that would result in excessive amounts of data, possibly straining the DB.
An error message will be thrown that approximates the data size and asks the user to set the option False if
they still want to proceed. If False the result datasets will be reshaped to an N-dimensional box based on the segment
(hard sweeps) dimensions, whenever that is possible. The ragged data format, where the result data is
indexed along the readout trigger index, is used only when necessary, i.e. if the number of readout triggers per
segment is not constant. Turn this option to True if you want the experiment to always produce ragged
data. This can be useful e.g. if the number of readouts per segment is not deterministic or known, and the
experiment may under some circumstances return ND-data and in some ragged data (forcing the data to be always ragged
makes the result handling consistent). Configuration for the model, should be a dictionary conforming to [ ConfigDict ][pydantic.config.ConfigDict]. Extract state of the current experiment options as a dictionary. Any arbitrary type present is also converted to dict, and a __type__ attribute is added to the root
of that dict, so that from_dict() is able to convert them back.
The arbitrary types need to be specified in _class_name_to_class() and have the method to_dict implemented. A dict[str, Any] representing the state of the current experiment options. ValueError – if an arbitrary type does not have the method “to_dict” implemented. dict [ str , Any ] Construct an ExperimentOptions instance from specified state provided as a dictionary. Construction can be based on the type of the class, or just this base class if the type is not relevant.
If values contains '__type__' in a nested dictionary (as is typically inserted by to_dict() ), it will be silently removed.
The intended usage is that the '__type__' information is used to determine which arbitrary type was
converted to a dict and now needs to be converted back to the type. values ( dict [ str , Any ] ) – Dictionary to create the instance from. An instance of ExperimentOptions . ValueError – either if an arbitrary type has been used and it does not have a mapping in _class_name_to_class() , or if the arbitrary type does not have the method
    “from_dict” implemented. ExperimentOptions Inheritance previous experiment_options next experiment_utils By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

content:
Wraps SequenceExecuteResult.analyze() by recording any caught exception detail into the result. In the event of an exception, the real analysis is skipped and the latest sequence execution results are merely
conveyed to the returned analyze result in order to have the data available.

content:
Load all the observations for a given sequence and all of its child nodes. The observations are returned from any level of subsequences and their experiment nodes. The returned values
are mapped to tuples that contain the “path” of IDs for the sequences and/or experiment that created them.
For example, if a sequence with ID=0 has a subsequence with ID=1 which further has an experiment with ID=3
that creates an observation with dut_field “QB1.readout.amplitude”, the observation will be mapped to a path ("0","1","2","QB1.readout_amplitude") . sequence_run_id ( UUID ) – The sequence ID. tags ( list [ str ] | None ) – Optionally filter with these tags. title: exa.core.post_processing.excited_state_probability_computation.compute_single_qubit_probability_from_counter_results
description:
Compute single qubit state probabilities from the multi qubit counter results. For N qubits, the multi qubit states are written as binary numbers (of length N): 00…0, 00…1, …, 11…0 .
The counter retur...
content:
Compute single qubit state probabilities from the multi qubit counter results. For N qubits, the multi qubit states are written as binary numbers (of length N): 00…0, 00…1, …, 11…0 .
The counter returns the probabilities P(00…0), P(00…1), … P(11…1) . The single qubit probability that
a specific qubit is in the excited state can be obtained as the sum of all the probabilities where that qubit
is in the excited state. For three qubits, e.g., the probability that the first qubit is in excited state is
given as P(E_1) = P(001) + P(011) + P(101) + P(111) , and similarly the probability for the second qubit is P(E_2) = P(010) + P(011) + P(110) + P(111) . data ( DataArray ) – Data containing the multi qubit counter results. qubit_basis_coordinate ( str ) – The name of the multi qubit basis coordinate. qubits_list ( list [ str ] ) – The full list of qubit names for which the counter was used. The order of the list defines the
order of the multi qubit states such that the first qubit in the list corresponds to the smallest digit
in the binary representation of the multi qubit states. qubit ( str ) – The name of the qubit for which to return the probability. get_excited_state ( bool ) – If set False , will return the ground state probability. Otherwise returns the exicted
state. Data array containing the given single qubit probability. Data array containing the given single qubit probability. title: Fitter
description:
Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.fitter Bases: object Fitter object that stores the models used for model-selection. To get started, create an instance of the fitter and add the models
you woul...
content:
Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.fitter Bases: object Fitter object that stores the models used for model-selection. To get started, create an instance of the fitter and add the models
you would like to compare. Calling fit() fits all the models
to the given data, and selects the best one based on Bayesian information
criterion. Example: from exa.core import model_selection_fitter as msf
import xarray as xr
import numpy as np fitter = msf.Fitter()
model = msf.models.LinearModel()
fitter.add_model(model)
# Add another linear model with fixed offset.
model_fixed = msf.models.LinearModel(name=”Fixed”)
model_fixed.set_param_hint(“b”, value=0.1, vary=False)
fitter.add_model(model_fixed)
data = xr.DataArray(np.linspace(-2,2,21) + 0.5, dims=[‘time’], coords={“time”: np.linspace(-1, 1, 21)})
fit_result = fitter.fit(data=data, x=”time”, plot_fit=True) Create a new Fitter instance. Methods add_model Adds a model to the fitter. fit Fits all the models known to the fitter and returns the best model. plot Plots the selected quantity. Adds a model to the fitter. When calling fit method, all the added models are fit and the best
model is selected. model ( Model ) – Model to add. None Fits all the models known to the fitter and returns the best model. The independent variables are first extracted from the dataset. After that, complex action is applied
to all the data, and the remaining dimensions are reduced by first taking only the indices given by take_index . Reduction action is then applied to all extra dimensions. Finally, the fit is done
separately for all the remaining coordinates. At each step of the fit, all the models are fitted to the data, and the best model is chosen using
the Akaike information criterion adjusted for small sample sizes. data ( Dataset | DataArray ) – Dataset with the data to be fitted. Can be also DataArray, in which case datavar is ignored. datavar ( str ) – Data variable name. Defaults to None. plot_fit ( bool ) – If True , the best fit is plotted and shown immediately. add_plot_to_dataset ( bool ) – If True , plot of the fit is created and added to the dataset.
If performance is critical, set this to False and use the “plot_definitions” return callable instead. use_outlier_detection ( bool ) – If True , uses leave-one-out outlier detection. take_indices ( tuple [ int ] | None ) – Picks only the extra dimensions specified by the tuple. complex_action ( Literal [ 'real' , 'imag' , 'rotate_to_real' ] ) – Converts complex values to real. Either ‘real’, ‘imag’, ‘rotate_to_real’.
If None, no conversion is done. reduction_action ( Literal [ 'mean' , 'median' ] | None ) – Applies the given operation to reduce the remaining dimensions. Either ‘mean’,
‘std’ or None. fitter_options ( dict [ str , Any ] | None ) – Key-value pairs for setting lmfit fitter options. If using lmfit models,
these are the fitter options accepted by lmfit. If not options are specified,
defaults to fitter_options = {"method": "leastsq", "nan_policy": "omit"} Some fitter_options also have impact on how msf does fitting:
*  nan_policy: if number of independent variables is > 1, changed to “raise”. outlier_detection_options ( dict [ str , Any ] | None ) – Key-value pairs for configuring outlier detection. override_model_initial_guess ( bool ) – If True, initial guess is done using parameter values.
If False model.guess function is used instead. extra_parameter_penalty_factor ( float ) – Add an extra penalty on having more parameters in the model. Used to select the best model. select_by_bic ( bool ) – If true, select the best fit based on the bayesian information criterion (BIC). If false,
select based on the Akaike Information Criterion corrected for small sample sizes. weights ( DataArray | None ) – Weight factor used to scale the residuals. The weight array must have the same shape as the data.
Weights can also be applied through fitter_options, but then the same weights are used for all
data points. **independent_vars ( str | list [ str ] | dict [ Any , Any ] | None ) – Maps the given coordinate names in the dataset to the independent variables of the model. For example,
if the x-coordinate of the model is called x, and the corresponding coordinate in the dataset
is ‘time’, give x=’time’ as the argument. If the model acts on multidimensional data, this can be
specified by giving a list of coordinates. For example x = ['time', 'frequency'] . fit_result: Data array which elements are the ModelResult s and the coordinates are the remaining coordinates of the dataset an extra dimension that contains the names of the fitted models. fit: The evaluated values of the fitted models. initial_guess: The values for the initial guess. uncertainty: The evaluated values for the uncertainty in the fitted data points. plots: Plot of the fit if add_plot_to_dataset is True . plot_definitions: a callable that plots a matplotlib figure, and suggested arguments for the callable. best_model: The best ModelResult for each of the remaining coordinates. best_model_index: The index for the best model for each of the extra dimension. model_probabilities: Probability that each of the model is the best according to AIC. AICs: Akaike information criterion for all the models. AICcs: Akaike information criterion for small samples of all the models. redchis: Reduced chi-square for all the models. r2s: R2 values for all the models. parameters: Fitted parameter values for the best model as separate datavars. parameter_stderr: Standard errors for all the parameters as separate datavars. coordinates of the dataset an extra dimension that contains the names of the fitted models. fit: The evaluated values of the fitted models. initial_guess: The values for the initial guess. uncertainty: The evaluated values for the uncertainty in the fitted data points. plots: Plot of the fit if add_plot_to_dataset is True . plot_definitions: a callable that plots a matplotlib figure, and suggested arguments for the callable. best_model: The best ModelResult for each of the remaining coordinates. best_model_index: The index for the best model for each of the extra dimension. model_probabilities: Probability that each of the model is the best according to AIC. AICs: Akaike information criterion for all the models. AICcs: Akaike information criterion for small samples of all the models. redchis: Reduced chi-square for all the models. r2s: R2 values for all the models. parameters: Fitted parameter values for the best model as separate datavars. parameter_stderr: Standard errors for all the parameters as separate datavars. Xarray Dataset containing the following data variables Plots the selected quantity. quantity ( str | list [ str ] ) – Name of the quantity (datavar) or quantities to plot. indices ( list [ tuple [ int ] | int ] | None ) – Coordinate indices to select for plotting. Can be either provided as a flat list of indices or a list
of tuples of indices. coordinate ( str | list [ str ] | None ) – Coordinate to plot. Can also provide a list of coordinates for mult-dimensinal plots. result_index ( int ) – index of the fit result to use for plotting. ax ( Axes | None ) – Axes object for plotting. If None, a new axes is created. plot_style ( Literal [ 'point' ] ) – Style of the plot. uncertainty_style ( Literal [ 'errorbar' , 'fill' ] ) – Style for uncertainties, options are ‘errorbar’ or ‘fill’. Matplotlib figure which contains the axes. FigureBase | None Inheritance previous fitter next fitting By Author name not set © Copyright 2019-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 20.0.0. Full path: exa.core.provider.provider Unified execution and storage runtime for the EXA core. This module provides the ExaRuntime , a process-wide singleton that acts
as the central access point for quantum job execution and data persistence.
By utilizing the standardized ExecutorInterface and StorageInterface ,
it decouples high-level experiment logic from specific backend implementations
(e.g., IQM Server, local simulators, or mock hardware). The runtime is designed to be initialized once during the application startup
using a concrete provider helper, after which the global executor and storage
instances can be accessed throughout the process. description: Module: exa.core.sequence.sequence Bases: ABC Base class for Sequences. New sequences are defined by subclassing this. A subclass of Sequence should at least define name as a class attribute, and impl...
content:
Module: exa.core.sequence.sequence Bases: ABC Base class for Sequences. New sequences are defined by subclassing this. A subclass of Sequence should at least define name as a class attribute, and implement execute() , which is the main body of the sequence execution. observation_stash ( ObservationStash | None ) – If provided, the observations created by the execution nodes will not
be saved to the DB but to the given stash instead. In this case, any subsequences will
by default copy that stash, add their observations to the copy, and only at the end of
the subsequence execution, save them to the parent’s stash. The user may turn off the merging
of stashes via the attribute save_stash and/or use a different stash (or no stash)
for a given execution node in the actual implementation of execute() . kwargs – All keyword arguments to the constructor are copied to options attribute.
The execute() can refer to the options to modify the behavior of the execution.
The meaning of the options depends entirely on how they are used by execute() .
The user may apply options to specific execution nodes via prefixing them with the node’s class names.
E.g. to apply option foo = 1 for experiment class MyExperiment that is a part of the
subsequence MySequence , the user should add MySequence_MyExperiment_foo = 1 to the kwargs. Attributes default_options Required keys for the sequence options and their default values. ignore_analyze_errors Ignore analyze errors for this sequence and its subsequences. save_stash Whether to save this sequence's stash to the parent sequence's stash (or the DB if the parent does not have stash). name Identifier of the sequence type. options Options that modify the execution. Methods analysis Function that performs sequence-level analysis based on the results of the executed nodes. context Generate a context manager inside execute() . execute Executes the sequence. set_attribute_options Set the attribute values from options for the options defined in ATTRIBUTE_OPTIONS . Identifier of the sequence type. Function that performs sequence-level analysis based on the results of the executed nodes.
It must take a SequenceResult as the first argument and return a SequenceAnalyzeResult .
Other arguments are optional. analysis should be given as a class attribute, decorated with staticmethod .
If a subclass does not define analysis , default_analysis() is used. result ( SequenceExecuteResult ) SequenceAnalyzeResult Required keys for the sequence options and their default values. ExperimentTracker or a subclass of it.
This class will be used when creating a tracker object in the execution context with track() .
Giving your own tracker class allows modifying the execution of all experiments, for example by wrapping
the run logic with custom conditions. alias of ExperimentTracker SequenceExecutor or a subclass of it.
This class will be used when executing a sequence, and can be used to modify the sequence execution. alias of SequenceExecutor Whether to save this sequence’s stash to the parent sequence’s stash (or the DB if the parent does not have
stash). This attribute has an effect only if set at the subsequence level, and effect will not propagate to
further subsequences. This attribute is also settable by including save_stash in the sequence options. Ignore analyze errors for this sequence and its subsequences. The observations and other analyze results will
be retained if they were created successfully, but any analyze errors will still be shown in the report. If set,
as True or False , the effect will propagate recursively to all subsequences and their experiments.
This attribute is also settable by including ignore_analyze_errors in the sequence options. Options that modify the execution. The values are either class-level defaults from default_options or kwargs given in the constructor. Options must contain only basic Python types. Generate a context manager inside execute() . sequence_run_id ( UUID | None ) – If specified uses this id for the sequence. A new instance of SequenceContext. SequenceContext Set the attribute values from options for the options defined in ATTRIBUTE_OPTIONS . Executes the sequence. This is the main body of the execution code and should be implemented in a subclass. Inside this method A SequenceContext should be created by making a with self.context() as context: statement. Under the with statement, all calls to Experiment.run() , Experiment.analyze() , and Sequence.execute() (of subsequences) should be made using the methods of context .
Otherwise, those actions will not be tracked. The method must end with return context.to_result() , called outside the scope of the above-mentioned with statement. It converts the captured results for further processing. A new instance of SequenceExecuteResult. Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.models.model_utils Bases: Model Base class for the model selection fitter’s models. Every model in this package needs its make_params and set_param_hint decorated the same way,
so this wires that up once rather than in each model. The model function will normally take an independent variable

data to model some data as for a curve-fitting problem. func ( callable ) – Function to be wrapped. independent_vars ( list of str , optional) – Arguments to func that are independent variables (default is
None). param_names ( list of str , optional) – Names of arguments to func that are to be made into
parameters (default is None). nan_policy ( {'raise' , 'propagate' , 'omit'} , optional ) – How to handle NaN and missing values in data. See Notes below. prefix ( str , optional ) – Prefix used for the model. name ( str , optional ) – Name for the model. When None (default) the name is the same
as the model function ( func ). **kws ( dict , optional ) – Additional keyword arguments to pass to model function. Notes 1. The model function must return an array that will be the same
size as the data being modeled. 2. Parameter names are inferred from the function arguments by default,
and a residual function is automatically constructed. 3. Specifying independent_vars here will explicitly name the
independent variables for the Model.  in contrast, param_names is
meant to help infer Parameter names for keyword arguments defined with **kws in the Model function. 4. nan_policy sets what to do when a NaN or missing value is
seen in the data. Should be one of: ‘raise’ : raise a ValueError (default) ‘propagate’ : do nothing ‘omit’ : drop missing data Examples The model function will normally take an independent variable

title: SequenceContext
description: Module: exa.core.sequence.context Bases: object A stateful object that provides the tools for Sequence execution and captures the inputs and outputs. SequenceContext is a context object that captures ...
content:
Module: exa.core.sequence.context Bases: object A stateful object that provides the tools for Sequence execution and captures the inputs and outputs. SequenceContext is a context object that captures the run IDs, analysis results,
and analysis arguments for each Experiment or Sequence execution done within the context. A user does not need to construct a SequenceContext. The intended way is to use it as a context manager,
see Sequence.context() . If exceptions are caught in execute_sequence and execute_experiment , error summary and traceback are stored
in results. Execution errors are stored in sequence result data which will be stored to persistence.
On the contrary, analysis errors are stored only locally in analyze results. Logging of errors is handled exclusively in __exit__ . data ( SequenceData ) – The serializable part of the Sequence that will be executed with this context. tracker_class ( type [ ExperimentTracker ] ) – Optional subclass of ExperimentTracker .
This class will be used when creating a tracker object with track() . observation_stash ( ObservationStash | None ) – The stash to save observations to instead of the DB. sequence_executer_class – Will be used when executing a sequence. attribute_options ( dict [ str , Any ] | None ) sequence_executor_class ( type [ SequenceExecutor ] ) sequence_run_id ( UUID | None ) Attributes sub_stashes Stores the observation stashes of any subsequences executed in this context (mapped to the sequence_run_id ). Methods end_tracking Get the captured data from an ExperimentTracker instance and store it to the context. execute_experiment Run a single experiment and its analysis. execute_sequence Execute and analyze another sequence in this context. to_result Converts the captured execution results into a SequenceExecuteResult data object. track Create a tracker object that wraps an Experiment instance and captures the actions done with it. Stores the observation stashes of any subsequences executed in this context
(mapped to the sequence_run_id ). Run a single experiment and its analysis. This includes: running the experiment on hardware analyzing the execution results with given arguments tagging the observations from the analysis. Note: the tags entry of Sequence.options will be
used for tagging, if any. saving the observations. Under the hood, the Experiment is wrapped with tracker_class , which means that a tracker class can be
used to customize the behavior without calling track() explicitly. experiment ( Experiment | type [ Experiment ] ) – The experiment to execute.
Can be either an instance or a class, in which case a new instance is created. custom_analysis ( Callable [ [ ... ] , AnalyzeResult ] | None ) – Custom analysis function for the experiment. run_args ( dict [ str , Any ] | None ) – Arguments to pass to the experiment.run , most commonly at least the list of components. analyze_args ( dict [ str , Any ] | None ) – Arguments to pass to the experiment.analyze . observation_stash ( ObservationStash | None ) – The stash to save observations to instead of the DB. If not provided, will use
the stash in self._observation_stash , and if that is empty as well, the observations will
be saved to the DB. The result of the experiment.analyze . AnalyzeResult Execute and analyze another sequence in this context. The analyze_results of each Experiment or sub-sequence within sequence are captured. If sequence does not have a stash and the context has self._observation_stash populated, will copy
the contents of self._observation_stash and run sequence on that stash. At the end of execution,
the stash of sequence will be saved (i.e. either merged to self._observation_stash or if that does not
exist, saved to the DB) based on the value of the attribute option save_stash . sequence ( _Sequence ) – The sequence instance to execute. analyze_args ( dict [ str , Any ] | None ) – Arguments to pass to the sequence.analyze . The analyzed result of executing sequence . SequenceAnalyzeResult Converts the captured execution results into a SequenceExecuteResult data object. As a side effect, the final result of this sequence is saved to persistence. The result is marked final after
which further changes to it are prevented. Thus, this method is callable only once per object. Should be called at the end of Sequence.execute() . A new instance of SequenceExecuteResult. SequenceExecuteResult Create a tracker object that wraps an Experiment instance and captures the actions done with it. As an alternative to execute_experiment() , the tracker allows a more fluent workflow with the
experiment instance.
The tracker behaves like a normal Experiment.
The use cases are, for example, tuning settings, sweep ranges, and options before running. The tracker should only be used for one round of run & analyze . After this, end_tracking() should be called. experiment ( Experiment | type [ Experiment ] | ExperimentTracker ) – An Experiment instance or an Experiment class. In case of class, a new instance is created. observation_stash ( ObservationStash | None ) – The stash to save observations to instead of the DB. If not provided, the observations DB. ( will be saved to the ) A new instance of ExperimentTracker. The created class is determined be tracker_class . ExperimentTracker Get the captured data from an ExperimentTracker instance and store it to the context. This should be called after performing the desired run and analyze actions with the
tracker, so that the results and used arguments are stored. tracker ( ExperimentTracker ) – the instance to get data from. The AnalyzeResult captured by the tracker, if any. AnalyzeResult Bases: Exception Internal helper type for propagating analysis errors. Analysis error can happen: subsequence or experiment analysis in execute_sequence method inside sequence.execute . in sequence analysis in execute_sequence method. Bases: Exception Internal helper type for propagating child sequence execution errors to upper level context. Bases: Exception Internal helper type for propagating internal sequence execution errors to upper level context. description:

content:
Decorates make_params to drop guesses for parameters a hint holds fixed or ties with expr . lmfit.Model.make_params writes its keyword arguments into the parameters it has already built from
the hints, and lmfit.Parameter.set clears the expression of any parameter it is given a value for.
A guess for a parameter a hint holds fixed therefore moves it off the pinned value while leaving it
fixed, and a guess for a parameter a hint ties to another with expr cuts that tie altogether. What
a fit never moves on its own is the caller’s to set, so the guesses for both kinds are dropped here and
the hints stand. make_params ( Callable [ [ ... ] , Parameters ] ) – The model’s make_params method, wrapped so every guess it is given passes through
this filter first. A make_params that silently drops the guesses for parameters its hints already settle. title: exa.core.util.qubit_utils.simple_transmon_ge_frequency
description: Simplified model for transmon dispersion. The transmon dispersion can be derived from koch2007 by calculating \(E_1 - E_0\) using equation 2.11 and then substituting \(E_j\) with equation 2.18. To red...
content:
Simplified model for transmon dispersion. The transmon dispersion can be derived from koch2007 by calculating \(E_1 - E_0\) using equation 2.11 and then substituting \(E_j\) with equation 2.18. To reduce the number of unknown parameters, \(E_c\) is ignored here and assumed to
be accounted for by f_sweet_spot . This results in a slight inaccuracy in the model

content:
Save the result of a sequence to persistence. This function can be called repeatedly on the same sequence. Subsequent calls will update the data in the database.
Thus, for incremental saving, a sequence will call this function with updated results after each run. This function does not save the results of child sequences recursively. Before calling this function, metadata has to exist in persistence so that results can be linked.

content:
ESPRIT method. Estimate parameters assuming data is a sum of complex exponentials: \(\Sigma_n A_n \exp (2 \pi i f_n) + N\) where \(N\) is noise. \(n\) is estimated: by some AIC-based guess based on the RSS after denoising if eps is given: by truncating based on singular values

description: Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.models.double_exponential_decay_model Bases: BaseModel Lmfit model for double-exponential decay w. This model describes data that decays as the sum of two expon...
content:
Module: exa.core.model_selection_fitter.models.double_exponential_decay_model Bases: BaseModel Lmfit model for double-exponential decay w. This model describes data that decays as the sum of two exponential components The model function is: a1 : Initial guess 1.0 (no bounds). rate1 : Initial guess 2, lower bound 0.01, upper bound 5.0. a2 : Initial guess 0.1 (no bounds). rate2 : Initial guess 1.05, lower bound 0.01, upper bound 2.0. Initializes the DoubleExponentialDecay model. args – Passed to parent __init__. independent_vars ( list [ str ] | None ) – Independent variable names. kwargs ( Any ) – Passed to parent __init__. Attributes Methods guess Estimate initial parameters for double-exponential decay with offset. Estimate initial parameters for double-exponential decay with offset. For non-trivial data, it estimates the amplitude as the difference between the first and
last data points, and the offset as the last data point. If the amplitude is close to zero, it uses the range of the data as the amplitude and the
minimum value as the offset. The decay constant (tau) is estimated by finding the point where the data falls
to 1/e of its initial amplitude above the offsets. If the initial x is 0 the amplitude a1 is the first data point.
otherwise we set it to 1.0 If this estimation fails, a default value is used. The method ensures rate1 is positive
and not too small We set a2 to a1/10 and rate2 to rate1*10 data ( ndarray ) – Dependent variable data. x ( ndarray ) – Independent variable data. kws – Values for the model parameters. title: Portfolio Optimization
description: The purpose of this notebook is to showcase the QAOA library working from the problem definition all the way to execution on a real hardware. In particular, here we use QAOA to solve a particular inst...
content: The purpose of this notebook is to showcase the QAOA library working from the problem definition all the way to execution on a real hardware. In particular, here we use QAOA to solve a particular instance of portfolio optimization. First, we describe the problem: we have n_assets assets, each with an expected_return . The variable containing the covariances and variances is called cov_mat . The goal is to choose a set of assets which maximize the yield, while minimizing the covariance, weighted by the investor’s risk_aversion (the higher, the more likely the investor is to avoid risk). The budget says how many assets we can buy. Within the QAOA library, quadratic binary optimization problems are represented as objects of BinaryQuadraticModel or ConstrainedQuadraticModel from the dimod package ( read more about the models here ). In order to define a custom constrained problem in our QAOA library ( ConstrainedQuadraticInstance ), we need to create a custom object of ConstrainedQuadraticModel , by defining the objective and the constraint. The objective is the expected return minus the variance of the portfolio weighted by the risk aversion. The constraint has the identity matrix on the left-hand side (i.e., the number of selected assets) and the budget on the right-hand side. In the following, we set up the connection to Resonance and define a simulator backend of the Garnet QPU. Note: in general, you also need to specify the ‘usage mode’. For running on a real machine (in pay-as-you-go usage mode), the url would change to https://resonance.iqm.tech/garnet. For a specific timeslot the url would change to https://resonance.iqm.tech/garnet:timeslot Create the QUBO QAOA instance from the problem instance and train it. The train method has several possible parameters, but here the default setting is used (which uses analytical formulas since the QAOA has one layer). Sample for a solution from the QAOA and post-process the result (removing the samples violating the constraint). The sample method of my_qaoa typically expects a number of shots. By omitting this parameter, it defaults to 20 000, the default maximum number on Resonance. The format of the samples is a dictionary whose keys are bitstrings (the individual samples that were taken) and whose values are integers (the number of times each sample was taken). We may now examine the found solutions. previous Sparse Maxcut next Training the QAOA By IQM QAOA developers © Copyright 2021-2026, IQM. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Circuit Synthesis
description: The purpose of the notebook is to illustrate the circuit-synthesis tools available in the IQM QAOA Library (as of May 2026; likely to be moved elsewhere in the future). In this case, we are interestin...
content:
The purpose of the notebook is to illustrate the circuit-synthesis tools available in the IQM QAOA Library (as of May 2026; likely to be moved elsewhere in the future). In this case, we are interesting in synthesizing phase-polynomial quantum circuits. We consider a diagonal Hamiltonian $$
H = \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{i_1 < \cdots < i_k} c_{i_1 \cdots i_k} \prod_{m=1}^k Z_{i_m}
$$
and we time-evolve with respect to this Hamiltonian. That is, we want to implement the unitary:
$$
U(\varphi) = \text{e}^{-\text{i} \frac{\varphi}{2} H} = \prod_{k=1}^n \prod_{i_1 < \cdots < i_k} R_{Z_i \cdots Z_{i_k}} !\left( \varphi , c_{i_1 \cdots i_k}\right)
$$ The following two modules are completely independent from the rest of the IQM QAOA Library and therefore can be separated in the future into its own repository. Connect to Resonance and create Qiskit backend from it. Extract info from the Qiskit backend object (mostly QPU topology). The user has to manually specify a mapping between hardware qubits on the QPU (by convention labelled by integers starting from 0) and the variables of the problem (here labelled by letters “a”, “b”, “c”, “d”). There are two “regimes” of using the CircuitSynthesis class: Starting from a given higher-order Hamiltonian that we want to represent. Start by constructing a circuit (composed of CNOTs and RZs) and get a Hamiltonian from it. Start from a given higher-order Hamiltonian. Apply some CNOTs to the circuit synthesis object. Build the qiskit circuit, providing the bp object of interactions. Note three things: The dark blue identity gates are used to label which parities are assigned to which qubit. The build_qiskit method automatically adds RZ gates to where they are needed to represent the input Hamiltonian. The warning is raised because we provided a Hamiltonian, but didn’t execute all of its interactions. Now we do the opposite approach: We construct a circuit first and then “find out” what Hamiltonian it represents. This time we interleave the CNOT gates with RZ gates. Now we have two options: Examine what kind of Hamiltonian we represent by our circuit. title: Training the QAOA
description: In this notebook we showcase (and compare) various strategies of training the QAOA, that is finding the optimal values for the variational parameters (also known as QAOA angles ). We start by generati...
content: In this notebook we showcase (and compare) various strategies of training the QAOA, that is finding the optimal values for the variational parameters (also known as QAOA angles ). We start by generating a quasi-random instance of the maxcut problem (with 10 nodes). Generate a QAOA instance from the problem instance. We use the TreeQAOA class, which is identical to the QUBOQAOA class, but it contains one extra way to “train” the QAOA parameters. For training the QAOA, we will use various estimators . An estimator is a function (technically a class with a method) which takes a QAOA object and calculates/estimates the expectation value of the Hamiltonian. Similarly, a sampler takes a QAOA object and generates samples (measurement results) of possible solutions. Here we also set up a variable results to store the results of our experiments, for comparison. It’s a dictionary of dictionaries, keyed first by the training method and then by the QAOA number of layers. We start with EstimatorSingleLayer . For single-layer QAOA, the expectation values of 1- and 2-qubit operators can be calculated analytically. This estimator does the calculation. Next, we train using EstimatorStateVector . This estimator runs the statevector simulation of the QAOA circuit to calculate the expectation value of the Hamiltonian. Next, we train using EstimatorFromSampler together with SamplerSimulation . This estimator calls a given sampler and uses the obtained samples to estimate the expectation value (by calculating the energy of each of the samples and averaging them out). The SamplerSimulation runs the simulation of the QAOA circuit, including the measurements. Next, we again use EstimatorFromSampler together with SamplerSimulation . But this time we calculate not the expectation value , but the conditional value at risk at 0.1 level. We use this value in training the QAOA, possibly changing the performance. Next, we train using EstimatorFromSampler again, but this time together with SamplerResonance . This sampler actually runs the circuit via Resonance, IQM’s cloud quantum computing platform. WARNING When running training using this estimator, Resonance is used for every training cycle, potentially taking a lot of time (even when using a mock QC)! The if clause surrounding the cell makes sure that it’s skipped during testing (because it’s too slow). Now we “train” the angles by setting them to the Tree QAOA angles. The Tree QAOA angles are the optimal angles for problems on regular infinite random graphs, where the neighborhood of each node is a tree graph. These angles are pre-calculated for various values of graph regularity and parameters of the Hamiltonian. The method set_tree_angles looks at the parameters of our problem and sets the QAOA angles to the corresponding Tree QAOA angles. While these angles aren’t likely the most optimal angles for our problem, they are likely to produce good results and it allows us to skip conventional QAOA training completely. More reading on Tree QAOA For comparison we now repeat all of the above (except for EstimatorSingleLayer ) for QAOA with 2 layers and summarize the data in a table. We expect the Statevector , Simulated Samples and the Single Layer methods to perform the best (although none of them is scalable). Using CVaR instead of the mean gives better results, but this is expected, given that we’re looking at a tail of a distribution. Whether it actually helps in training the QAOA is not clear. We expect all methods to improve with increasing p . previous Portfolio Optimization next Circuit Synthesis By IQM QAOA developers © Copyright 2021-2026, IQM. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: SK Model and Transpilation
description: The purpose of this notebook is to showcase the QAOA library working from the problem definition all the way to execution on a real hardware. In particular, here we use QAOA to solve an instance of th...
content: The purpose of this notebook is to showcase the QAOA library working from the problem definition all the way to execution on a real hardware. In particular, here we use QAOA to solve an instance of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model, a very densely connected problem, to illustrate the advantage of using our custom transpiler over the Qiskit default transpiler. The SK model describes a number of binary variables, every pair of which interacts with a random interaction strength. We will solve a problem of size problem_size , i.e., this will be the number of binary variables and also the number of qubits that we use. The number of shots is set to default maximum on Resonance. We create an instance of the SK model of size problem_size . We specify the random distribution of the interactions between the variables to be “gaussian” (with mean 0 and variance 1). A few other distributions are possible (e.g., “uniform” or “rademacher”). We print out the largest, lowest and average energy of the model, calculated by brute-forcing over all possible bitstrings of length problem_size . This may be slow if problem_size has been set higher than ~30. In the following, we set up the connection to Resonance and define a simulator backend of the Garnet QPU. Note: in general, you also need to specify the ‘usage mode’. For running on a real machine (in pay-as-you-go usage mode), the url would change to https://resonance.iqm.tech/garnet. For a specific timeslot the url would change to https://resonance.iqm.tech/garnet:timeslot Create the QUBO QAOA instance from the problem instance, train it and then construct the QAOA circuits using 4 different methods: The perfect circuit without any transpilation. The circuit transpiled for IQM hardware, using Qiskit default transpilation function. The circuit transpiled for IQM hardware, using our custom transpiler. The circuit transpiled for IQM hardware, using the swap network strategy. The train method has several possible parameters, but here the default setting is used (which uses analytical formulas since the QAOA has one layer). Run the perfect circuit on perfect (noiseless simulator), print out the average energy of the samples. Run the Qiskit-transpiled circuit on our hardware, print out the average energy of the samples and the number of gates used. Run the custom-transpiled circuit on our hardware, print out the average energy of the samples and the number of gates used. Run the swap-network-transpiled circuit on our hardware, print out the average energy of the samples and the number of gates used. If everything went as expected, the hardwired transpiler and the swap network transpiler should perform better than the qiskit default transpiler. The hardwired transpiler minimizes the number of 2QB gates used whereas the swap network transpiler minimizes the overall depth of the circuit. Based on the average energy obtained with the two approaches, we can judge which is better for our hardware (and this particular problem size). previous Usage Examples next Sparse Maxcut By IQM QAOA developers © Copyright 2021-2026, IQM. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Sparse Maxcut
description: The purpose of this notebook is to showcase the QAOA library working from the problem definition all the way to execution on a real hardware. In particular, here we use QAOA to solve an instance of a ...
content:
The purpose of this notebook is to showcase the QAOA library working from the problem definition all the way to execution on a real hardware. In particular, here we use QAOA to solve an instance of a random sparsely-connected max-cut problem. Maxcut is a graph problem, but internally the QAOA library converts it to a quadratic binary optimization problem (QUBO). We will solve a problem of size problem_size , i.e., this will be the size of the graph, the number of binary variables and also the number of qubits that we use. The number of shots is set to default maximum on Resonance. We create an instance of the max-cut problem of size problem_size , on a 3-regular random graph.
We print out the largest, lowest and average energy of the model, calculated by brute-forcing over all possible bitstrings of length problem_size . This may be slow if problem_size has been set higher than ~30. In the following, we set up the connection to Resonance and define a simulator backend of the Garnet and Sirius QPUs. We will run the QAOA on both and compare the results. Note: in general, you also need to specify the ‘usage mode’. For running on a real machine (in pay-as-you-go usage mode), the url would change to https://resonance.iqm.tech/garnet. For a specific timeslot the url would change to https://resonance.iqm.tech/garnet:timeslot Create the QUBO QAOA instance from the problem instance and train it. The train method has several possible parameters, but here the default setting is used (which uses analytical formulas since the QAOA has one layer). Once the QAOA is trained, we can use the QPU to sample from it and to use the samples for estimating the expected value of the Hamiltonian. For that we need to define a sampler and an estimator . There are several other samplers and estimators available in the QAOA library. Here we use the sampler which samples from a given QPU (via Resonance) and the estimator which uses this sampler to provide samples from which the expected value of the Hamiltonian is calculated. We don’t need the samples here for anything, so we’ll discard them. Same as the above, except on the star QPU. Running circuits on the star uses fewer 2QB gates, but requires considerably larger circuit depth (because only one 2QB gate can be done at a time). previous SK Model and Transpilation next Portfolio Optimization By IQM QAOA developers © Copyright 2021-2026, IQM. title: goemans_williamson
description: Runs the Goemans-Williamson algorithm for maxcut, returning a solution bitstring. The Goemans-Williamson is a randomized algorithm for maxcut, with a guaranteed approximation ratio of around 0.87856 ....
content:
Runs the Goemans-Williamson algorithm for maxcut, returning a solution bitstring. The Goemans-Williamson is a randomized algorithm for maxcut, with a guaranteed approximation ratio of around 0.87856 . The algorithm was first described in [ 1 ] . Steps: Relax the problem to a semidefinite program (SDP) with each variable represented by a multi-dimensional vector
on a unit sphere. Solve the SDP. Generate a random hyperplane through the origin. Assign the variables to 0 or 1 based on which side of the plane their multi-dimensional vector lies. max_cut_problem ( MaxCutInstance ) – A problem instance of maxcut to be solved (approximately). seed ( int | None ) – An optional seed to fix the rotation of the random hyperplane. A bitstring solution. str previous maxcut next greedy_max_cut By IQM QAOA developers © Copyright 2021-2026, IQM. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

Module: iqm.qaoa.tree_qaoa Bases: QUBOQAOA The class for tree QAOA with QUBO cost function. The class inherits everything from QUBOQAOA , but adds one more method set_tree_angles() , which sets angles according to the tree schedule.
The tree schedule uses QAOA angles precalculated numerically for a class of high-girth regular graph problems with
uniform Hamiltonian. For more details see [ 8 ] . problem ( QUBOInstance | ConstrainedQuadraticInstance ) – A QUBOInstance object describing the QUBO problem to be solved. num_layers ( int ) – The number of QAOA layers, commonly referred to as p in the literature. betas ( Sequence [ float ] | np.ndarray | None ) – An optional list of the initial beta angles of QAOA. Has to be provided together with gammas . gammas ( Sequence [ float ] | np.ndarray | None ) – An optional list of the initial gamma angles of QAOA. Has to be provided together with betas . initial_angles ( Sequence [ float ] | np.ndarray | None ) – An optional list of the initial QAOA angles as one variable. Shouldn’t be provided together
with either betas or gammas . Attributes Methods set_tree_angles A method for setting iqm.qaoa.generic_qaoa.QAOA.angles according to the tree schedule. A method for setting iqm.qaoa.generic_qaoa.QAOA.angles according to the tree schedule. The tree schedule is designed for problems with uniform 1-body local field, unit 2-body interactions and
uniform node degree. Therefore, when given a generic problem, the algorithm first calculates the average
degree d_av , the average local field h_av and the average interaction strength j_av (which is used
to renormalize the local field). The angles are then looked up in the saved files for the nearest implemented
degree and local field. For \(p > 6\) QAOA, the angles are interpolated from the calculated angles for \(p = 6\) . The method doesn’t output anything, but it modifies iqm.qaoa.generic_qaoa.QAOA.angles in-place. verbose ( bool ) – Should the method print out informative text about what it did?
