title: Clifford data regression
description: Clifford data regression (CDR) runs a set of training circuits with the same structure as the target circuit but made of Clifford gates, so their noiseless values are computed exactly and cheaply. A l...
content: Clifford data regression (CDR) runs a set of training circuits with the same structure as the target circuit but made of Clifford gates, so their noiseless values are computed exactly and cheaply. A line fitted from the measured to the exact values of the training circuits is then applied to the measured value of the target. ErrorReductionWorkflow runs in four steps, plan , submit , collect and estimate , and each step stores its result on the workflow. The workflow can be saved after any step and reloaded in a later session. See the IQM Resonance documentation for how to connect. The workflow submits the circuits through the backend’s client. Two 6-qubit GHZ circuits with a small RX rotation on every qubit, differing in the angle, so neither is Clifford. The observable is the ring of nearest-neighbour ZZ terms, H = Z0 Z1 + Z1 Z2 + ... + Z5 Z0 . Pauli labels are little-endian: the rightmost character is classical bit 0. CDR decides which circuits run on the QPU: the number of training circuits, and how they are chosen ( strategy ); the shots of the target circuit and of each training circuit; the twirling instances of the target and of each training circuit. A budget left unset in CDR comes from the workflow ( shots ) or the twirling configuration ( num_twirling_instances ). A budget set in CDR wins, with a warning if you also gave a different value to the workflow or the twirling configuration. CDREstimation , given later to estimate , is free to change: whether to fit each Pauli term separately ( combine="per_term" ) or the whole observable ( combine="group" ). plan is free and shows the cost before anything runs. The target and the training circuits use different shots per circuit, so they become separate jobs. submit sends every job to the QPU and returns once they are queued. collect waits for the jobs and keeps the counts. Save the workflow to keep them. Estimation makes no use of the quantum computer, so try different settings freely. A later session starts by loading the saved workflow. Plotting the fit shows how well the training circuits constrain the line, and whether the target lies inside their range. previous Zero-noise extrapolation next API Reference By IQM Error Reduction Tools developers © Copyright 2024-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 0.4.0. title: Readout error mitigation and circuit randomization
description: Readout error mitigation and circuit randomization are techniques with a wide scope. They directly improve the bitstring distribution obtained from a circuit run and they can thus be used both for sam...
content:
Readout error mitigation and circuit randomization are techniques with a wide scope. They directly improve the bitstring distribution obtained from a circuit run and they can thus be used both for sampling problems, i.e. problems where the bitstring distribution is what matters, and for observable problems, i.e. scenarios where the expectations values of observables (typically Paulis) are the quantities of interest. As the name suggests, readout error mitigation reduces the impact of errors happening when qubits are measured at the end of a computation. As for circuit randomization, the main targets are coherent errors (like systematic over or under rotations), which are transformed into less detrimental and easier to handle stochastic errors. This is what, more generally, circuit twirling does. Our approach can be seen as a specific limit of twirling (hence the naming spanning from twirling to circuit randomization). These two techniques can be run in isolation or together. Importantly, they can be also combined with other error mitigation techniques (such as ZNE and CDR) as shown in other dedicated tutorials. This notebook, which runs on hardware, covers: Implementation of twirling alone Implementation of REM alone Implementation of REM and twirling together Advantages in specifying which expectation values the user cares about, when using REM. Asynchronous execution, and reusing a characterization you already paid for Edit this cell: use your own token to connect to the desired quantum computer. In this tutorial, we consider two simple circuits. They’re chosen to specifically highlight the features and advantages associated with circuit randomization and REM. "rotations" : One layer of random single-qubit rotations, no two-qubit gates. The outcome is dominated by SPAM errors, so it’s a great testbed for REM. It is less indicative for the performance of circuit randomization. "ghz" : an entangled GHZ chain. Two-qubit gates and real correlations, so circuit
randomization matters more and the four-way comparison in section 3 becomes meaningful. Feel free to pick one by specifying the CIRCUIT below and re-run from there. Both are simple, and both have a classically computable exact distribution – which is the
only reason we can say whether mitigation helped rather than just changed the numbers. Let’s create and transpile the chosen circuit. A circuit gets randomized into several equivalent variants, whose counts are then summed. It reshapes the noise so that what is left is closer
to a simple stochastic error, which is less detrimental and easier to handle (e.g. by other error mitigation techniques like ZNE that’ll sit on top). Circuit randomization is performed by the CircuitTwirler class, according to the specifications listed in a TwirlingConfiguration object. The latter allows us to specify which kind of randomization we want to perform. We can do that by specifying three parameters: readout_twirl_strategy: Literal["LOCAL", "MINIMAL", "HADAMARD", "NONE"] = "LOCAL" circuit_twirling: bool = True num_twirling_instances: int = 20 The first choice we face is which part of the circuit we want to randomize. We have four options: No randomization, the trivial one. Obtained with circuit_twirling=False and readout_twirl_strategy = "NONE" . Measurement twirling: Randomization only of the last single-qubit gates per qubit before the final measurements. This requires classically undoing such randomizations with classical bitflips applied in post-processing on the measured bistrings (automatically handled by the library). Obtained with circuit_twirling=False and readout_twirl_strategy different from "NONE" . Whole circuit randomization ( Recommended ): All single qubit gates in the circuit are randomized (which might still require adding classical bitflips on the measured bitstrings). Obtained with circuit_twirling=True and readout_twirl_strategy different from "NONE" . Circuit randomization without measurement twirling: All single qubit gates are randomized with the constraint that no measurement twirling is performed (so no classical bitflips need to be applied). Obtained with circuit_twirling=True and readout_twirl_strategy = "NONE" . Then we need to decide how many randomizations to perform. If we want to perform measurement twirling (i.e. readout_twirl_strategy different from "NONE" ), we have three choices: strategy number of randomizations what it does "MINIMAL" 2 two flip patterns: all-identity and all-flip "LOCAL" 4 all possible twirling combinations for all neighbour qubits "HADAMARD" up to twice the number of qubits a Hadamard-matrix set of patterns, the most thorough As for the randomization of gates in the bulk of the circuit, we can simply specify an integer num_twirling_instances . Note that, when we randomize the whole circuit, the total number of randomizations is chosen to be the multiple of the randomizations needed by readout twirling that is closest to the specified num_twirling_instances . NOTE : Regardless of the type of desired randomization, the total shot budget is divided among the random instances. So randomization comes with no extra shots. Only the number of submitted circuits increases. In general REM does not need twirling. It works by Characterizing the measurement errors (running a small job on the QPU) Post-processing the raw counts according to the characterization to produce mitigated counts. For the sake of clarity, in this Section, we simply perform REM without any circuit randomization, although this is not the recommended approach. Note that mitigated_distributions holds quasi-probabilities and it can thus feature small negative entries. nearest_probability=True (the default)
projects them back to a genuine distribution. This is the intended combination, as readout twirling symmetrizes the readout errors and kills most of the spatial correlations. As discussed in Section 1, we’ll then use a readout_twirl_strategy different from "NONE" . We are free to choose whether we want to
also randomize other single-qubit gates in the rest of the circuit or not by playing with the boolean parameter circuit_twirling . We can also tweak parameters of the readout error characterization, by passing a custom RECConfiguration object. Here’s a summary of the results obtained so far. If what you want is a Pauli observable (or a set of Pauli observables) it is convenient to pass observables= and the workflow computes the
expectation values from the mitigated distribution for you. This is not just a convenience function but it affects the REM post-processing.
If the observables one is interested in have low weight, explicitly passing them results in More precise mitigated results Possibly faster post-processing time (if the qubit number is large and the raw bitstring distribution has a large entropy) If what you want is the distribution – sampling, a histogram, a total variation
distance – take mitigated_distributions directly and skip observables entirely. That is
what sections 2 and 3 did. run() blocks. submit() returns as soon as the jobs are queued, which is what you want if
the QPU has a queue and you would rather not hold the kernel open. The workflow itself can be saved and reloaded, so “later” can mean a different kernel/computer/process. The readout error characterization is quick but still requires QPU time. To speed up the execution of experiments, it can be useful to save it once and reuse it for subsequent circuit runs. A characterization is only valid for the qubits it measured and only as long as the
device has not drifted. Reuse it across a session, not across a recalibration. previous Examples next Zero-noise extrapolation By IQM Error Reduction Tools developers © Copyright 2024-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 0.4.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Zero-noise extrapolation
description: ZNE runs copies of your circuit with more noise than the original, then extrapolates the measured values back to the zero-noise limit. Noise is amplified by global folding: U becomes U(U†U)^s , so eve...
content: ZNE runs copies of your circuit with more noise than the original, then extrapolates the measured values back to the zero-noise limit. Noise is amplified by global folding: U becomes U(U†U)^s , so every gate runs 1 + 2s times. You choose the noise factors 1 + 2s , which are odd integers starting at 1. An observable is a weighted sum of Pauli terms, and ZNE fits each Pauli term on its own. ErrorReductionWorkflow runs in four steps, plan , submit , collect and estimate , and each step stores its result on the workflow. The workflow can be saved after any step and reloaded in a later session. See the IQM Resonance documentation for how to connect. The workflow submits the circuits through the backend’s client. Two 4-qubit GHZ circuits with a small RX rotation per qubit, differing in the angle, so neither is Clifford. We measure ZZZZ and ZZII + 0.75 ZIZI . That is three Pauli terms, so three fits per circuit. Pauli labels are little-endian: the rightmost character is classical bit 0. ZNE decides which circuits run on the QPU and cannot change once they are submitted. ZNEEstimation , given later to estimate , is everything you can redo for free once the data exists. Costs QPU time (fixed once the circuits are submitted) parameter options default ZNE.noise_factors odd integers in increasing order, starting at 1 (1, 3, 5) shots total shots of each noise factor, split over its twirling instances 20_000 twirling_configuration.readout_twirl_strategy "LOCAL" , "MINIMAL" , "HADAMARD" , "NONE" "LOCAL" twirling_configuration.circuit_twirling True , False True twirling_configuration.num_twirling_instances any positive int 20 twirling_configuration None executes every circuit once, without twirling  rec_configuration.num_circuits , rec_configuration.shots size of the readout characterization job; rec_configuration=None skips it 50 , 10_000 Free to redo ( ZNEEstimation and the options of estimate , no QPU involved) parameter options default extrapolation_type "Poly" , "Exp" "Poly" degree any int up to one less than the number of fitted points, for "Poly" only None , i.e. Richardson noise_factors any two or more of the executed noise factors, or None for all of them None apply_rem True , False , or None to mitigate whenever readout errors were characterized None bootstrap_samples 0 for no uncertainties, or the number of resamples of the counts 0 plan is free and shows what will run. submit returns once the jobs are queued. collect waits for them and keeps the counts, which is the expensive data. Save the workflow to keep them. Everything below needs no quantum computer, so a later session starts here. Uncertainties come from resampling the measured counts and repeating the whole estimation, so leave bootstrap_samples at 0 while you are still choosing a fit. One panel per Pauli term, which is what was fitted. ideal adds the noiseless reference to each panel. a polynomial of the given degree ; degree=None is Richardson extrapolation, the polynomial through every fitted point; extrapolation_type="Exp" fits a * exp(b * x) . The circuits are already executed, so which of them to fit through is free to change. noise_factors= selects from the executed noise factors, and None fits all of them. A noise factor that was not executed is refused. previous Readout error mitigation and circuit randomization next Clifford data regression By IQM Error Reduction Tools developers © Copyright 2024-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 0.4.0. title: iqm.error_reduction_tools.readout_characterization.visualization.visualize_time_stability
description:
Visualize temporal stability of readout characterization data across multiple runs. Creates a two-panel visualization to assess the temporal stability of readout
measurements. The first panel shows th...
content:
Visualize temporal stability of readout characterization data across multiple runs. Creates a two-panel visualization to assess the temporal stability of readout
measurements. The first panel shows the distribution of measurements across
qubits with violin plots, individual data points, and error bars representing pure
statistical uncertainty. The second panel displays the ratio of total standard
deviation to shot-noise standard deviation for each qubit. data ( ndarray ) – 2D array of shape ( num_runs , num_qubits ) containing measurement data
from multiple characterization runs. std_shots ( ndarray ) – Array of shot-noise standard deviations for each qubit, representing
pure statistical uncertainty expected from finite sampling. threshold_err ( float ) – Threshold value for acceptable error level, displayed as a
horizontal line in the first panel. Default is 0.1 (10%). threshold_ratio ( float ) – Threshold value for the ratio of standard deviations, displayed
as a horizontal line in the second panel. Default is 3. upper_y_label ( str | None ) – Label for the y-axis of the first panel. If None , no label is set. None . Displays a matplotlib figure with two subplots. None Note The first panel shows violin plots with overlaid scatter points (with jitter)
and error bars representing shot-noise limited uncertainty. The second panel uses a logarithmic y-scale to show the ratio of total
standard deviation to shot-noise standard deviation. A ratio near 1 indicates
that the measurement is shot-noise limited, while higher ratios suggest
additional sources of variability (e.g., temporal drift). Horizontal reference lines at y=1 and y=threshold_ratio help identify qubits
with excessive time-dependent variability. previous iqm.error_reduction_tools.readout_characterization.visualization.visualize_state_dep_matrix next iqm.error_reduction_tools.rem By IQM Error Reduction Tools developers © Copyright 2024-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 0.4.0. content:
Visualize readout error correlations overlaid on QPU topology. Creates a network graph showing qubits positioned according to their physical
layout, with directed edges representing correlation strength and sign.
Qubits are colored by readout line grouping. correlation_matrix ( ndarray ) – NxN array of correlation coefficients. Element [i,j]
represents correlation from qubit i to qubit j. topology ( QPUTopology ) – QPUTopology defining qubit positions and readout lines.
Use topology_from_qc() to obtain a fully-populated instance from a connected quantum computer. thresholds ( tuple [ float , float ] | None ) – Optional (upper, lower) thresholds for edge filtering.
Only correlations ≥upper or ≤lower are displayed.
If None , all edges are shown. vmax ( float | None ) – Colormap saturation value. Correlations are mapped to
[-vmax, +vmax] range (red=negative, blue=positive). qubit_labels ( list [ str ] | None ) – List of qubit labels corresponding to the correlation matrix rows/columns.
If None , assumes matrix represents all topology qubits in order.
Can be a subset to visualize only specific qubits (unlisted qubits appear faded). title ( str | tuple [ int , str ] ) – Plot title. String or tuple (error_id, title_string). edge_curvature ( float ) – Curvature radius for edges (0=straight, 0.2=default curve). show_plot ( bool ) – If True , displays plot and returns None . If False , returns Figure . Matplotlib figure if show_plot=False , otherwise None . Figure | None Note Arrows point from dimension 1 to dimension 2 of correlation_matrix.
E.g., arrow QB0→QB1 shows correlation_matrix[QB0_idx, QB1_idx] . previous iqm.error_reduction_tools.readout_characterization.visualization.plot_error_probabilities next iqm.error_reduction_tools.readout_characterization.visualization.visualize_state_dep_matrix By IQM Error Reduction Tools developers © Copyright 2024-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 0.4.0. title: iqm.error_reduction_tools.rem.rem_processors.ReadoutErrorMitigation
description:
Bases: object Apply readout error mitigation to measurement counts, with optional twirling support. This class performs tensor-product inversion of readout confusion matrices
to correct measurement er...
content:
Bases: object Apply readout error mitigation to measurement counts, with optional twirling support. This class performs tensor-product inversion of readout confusion matrices
to correct measurement errors. Supports both standard and symmetrized
(twirled) characterization data. Methods _mitigate (counts, cl_index_to_qubit_name[, ...]) Apply readout error mitigation to the given counts. _normalize_observables (observables, ...) Normalize observables to the canonical qubit-name list format. _symmetrize_copy (charact_data) Return a symmetrized copy of characterization data without modifying the original. _validate_charact_data () Validate the characterization data format. _validate_counts_and_mapping (counts, ...) Validate the counts format and qubit mapping. _warn_high_error_rates (charact_data) Emit warnings for qubits whose readout error rate is >= 20%. from_client (client[, qubits, ...]) Create ReadoutErrorMitigation by running characterization on a quantum computer. get_calibration_data () Get the calibration data for all qubits. mitigate_counts (experiment_counts, ...[, ...]) Mitigate a list of measurement count dictionaries for one or more observables. symmetrize_charact_data () Symmetrize the characterization data by averaging error rates. readout_errors ( dict [ str , AssignmentMatrix ] | dict [ str , float ] ) max_entropy ( float ) Create ReadoutErrorMitigation by running characterization on a quantum computer. Runs the full characterization workflow on the quantum computer and then
returns an initialized ReadoutErrorMitigation instance. client ( IQMClient ) – Client for connecting to an IQM quantum computer. qubits ( list [ str ] | None ) – List of qubit names to characterize (e.g., [“QB1”, “QB2”]). If None,
characterizes all qubits available on the client. number_of_circuits ( int ) – Number of calibration circuits to generate. shots ( int ) – Total shots for characterization, distributed across all circuits. symmetrize ( bool ) – If True, generates complementary I/X preparation pairs. seed ( int | None ) – Random seed for reproducible characterization. equatorial_randomization ( bool ) – If True, randomizes X gate phases. max_entropy ( float ) – Maximum allowed Shannon entropy (in bits) threshold. ReadoutErrorMitigation instance with characterization data. ReadoutErrorMitigation Example Get the calibration data for all qubits. Dictionary mapping qubit names to their calibration matrices (2x2 numpy arrays). dict [ str , ndarray ] Symmetrize the characterization data by averaging error rates. Converts matrices to symmetrized scalar error rates by averaging P(0|1) and P(1|0).
If data is already scalar, this method has no effect. None Mitigate a list of measurement count dictionaries for one or more observables. Bitstrings and bit indices follow little-endian (Qiskit) convention:
bit index 0 is the rightmost character of the bitstring. experiment_counts ( list [ SampledDistribution ] ) – Measurement count dictionaries.
Each dict maps bitstrings (e.g., "0101" ) to shot counts.
Bitstrings follow little-endian convention
(rightmost character = bit index 0). qubit_to_bit_mapping ( dict [ str , int ] | TwirledCircuit | list [ TwirledCircuit ] ) – A property of the transpiled circuit: it maps every measured
qubit name to its classical bit index and is fixed once the circuit has been run. Accepts multiple formats (auto-detected): dict (canonical): {"QB5": 0, "QB12": 1, "QB3": 2, "QB7": 3} TwirledCircuit : extracts the mapping from its measurement keys list[TwirledCircuit] : extracts from the first circuit A property of the transpiled circuit: it maps every measured
qubit name to its classical bit index and is fixed once the circuit has been run. Accepts multiple formats (auto-detected): dict (canonical): {"QB5": 0, "QB12": 1, "QB3": 2, "QB7": 3} TwirledCircuit : extracts the mapping from its measurement keys list[TwirledCircuit] : extracts from the first circuit observables ( list [ list [ str ] | str | list [ int ] ] | None ) – Observables to mitigate and compute ZZ…Z expectation values for. observables is a list of qubit-name subsets; for
each subset the raw counts are first marginalized to the corresponding bit indices
(looked up from qubit_to_bit_mapping ), then readout-error-mitigated, and finally a
ZZ…Z expectation value is computed. Supports three formats per element (auto-detected): Qubit names (current): [["QB3", "QB5"], ["QB1"]] Pauli strings (Z/I only): ["IIIZZIZI", "ZIIIIIIII"] Bit indices : [[2, 4], [0]] If None , a single observable covering all qubits
in qubit_to_bit_mapping is used.  Formats can be mixed
within a single call. Observables to mitigate and compute ZZ…Z expectation values for. observables is a list of qubit-name subsets; for
each subset the raw counts are first marginalized to the corresponding bit indices
(looked up from qubit_to_bit_mapping ), then readout-error-mitigated, and finally a
ZZ…Z expectation value is computed. Supports three formats per element (auto-detected): Qubit names (current): [["QB3", "QB5"], ["QB1"]] Pauli strings (Z/I only): ["IIIZZIZI", "ZIIIIIIII"] Bit indices : [[2, 4], [0]] If None , a single observable covering all qubits
in qubit_to_bit_mapping is used.  Formats can be mixed
within a single call. twirled ( bool ) – If True , symmetrize the characterization data before mitigation
by averaging P(0|1) and P(1|0) into a single error rate per qubit.
This is appropriate when the counts were obtained using readout
twirling.  The original charact_data on the instance is not modified; a temporary symmetrized copy is used.  Default is False . force_mitigation ( bool ) – If True, apply mitigation even if complexity exceeds threshold. nearest_probability ( bool ) – If True, project each quasi-probability distribution onto the
nearest valid probability distribution using mthree ’s nearest_probability_distribution method. Eliminates negative values
at the cost of a small bias. Default is True. client ( IQMClient | None ) – Optional client for automatic characterization of missing qubits on the quantum computer. auto_characterize_shots ( int ) – Shots to use when auto-characterizing (default: 10000). auto_characterize_circuits ( int ) – Number of circuits for auto-characterization (default: 20). "mitigated_counts" : list[list[dict[str, float]]] — result["mitigated_counts"][i][j] is the mitigated quasi-probability
distribution for circuit i under observable j . "expectation_values" : list[list[float]] — result["expectation_values"][i][j] is the ZZ…Z expectation value
for circuit i under observable j . "characterization_performed" : bool — True if auto-characterization ran. "mitigated_counts" : list[list[dict[str, float]]] — result["mitigated_counts"][i][j] is the mitigated quasi-probability
distribution for circuit i under observable j . "expectation_values" : list[list[float]] — result["expectation_values"][i][j] is the ZZ…Z expectation value
for circuit i under observable j . "characterization_performed" : bool — True if auto-characterization ran. Dictionary containing ValueError – If experiment_counts or qubit_to_bit_mapping are empty, if any
    observable qubit is not in qubit_to_bit_mapping , or characterization
    data is missing and no client is provided. title: iqm.error_reduction_tools.workflow.ErrorReductionWorkflow
description: Bases: object Workflow to estimate observables of target circuits with an error reduction technique. The four stages are separate methods, and each stores its output on the workflow: plan() sets execu...
content:
Bases: object Workflow to estimate observables of target circuits with an error reduction technique. The four stages are separate methods, and each stores its output on the workflow: plan() sets execution_plan , submit() sets submission , collect() sets counts , and estimate() sets result . run() does all four in one call. submit() and collect() use the quantum computer. plan() and estimate() do not,
and can be repeated with other settings. save() and load() can be used after the collection and before the estimation, respectively,
to store and retrieve the workflow state from a file. targets ( Sequence [ object ] ) – Circuits whose observables are estimated, transpiled to the native gate set and the physical qubits
of the quantum computer: iqm.pulse.Circuit , qiskit or Qrisp circuits, or anything else canonicalize_circuit() accepts. They are converted
to iqm.pulse.Circuit . observables ( ObservableLike | Sequence [ ObservableLike ] ) – One observable or a sequence of observables, each a sum of I/Z Pauli terms, applied to every
target. See build() . technique ( Technique ) – The error reduction technique, e.g. ZNE or CDR . client ( IQMClient ) – Client connected to the IQM quantum computer the circuits run on. compilation_options ( dict [ str , Any ] | None ) – Extra entries for the compiler context, e.g. a dynamical decoupling strategy. The
readout calibration job is compiled without them. twirling_configuration ( TwirlingConfiguration | None ) – Twirling configuration, or None to execute every variant once as it is. rec_configuration ( RECConfiguration | Mapping [ str , np.ndarray ] | None ) – Readout error characterization configuration, or None for no readout error
mitigation. Readout assignment matrices of an earlier characterization, e.g. the readout_errors of another workflow, are used instead of a new calibration job. shots ( int | None ) – Total shots of each variant, split over its twirling instances. None uses 20 000. A technique can
set its own shots for some variants, which override these with a warning. backend ( IQMBackendBase | None ) – IQM Qiskit backend the targets were transpiled for, used to name the qubits of qiskit and Qrisp
targets. None names qubit i QB{i + 1} . TypeError – If a target is of an unsupported type. ValueError – If the reused readout assignment matrices do not cover every measured qubit. Attributes circuits Return the circuit of every twirling instance, nested by target, variant and instance. Methods _check_estimate_arguments (estimation, ...) Reject estimate() arguments that would fail, before any circuits run. _estimate_once (plan, counts, estimation, ...) Compute the term values of every variant and the estimate of every target from one set of counts. _require_executor () Return the executor, or explain that the stage needs one. _setup (targets, observables, technique, *, ...) Validate the inputs and set the initial state. collect () Wait for every job and store the counts of every twirling instance. estimate (estimation, *[, apply_rem, ...]) Estimate the observables of every target from the collected counts. load (path[, client, compilation_options]) Read a workflow written by save() . plan () Build the variants of every target, twirl them and group them into jobs. run (estimation, *[, apply_rem, ...]) Run every remaining stage, from planning to estimation, and wait for the quantum computer. save (path) Write the configuration, plan, submission, counts and readout errors to a JSON file. submit () Submit every job of the plan, planning first if needed. Build the variants of every target, twirl them and group them into jobs. The plan, also stored as execution_plan . RuntimeError – If the workflow has already been submitted. ValueError – If the executor cannot run twirled circuits, or the "LOCAL" strategy has no topology. ExecutionPlan Return the circuit of every twirling instance, nested by target, variant and instance. circuits[i][j][k] is twirling instance k of variant j of target i . The readout calibration
circuits belong to no target and are not included, see execution_plan . RuntimeError – If the workflow has not been planned. Submit every job of the plan, planning first if needed. The submission, also stored as submission . RuntimeError – If the workflow was loaded without a client, or has already been submitted. Submission Wait for every job and store the counts of every twirling instance. The counts, also stored as counts . RuntimeError – If the workflow was loaded without a client, has not been submitted, or the client is
    connected to another quantum computer than the one the jobs were submitted to. dict [ CircuitKey , dict [ str , int ]] Estimate the observables of every target from the collected counts. estimation ( Estimation ) – Post-processing settings of the technique, e.g. ZNEEstimation . apply_rem ( bool | None ) – Whether to mitigate readout errors. None mitigates them when they were characterized. bootstrap_samples ( int ) – Number of bootstrap samples for the standard deviations, 0 for none. Each sample
resamples the counts of every instance and repeats the whole estimation. bootstrap_seed ( int | None ) – Seed of the resampling. The estimate, also stored as result . RuntimeError – If no counts have been collected. ValueError – If the estimation does not match the technique, readout errors are to be mitigated but were
    not characterized, or bootstrap_samples is 1. EstimationResult Run every remaining stage, from planning to estimation, and wait for the quantum computer. Stages that have already run are not repeated, so a loaded or partly run workflow continues where it
stopped. The arguments are checked before anything is submitted. estimation ( Estimation ) – Post-processing settings of the technique, e.g. ZNEEstimation . apply_rem ( bool | None ) – Passed to estimate() . bootstrap_samples ( int ) – Passed to estimate() . bootstrap_seed ( int | None ) – Passed to estimate() . The estimate, also stored as result . ValueError – If an argument is invalid, see estimate() . EstimationResult Write the configuration, plan, submission, counts and readout errors to a JSON file. path ( str | Path ) – Destination file. None Read a workflow written by save() . path ( str | Path ) – The file. client ( IQMClient | None ) – Client connected to the quantum computer, needed to plan, submit or collect. None is enough to
estimate from saved counts. compilation_options ( dict [ str , Any ] | None ) – Extra entries for the compiler context, e.g. a dynamical decoupling strategy. The workflow, in the stage it was saved in. Any other sequence is a sequence

content:
Process an R gate: absorb pending operations, then optionally insert a twirling π rotation. First delegates to take_care_of_pending_operations to commute any accumulated
Z and π rotations into the gate parameters. Then, with probability twirling_prob (possibly adjusted by parity or readout twirling constraints),
inserts a new π rotation via insert_twirling_pi_rotation . Finally appends
the resulting PRX gate to the twirled circuit. operation ( CircuitOperation ) – The PRX CircuitOperation to process. twirled_circuit ( TwirledCircuit ) – The new circuit being built. rgen ( Generator ) – Random number generator for twirling decisions. registers ( TrackingRegisters ) – Tracking registers for Z, π-rotation state, etc. enforce_readout_twirling_basis ( str | None ) – If set (‘X’ or ‘I’), overrides twirling_prob
to enforce a specific readout twirling outcome on the last SQG. twirling_prob ( float ) – Probability of inserting a twirling π rotation. Defaults to 0.5. fix_axes ( bool ) – If True, the twirling π rotation axis is fixed to match the gate’s
phase rather than being uniformly random. Defaults to False. content:

title: iqm.error_reduction_tools.twirling.twirling_modifiers
description:
Module for Poor Man’s Pauli Twirling (PMPT) and circuit manipulation utilities. This module provides functions and classes for randomizing quantum circuits using
PMPT and readout twirling techniques, ...
content:
Module for Poor Man’s Pauli Twirling (PMPT) and circuit manipulation utilities. This module provides functions and classes for randomizing quantum circuits using
PMPT and readout twirling techniques, as well as helpers for circuit analysis and
gate manipulation. It is designed to work with Qiskit circuits transpiled to a
restricted gate set (typically R and CZ gates), and supports readout twirling,
Z rotation tracking, and logical equivalence checks. The main entry point is randomize_circuit , which returns a randomized circuit logically equivalent to
the input (considering readout twirling and suppression of Z rotations before measurement). Functions absorb_pending_pi_rotation (registers, qubit, ...) Absorb a pending π rotation (from the left) into the current R gate. insert_twirling_pi_rotation (registers, ...) Insert a new π rotation (to the right) after the current R gate for twirling. process_cz_gate (operation, new_circuit, ...) Process a CZ gate: propagate pending π-rotation parity as Z kicks. process_measure_gate (operation, new_circuit, ...) Process a measurement gate: record readout twirling character and append. process_r_gate (operation, twirled_circuit, ...) Process an R gate: absorb pending operations, then optionally insert a twirling π rotation. randomize_circuit (circuit, rgen[, ...]) Randomize a quantum circuit using Poor Man's Pauli Twirling (PMPT). take_care_of_pending_operations (registers, ...) Process pending Z and π-rotation operations before the current R gate. Classes TrackingRegisters ([virtual_z, extra_phi, ...]) Container for tracking registers during circuit randomization. decoupling.  For example: compilation_options = { "DDStrategy" : my_dd_strategy } Extra key-value pairs passed to the IQM

content:
Perform global folding directly on an IQM Pulse circuit. Implements the map U -> U (U^dagger U)^s on the native IQM Pulse representation, so every
gate is executed 1 + 2s times. The circuit must already be transpiled to the IQM native gate set, with every qubit measured after its last
gate. The measurements are excluded from the folded body and appended unchanged at the end. target_circuit ( Circuit | TwirledCircuit ) – The original noisy circuit to be amplified, as an Circuit or a TwirledCircuit . folds ( int ) – How many times to insert U^dagger U . 0 returns a copy of the input
circuit. s folds give a noise factor of 1 + 2s . name ( str | None ) – Name for the returned circuit. Defaults to the input circuit’s name (when
available) suffixed with the fold count. The noise amplified circuit, in the same representation as the input, with a TwirledCircuit keeping its rot_dict so that a folded randomized circuit can still be untwirled. The original
circuit is not modified. ValueError – If folds is not a whole number of at least 0, if the circuit contains
    a gate on a qubit after its measurement, if it has no foldable gates, or if it contains an operation
    with no well-defined inverse. content:
Readout twirling string generation utilities. This module provides helper functions to build per-qubit I/X twirling
strings used by REM workflows. The supported strategies are: Requires up to 2n strings for n active qubits. MINIMAL : Two alternating strings. LOCAL : 4 strings balancing nearest-neighbor pair combinations. The number of strings should be a multiple of 4, ideally four times the smaller
power of 2 greater than the largest control line length.
This ensures balanced coverage across all pairs of qubits connected by a control line. Note All strategies ensure that, for each qubit, the number of I and X operators is equal. title: iqm.error_reduction_tools.twirling.twirling_modifiers.randomize_circuit
description:
Randomize a quantum circuit using Poor Man’s Pauli Twirling (PMPT). Produces a new circuit that is logically equivalent to the input (up to
readout twirling characters recorded in TwirledCircuit.rot_d...
content:
Randomize a quantum circuit using Poor Man’s Pauli Twirling (PMPT). Produces a new circuit that is logically equivalent to the input (up to
readout twirling characters recorded in TwirledCircuit.rot_dict ),
but with the θ angle of (arbitrarily/randomly) selected existing single-qubit R gates
increased by π. The necessary bookkeeping for tracking the changes required downstream
to maintain logical equivalence is handled by the TrackingRegisters class internally,
so that no extra physical gates are added to the circuit. Algorithm overview (gate-by-gate processing): PRX (single-qubit R gate) — handled by process_r_gate : Absorb any pending virtual-Z and π rotations (stored in the TrackingRegisters )
into the gate parameters (see take_care_of_pending_operations , absorb_pending_pi_rotation ). With probability twirling_prob , insert a π rotation (with random φ angle) after
the gate and combine the two together (see insert_twirling_pi_rotation ).
On the last SQG of each qubit, the probability may be overridden to enforce a desired
readout twirling basis. CZ (two-qubit gate) — handled by process_cz_gate :
Propagate (pending) operations through the CZ gate, updating the TrackingRegisters . Measure — handled by process_measure_gate :
Record the net readout twirling basis (‘I’ or ‘X’) from the parity
of accumulated π rotations. Pending virtual-Z rotations are dropped. If the measured qubit
has no SQG and readout twirling enforces ‘X’, a final PRX(π, 0) is added before measurement
to ensure the correct readout twirling basis. Barrier / Delay — passed through unchanged. The recorded readout twirling characters can later be used by untwirl_counts to recover the original measurement statistics. Note Right now, there is no support for MOVE gates. If the input circuit contains MOVE operations,
a ValueError will be raised. circuit ( TwirledCircuit ) – The quantum circuit to randomize. rgen ( Generator ) – Random number generator for twirling decisions. drop_final_rz ( bool ) – If True, drop final virtual-Z rotations before measurements. readout_twirling ( bool | dict [ str , str ] ) – Controls readout twirling behavior:
- False : no readout twirling (last SQG forced to even parity).
- True : free twirling (no constraint on last SQG).
- dict : maps qubit names to ‘I’ or ‘X’ to enforce a specific basis. twirling_probabilities ( Iterable [ float ] | float | None ) – Probability of inserting a π rotation per SQG.
Can be a single float (broadcast), a per-gate iterable, or None (default 0.5). fix_axes ( bool ) – If True, twirling π rotations use the same phase as the gate
instead of a uniformly random phase. A new TwirledCircuit with randomized gates and rot_dict set to
the per-qubit readout twirling characters. ValueError – If twirling_probabilities length doesn’t match the number of
    single-qubit gates, or if an unsupported operation is encountered. TypeError – If readout_twirling has an invalid type. TwirledCircuit previous iqm.error_reduction_tools.twirling.twirling_modifiers.process_r_gate next iqm.error_reduction_tools.twirling.twirling_modifiers.take_care_of_pending_operations By IQM Error Reduction Tools developers © Copyright 2024-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 0.4.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: iqm.error_reduction_tools.utils.circuit_utils.TwirledCircuit
description:
Bases: object A quantum circuit wrapper that supports readout twirling and gate randomization. This class serves as a mutable working representation for building and manipulating
quantum circuits. It ...
content:
Bases: object A quantum circuit wrapper that supports readout twirling and gate randomization. This class serves as a mutable working representation for building and manipulating
quantum circuits. It tracks single-qubit gates, measurements, and
readout twirling state. Use to_circuit(name) to convert to the immutable Circuit . Note The operations are not stored as a Circuit . Circuit.instructions is an immutable tuple , which would be rebuilt on
every append_operation call. Instead, operations is kept as a mutable list[CircuitOperation] throughout circuit construction, and converted to Circuit on demand via to_circuit() . operations ( list [ CircuitOperation ] ) List of operations in the circuit. Dictionary for readout twirling rotations, if applied. Free-form annotations, like iqm.pulse.Circuit.metadata , e.g. the number of folds
of a folded circuit. Counter for single-qubit gates per qubit. List of qubits that are measured. List of all qubits involved in the circuit. Methods append_operation (operation) Append a deep copy of the operation to the circuit and update basic analysis. basic_analysis () Perform basic analysis on quantum circuit operations. get_rot_char_per_meas_key () Get rotation character per measurement key due to readout twirling. qubit_to_clbit () Map each measured qubit to the classical bit its outcome lands in. to_circuit (name) Convert to an immutable Circuit . Perform basic analysis on quantum circuit operations. This method analyzes the circuit operations to extract information about
single-qubit gates, measurements, and active qubits. It also validates
that no mid-circuit measurements are present. ValueError – If mid-circuit measurements are detected (when any qubit is measured more than once). None Note This method populates the following instance attributes: sqg_counter : Dictionary mapping qubit identifiers to the count of ‘prx’
operations performed on each qubit. measured_qubits : List of qubit identifiers that have measurement operations. active_qubits : List of all qubit identifiers that appear in any operation. The method iterates through all operations in the circuit and: Counts ‘prx’ (parametric rotation) operations per qubit Counts measurement operations per qubit Collects all qubits involved in any operation Validates that no qubit is measured more than once Append a deep copy of the operation to the circuit and update basic analysis. A deep copy is made to ensure that no external references to the operation
are retained, preventing shared-state bugs when the same source circuit
is randomized multiple times. operation ( CircuitOperation ) None Map each measured qubit to the classical bit its outcome lands in. Read from the measurement keys, so it agrees with the counts bitstrings. Falls back to
measurement order when the keys carry no classical bit index. Qubit name to classical bit index. dict [ str , int ] Get rotation character per measurement key due to readout twirling. Dictionary mapping measurement keys to rotation characters (‘I’ or ‘X’). dict [ str , str ] Convert to an immutable Circuit . name ( str ) – Name to assign to the circuit. A Circuit with the current operations as instructions, and metadata carried over. content:
Estimate the Shannon entropy of the measurement probability distribution. Computes \(H = -\\sum_i p_i \\log_2(p_i)\) from the observed counts
which quantifies the spread of the distribution.  Higher entropy means
more unique outcomes with similar probabilities, making mitigation
more expensive. counts ( dict [ str , int ] ) – Dictionary mapping bitstrings to their measured counts. Shannon entropy in bits.  Ranges from 0 (single outcome) to \(\\log_2(N)\) where N is the number of unique bitstrings. float previous iqm.error_reduction_tools.rem.rem_processors next iqm.error_reduction_tools.rem.rem_processors.should_apply_mitigation By IQM Error Reduction Tools developers © Copyright 2024-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 0.4.0. title: iqm.error_reduction_tools.twirling.twirling_api.TwirlingConfiguration
description: Bases: object Configuration for circuit twirling. Attributes circuit_twirling Whether to apply Pauli twirling to two-qubit gates ("Poor Man's Pauli Twirling"). num_twirling_instances Total number of r...
content:
Bases: object Configuration for circuit twirling. Attributes circuit_twirling Whether to apply Pauli twirling to two-qubit gates ("Poor Man's Pauli Twirling"). num_twirling_instances Total number of randomized variants per input circuit when circuit_twirling=True . readout_twirl_strategy Readout-twirling strategy. seed RNG seed for reproducibility. Methods __eq__ (other) Return self==value. __repr__ () Return repr(self). readout_twirl_strategy ( Literal [ 'LOCAL' , 'MINIMAL' , 'HADAMARD' , 'NONE' ] ) seed ( int | None ) circuit_twirling ( bool ) num_twirling_instances ( int ) Readout-twirling strategy. Supported values are "LOCAL" (4 strings, requires topology), "MINIMAL" (2 strings), "HADAMARD" (up to $2^n$ strings), and "NONE" to disable readout twirling entirely.
When "NONE" is combined with circuit_twirling=True , num_twirling_instances random
circuit-twirled variants are generated instead. RNG seed for reproducibility. None means non-deterministic. Whether to apply Pauli twirling to two-qubit gates (“Poor Man’s Pauli Twirling”). When False , the inserted Pauli rotations on single-qubit gates are suppressed;
readout twirling (if any) still works. Total number of randomized variants per input circuit when circuit_twirling=True . This budget is split evenly across the readout-twirling rot-strings (whose count is
fixed by readout_twirl_strategy ) so that every rot-string receives the same
number of independent Pauli randomizations. Reconciliation rules (a warning is emitted whenever the effective count differs
from the requested one): If num_twirling_instances is a multiple of the number of rot-strings,
it is used as-is. If it is not a multiple, it is rounded up to the next multiple. If it is smaller than the number of rot-strings, the number of rot-strings
is used (one Pauli randomization per rot-string). When circuit_twirling=False this field is ignored: each rot-string is emitted
exactly once. Default of 20 follows common Pauli-twirling practice (10–50 instances). previous iqm.error_reduction_tools.twirling.twirling_api.CircuitTwirler next iqm.error_reduction_tools.twirling.twirling_modifiers By IQM Error Reduction Tools developers © Copyright 2024-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 0.4.0. title: iqm.error_reduction_tools.cdr.cdr_training_set.generate_clifford_training_set
description: Generate Clifford training circuits for a target circuit. target_circuit ( Circuit ) – The target circuit, with its final measurements. observables ( Sequence ) – Diagonal observables indexed by class...
content:
Generate Clifford training circuits for a target circuit. target_circuit ( Circuit ) – The target circuit, with its final measurements. observables ( Sequence ) – Diagonal observables indexed by classical bit, in a format accepted by to_pauli_terms() . num_training_circuits ( int ) – Number of training circuits. Fewer are returned when there are not enough distinct
library assignments. strategy ( str ) – "pool_fps" evaluates a random pool of candidates and selects a spread subset with farthest_point_selection() . "optimize" searches, by coordinate descent over the gate choices,
for one circuit per value of a uniform grid of target values. pool_size ( int | None ) – Size of the candidate pool of "pool_fps" . None uses max(200, 50 * num_training_circuits) . coefficients ( Sequence [ float ] | None ) – Coefficients of the terms of the fitted observable, shape (num_terms,) . If given, both
strategies spread the combined value instead of the values of single terms. primary_index ( int ) – Observable that "optimize" spreads when coefficients is not given. target_grid ( Sequence [ float ] | None ) – Target values of "optimize" . None uses a uniform grid over [-1, 1] , or over the
reachable range of the combined value when coefficients is given. max_descent_passes ( int ) – Largest number of coordinate-descent passes per target value of "optimize" . max_opt_slots ( int ) – Largest number of slots that "optimize" changes, chosen at random on deep circuits. dedup ( bool ) – Whether to drop duplicate library assignments before selection. rng_seed ( int | None ) – Seed of the random number generator. None gives a different result on every call. identity_as_delay ( bool ) – Whether the identity in the library is a delay instead of prx(0, 0) . identity_delay ( float ) – Duration of the identity delay, in seconds. clifford_atol ( float ) – Tolerance for Clifford detection. progress ( bool ) – Whether to show tqdm progress bars. self_check ( bool ) – Whether to compare the fast evaluation with the Stim simulation once. build_stim_circuits ( bool ) – Whether to also store the Stim circuits of the selected circuits. validate_selected ( bool ) – Whether to check that the selected circuits are Clifford. verbose ( bool ) – Whether to print the number of selected circuits and their spread. The training set. ValueError – If strategy is neither "pool_fps" nor "optimize" . RuntimeError – If self_check is True and the two evaluations disagree. title: iqm-qubit-selector
description:
Picks the best set of qubits on an IQM QPU to run a given circuit on. Gate and readout fidelities vary from qubit to qubit and from coupler to
coupler, so where a circuit runs matters. IQM Qubit Selec...
content:
Picks the best set of qubits on an IQM QPU to run a given circuit on. Gate and readout fidelities vary from qubit to qubit and from coupler to
coupler, so where a circuit runs matters. IQM Qubit Selector enumerates the
placements the QPU’s couplings allow and ranks them with the latest
calibration metrics, without transpiling the circuit for any candidate. Set the IQM_TOKEN environment variable to your API token before connecting.
To place several circuits, fetch the architecture and metrics once and pass
them instead of the client, as select_layout(circuit, arch, metrics) . This
also works without a client, e.g. with metrics measured offline. SDK-agnostic. The core, iqm.qubit_selector.core , works on an iqm.pulse.Circuit , so circuits from IQM Pulse, Qiskit, Cirq and Qrisp
are all placed with the same call. Calibration-aware. Layouts are ranked by an error budget built from
two-qubit, single-qubit and, optionally, readout fidelities. score_layouts returns the breakdown for every candidate. Crystal and Star QPUs. On Star QPUs the resonator is handled
automatically; no extra arguments are needed. Extensible. The coupling graph, enumerators and cost model can be used
on their own, or replaced with your own. Version 2.0 replaces the Qiskit-based iqm.qubit_selector.qubit_selector and iqm.qubit_selector.qiskit_utils modules with iqm.qubit_selector.core . The
old modules are removed and there is no compatibility layer; see the changelog
for how to port existing code. The user guide, API reference and example notebooks are at docs.iqm.tech/iqm-qubit-selector . Note: uv is highly recommended
for practical Python environment and package management.
The supported Python versions are =3.11, <3.15. The following optional extras are available: notebook : Qiskit, Cirq and Qrisp support, and Jupyter for the notebooks All extras are inter-compatible and each adds more dependencies
on top of the base install. To install all of them: For reproducible installations, pinned dependency extras
are available: pin-iqm : pins inter-IQM package dependencies to exact
co-released versions. pin-all : like pin-iqm , but additionally pins all
transitive third-party dependencies. These can be combined with other extras. The following
combined extras are available: notebook-pin-iqm notebook-pin-all For example: All extras are inter-compatible, so you can combine multiple
extras with pinning as needed. Note: This package was tested at release time for clean
installation with uv 0.13.6 and pip 25.1.1 .
Other versions are likely to work but are not verified
per release. previous IQM Qubit Selector next Qubit Selector user guide By IQM Qubit Selector developers © Copyright 2022-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 2.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: Example: GHZ state on the best qubits
description:
We prepare a GHZ state with Qiskit and execute it on the optimal layout found by the core of IQM Qubit Selector
( iqm.qubit_selector.core ), and on the naive layout transpile_to_IQM picks by default. ...
content:
We prepare a GHZ state with Qiskit and execute it on the optimal layout found by the core of IQM Qubit Selector
( iqm.qubit_selector.core ), and on the naive layout transpile_to_IQM picks by default. The Hellinger fidelity to
the ideal GHZ distribution shows the difference. The example runs on a crystal QPU (Garnet) first, and then on a Star QPU (Sirius). Position i of a layout does not belong to virtual qubit i . It belongs to the i -th qubit of the converted
circuit in the selector’s order: the qubits with two-qubit gates first, then the others, each group sorted by name
(as strings, so QB10 comes before QB2 ). The converted circuit’s qubits are the physical qubits Qiskit picked, so selected_initial_layout follows each virtual qubit from the qubit Qiskit placed it on to the one the selector
chose. Pinning [backend.qubit_name_to_index(q) for q in best_layout] instead would scramble the qubits, and Qiskit
would add SWAPs to undo it. Switch on the logging of the selector to see what it does at each step: how many candidate layouts the enumerator
finds, whether the search budget cut it short, and the error budget of the best layout. The selector logs under iqm.qubit_selector ; the cell below shows its INFO messages in the notebook. Set the IQM_TOKEN environment variable to your IQM Resonance API token before starting the notebook. IQMProvider reads it from there, so the token never appears in the notebook. Transpile the circuit to the backend with transpile_to_IQM and convert it with qiskit_to_iqm . The transpiled
circuit already sits on physical qubits that Qiskit picked, which is the naive layout run below; the selector treats
those names as placeholders and may move the circuit elsewhere. Given the client, the selector fetches the
architecture and metrics of the default calibration set itself. Pin the best layout by turning it into the physical qubit index of each virtual qubit, which is the initial_layout Qiskit expects. The optimal layout puts the gates on the qubits and couplers with the best calibration metrics, which shows up as a
higher GHZ fidelity than the naive run. On Sirius every two-qubit gate goes through the computational resonator. The selector ranks the qubits with
fictional CZ fidelities that combine the resonator CZ and MOVE fidelities, and transpile_to_IQM adds the MOVE gates on the pinned qubits. The steps are the same as above. The 10-qubit GHZ state uses only part of Sirius, so there are layouts to choose from. previous Examples next API Reference By IQM Qubit Selector developers © Copyright 2022-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 2.0.0. title: Qubit Selector user guide
description: This guide shows how to choose the physical qubits a circuit runs on with IQM Qubit Selector, iqm.qubit_selector.core . The core enumerates the placements of the couplings that the QPU allows for and ...
content:
This guide shows how to choose the physical qubits a circuit runs on with IQM Qubit Selector, iqm.qubit_selector.core . The core enumerates the placements of the couplings that the QPU allows for and ranks them with
the latest calibration metrics, without transpiling the circuit for any candidate. It works on an iqm.pulse.Circuit , so it does not depend on the SDK the circuit was
written in: IQM Pulse, Qiskit, Cirq and Qrisp circuits are all placed with the same call. For a notebook you can run and check the output of yourself, see the examples . Note IQM provides access to its quantum computers via IQM Resonance – IQM’s quantum cloud service.
Please head over to our website to learn more. The steps are: Connect to a QPU and fetch its architecture and calibration metrics. Convert a circuit from your SDK to an iqm.pulse.Circuit . Rank layouts with select_layout() and score_layouts() . Tune the ranking: readout, excluded qubits, search budget, what-if metrics. Run the circuit on the selected layout. Install the iqm-qubit-selector distribution package from the Python Package Index (PyPI). It brings IQM Client,
IQM Pulse and IQM Station Control Client along, which is all iqm.qubit_selector.core needs for circuits
written in IQM Pulse: Qiskit is not installed by default. To prepare circuits in Qiskit, Cirq or Qrisp, connect with IQMProvider , or run the example notebooks, install the notebook feature as
well. It brings IQM Client with its Qiskit, Cirq and Qrisp adapters, and Jupyter: Set the IQM_TOKEN environment variable to the API token obtained from the IQM Server web dashboard. IQMClient and IQMProvider read it from
there, so the token does not have to appear in your code or notebooks. Connect with IQMProvider . The backend carries both the client and the
architecture of the QPU: Without Qiskit, connect with from_url() instead. The selector needs two inputs besides the circuit: the DynamicQuantumArchitecture of the
QPU, which says which gates act on which qubits, and a MetricsData with the gate and readout fidelities of the latest
calibration. get_metrics_data() fetches the metrics of a calibration
set and keeps what the cost model uses: CZ fidelities per qubit pair ( two_qubit ), PRX fidelities per qubit
( single_qubit ) and readout metrics per qubit ( readout , keyed by ReadoutMode ). Pass the calibration set of the architecture, so that the
metrics match it; without one, the server’s current default calibration set is used: get_full_metrics_data() returns everything it parses
as a FullMetricsData , including Clifford fidelities and T1 / T2 times. These are for reference only and are not used for ranking: The selector only looks at which qubits a circuit uses and how many gates act on each qubit and qubit pair. Any
circuit that can be expressed as an iqm.pulse.Circuit can therefore
be placed. The circuit’s qubit names only identify its qubits; the selector decides which physical qubits they go to. The examples below all build a GHZ circuit on six qubits. CircuitOperationList builds a circuit from native IQM operations, on
placeholder qubits QB1 to QBn . A measure operation acts on any number of qubits, so it is added with add_op() : Transpile the circuit to the backend with transpile_to_IQM() , then convert
it with qiskit_to_iqm() , which returns the converted circuits and a compiler.
The transpiled circuit already sits on physical qubits that Qiskit picked; the selector treats those names as
placeholders and may move the circuit elsewhere: serialize_circuit() converts a Cirq circuit in native IQM gates ( PhasedXPowGate to prx , CZ to cz , measurements to measure ) on NamedQid qubits named like IQM qubits: transpile_to_iqm() converts the circuit to native IQM gates and needs the connectivity of the
circuit’s qubits as pairs of indices. Since the selector chooses the physical qubits afterwards, allow every pair to
interact so that the transpiler adds no SWAPs. qrisp_to_iqm_converter() then produces the iqm.pulse.Circuit : select_layout() returns the best num_layouts layouts as (layout, error) pairs, best first. The error is the estimated probability that at least one gate or readout
fails, so lower is better. The call is the same for every SDK; the results can differ slightly because each SDK
decomposes the GHZ circuit into a different number of gates: The QPU can also be given as a client, and the selector fetches the architecture and metrics of the default
calibration set itself: Give either a client alone, or arch and metrics without one. The selector fetches on every call, so when placing
several circuits, or scoring with freshly measured metrics, fetch arch once, as above, and pass it with the
metrics. A layout lists one physical qubit per circuit qubit. Position i belongs to the i -th circuit qubit in this
order: the qubits with two-qubit gates first, then the others, each group sorted by name. Names sort as strings, so QB10 comes before QB2 . The helper below turns a layout into an explicit mapping; use it whenever you place
the circuit yourself: Each layout is scored as an error budget in nats: every gate or readout with fidelity F adds -ln(F) , and total is the sum. A difference of d nats between two layouts means the better one is exp(d) times more
likely to run without error. The error of select_layout() is 1 - exp(-total) ; for deep circuits it approaches 100% for every candidate, while total still tells them apart. score_layouts() returns every candidate as a LayoutScore , sorted by total , with the two-qubit, single-qubit and readout
terms that make it up: readout_mode selects which readout metric enters the score: ReadoutMode.NONE (default): readout is not scored. ReadoutMode.FIDELITY : single-shot readout fidelity. Use it when you do not mitigate readout errors. ReadoutMode.QNDNESS : how well the measured state survives the measurement. Use it when the circuit keeps using
a qubit after measuring it. remove_qubits_list keeps qubits out of every layout, for example qubits you know to be faulty although their
metrics do not show it. They are removed from the coupling graph before the search, so they do not connect other
qubits either: max_num_layouts caps the number of candidate layouts that are scored. The default, 20000, spreads the candidates
over the whole QPU for chips of up to about 150 qubits. A larger budget finds more candidates in each region, at the
cost of a slower search: When the budget is too small to cover every candidate, the enumerators sample with a fixed seed, so the same inputs
always give the same ranking. Pass seed to make_enumerator() to draw a
different sample; see Building blocks . MetricsData is a plain dataclass, so you can edit the metrics to see
how the ranking reacts. Two-qubit fidelities are keyed by two_qubit_key() in both orientations. Here the couplers the best layout uses are made much worse, and the selector moves the circuit
elsewhere: You can also build MetricsData from scratch, for example from your own
characterisation data. two_qubit_fidelities() stores each pair in both
orientations. A readout mode you never score may be left out. A qubit or pair without a metric gives every layout
that uses it infinite error, so it is never selected, and a fidelity outside (0, 1] raises ValueError : score_layouts() chains four steps, each available on its own: iqm.qubit_selector.core.ir reads the circuit: two-qubit gate counts per pair
( interactions_from_circuit() ), single-qubit gate counts per qubit and the
measured qubits. build_coupling_graph() turns the architecture into a networkx graph of coupled qubits. make_enumerator() picks the enumerator for that graph: VF2Enumerator searches the graph for placements of the circuit’s
interactions, and AllToAllEnumerator picks qubit sets directly when
every pair is coupled. A cost model, here FastEdgeCost , scores the layouts and sorts them. To rank with your own cost model, subclass CostCalculatorBase and implement score_single_layout() . It returns a LayoutCost (or a subclass), and the base class takes care of scoring and
sorting. This one ranks on the two-qubit gates only: Layout selection does not depend on the SDK, but running the circuit does. With Qiskit, pin the circuit’s virtual
qubits to the selected physical qubits with initial_layout when transpiling it. For that, the selector should see the circuit’s virtual qubits rather than the physical qubits of a default
placement. Convert the circuit to native IQM gates without placing it, with virtual qubit i named QB{i+1} ,
and turn the selected layout into the physical qubit index of each virtual qubit: Then transpile with that layout pinned, and run. transpile_to_IQM() works on crystal and Star QPUs alike; on a Star QPU it
also adds the MOVE gates: The qubit_selector_core_qiskit_example notebook in the examples runs a GHZ circuit this way on a
crystal and a Star QPU, and compares it with the placement transpile_to_IQM picks without initial_layout . On a Star QPU, such as sirius , the qubits do not couple to each other directly. Every two-qubit gate goes through
a computational resonator: a MOVE gate moves the state of one qubit into the resonator, a CZ acts between the
resonator and a second qubit, and another MOVE moves the state back. The calls stay the same: Three things happen behind the scenes: Fictional CZ fidelities. A logical CZ(q1, q2) runs as MOVE(q2, r) CZ(q1, r) MOVE(q2, r) through a
shared resonator r , so its fidelity is F_cz(q1, r) * F_move(q2, r) ** 2 , with the better choice of MOVE qubit kept. get_metrics_data() returns these qubit-qubit
fidelities in two_qubit , computed from the measured resonator fidelities by fictional_two_qubit_fidelities() . A collapsed coupling graph. build_coupling_graph() replaces the
resonator loci with the qubit pairs that MOVE + CZ can couple. With a single resonator every pair can, so the
graph is complete and make_enumerator() picks AllToAllEnumerator , which ranks sets of qubits directly. MOVE gates are removed from the circuit. A Qiskit circuit transpiled with transpile_to_IQM() for a Star QPU contains MOVE gates. The selector
removes them to recover the qubit-qubit interactions, so the circuit can be passed as it is. For the same reason, a Qrisp circuit for a single-resonator Star QPU can be transpiled with all-to-all connectivity,
as in the Qrisp example above. The API reference documents every function and class of iqm.qubit_selector.core . The examples include qubit_selector_core_qiskit_example , a ready-to-run notebook that
places a GHZ circuit on a crystal and a Star QPU and compares it with the default placement. previous iqm-qubit-selector next Examples By IQM Qubit Selector developers © Copyright 2022-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 2.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: AllToAllEnumerator
description: Module: iqm.qubit_selector.core.enumerator Bases: BaseEnumerator Enumerate layouts on a complete coupling graph. Every k -subset of the QPU’s qubits is a valid layout here, so VF2 would prune nothing;...
content:
Module: iqm.qubit_selector.core.enumerator Bases: BaseEnumerator Enumerate layouts on a complete coupling graph. Every k -subset of the QPU’s qubits is a valid layout here, so VF2 would prune nothing; the subsets
are generated directly instead. Only one assignment of logical to physical qubits is tried per set. Trying all k! would use up
the budget on reshuffling a few sets, and on a randomised 20-qubit star the best assignment beat
the canonical one by only about 0.02 nats (under 2% relative error). VF2Enumerator makes
the same trade-off. When C(N, k) exceeds max_num_layouts , a seeded uniform sample of the subsets is returned;
taking them in label order would never reach the high-numbered qubits. node_labels ( list [ str ] ) – Names of the QPU’s qubits. max_num_layouts ( int ) – Maximum number of layouts to return. seed ( int | None ) – Seed for the sample; None for a fresh draw on every call. Methods enumerate Return up to max_num_layouts qubit sets of size num_circuit_qubits . Return up to max_num_layouts qubit sets of size num_circuit_qubits . The interaction graph is only validated: on a complete graph any qubit set can host it. interaction_graph ( dict [ frozenset [ str ] , int ] ) – 2-qubit interaction graph over logical qubit names. num_circuit_qubits ( int ) – Number of qubits in the circuit. Layouts in node_labels order. ValueError – If the circuit needs no qubits, more qubits than the QPU has, or fewer
    qubits than its interaction graph involves. list [ list [ str ]] Inheritance previous iqm.qubit_selector.core.enumerator.make_enumerator next BaseEnumerator By IQM Qubit Selector developers © Copyright 2022-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 2.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: cost
description:
Full path: iqm.qubit_selector.core.cost Cost models for ranking candidate layouts. Costs are error budgets in nats: sums of -log(fidelity) rather than products of fidelities.
A routed circuit with a f...
content:
Full path: iqm.qubit_selector.core.cost Cost models for ranking candidate layouts. Costs are error budgets in nats: sums of -log(fidelity) rather than products of fidelities.
A routed circuit with a few thousand CZ gates has a fidelity product around 1e-6 , so 1 - product rounds every candidate to 100% even when they differ by orders of magnitude, while
the sums still tell them apart. Rank on LayoutCost.total ; LayoutCost.error is for
display. A new cost model subclasses CostCalculatorBase and implements score_single_layout() . Classes CostCalculatorBase Base class of the cost models: subclasses score one layout, this class ranks many. FastEdgeCost Score layouts from QPU metrics alone, without transpiling the circuit. LayoutCost A layout and its total error budget. LayoutScore A LayoutCost split into the terms FastEdgeCost scores. Inheritance previous core next CostCalculatorBase By IQM Qubit Selector developers © Copyright 2022-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 2.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

content:
Return the best num_layouts layouts for circuit with their total errors. The errors are 1 - exp(-total) and saturate at 1.0 for deep circuits, where every candidate
then looks equally bad; use score_layouts() in that case. Give the QPU as in score_layouts() . circuit ( Circuit ) – The circuit to place. arch ( DynamicQuantumArchitecture | None ) – Architecture of the target QPU. Leave out when client is given. metrics ( MetricsData | None ) – QPU metrics used for scoring. Leave out when client is given. client ( IQMClient | None ) – Client to fetch the architecture and metrics from. num_layouts ( int ) – Number of layouts to return. readout_mode ( ReadoutMode ) – Which readout metric to include, if any. remove_qubits_list ( list [ str ] | None ) – Physical qubits to keep out of every layout, e.g. known-bad ones. max_num_layouts ( int ) – Maximum number of candidate layouts to score; see score_layouts() . (layout, error) pairs, best first, so result[0][0] is the best layout. ValueError – If the QPU is not given as either client alone, or arch and metrics without a client. title: VF2Enumerator
description: Module: iqm.qubit_selector.core.enumerator Bases: BaseEnumerator Enumerate layouts with rustworkx VF2 subgraph monomorphism. VF2 tries the QPU’s qubits in index order, so a single capped search return...
content:
Module: iqm.qubit_selector.core.enumerator Bases: BaseEnumerator Enumerate layouts with rustworkx VF2 subgraph monomorphism. VF2 tries the QPU’s qubits in index order, so a single capped search returns layouts clustered in one
corner of the chip. Each search here therefore runs on a copy of the coupling graph renumbered by distance
from a different start qubit, and the searches take turns (see _round_robin() ), which gives
every qubit the same share of the budget as a starting point. Each search is capped at max_num_layouts VF2 states. rustworkx reports a capped search the same
way as an exhausted one, so matches can be missed without a truncation warning. coupling_graph ( Graph ) – QPU coupling graph; nodes are qubit names. max_num_layouts ( int ) – Maximum number of layouts to return, and the VF2 state limit of each search.
With fewer than the number of QPU qubits, some qubits never serve as a start; 10-15
times that number gave full coverage on a 150-qubit lattice. seed ( int | None ) – Seed for the start order and the placement of single-qubit-only qubits; None for a
fresh draw on every call. Methods enumerate Return up to max_num_layouts layouts that can host interaction_graph . Return up to max_num_layouts layouts that can host interaction_graph . VF2 matches only the core qubits. Single-qubit-only qubits need no coupling, so they are placed
on unused qubits afterwards; this keeps the VF2 pattern small. The interaction graph may be disconnected, e.g. CZ(QB1, QB2) and CZ(QB3, QB4) . Its
components may then land on non-adjacent parts of the QPU, which is a valid layout. interaction_graph ( dict [ frozenset [ str ] , int ] ) – 2-qubit interaction graph over logical qubit names. num_circuit_qubits ( int ) – Number of qubits in the circuit, including single-qubit-only ones. Layouts of physical qubit names, in the order BaseEnumerator.enumerate() describes. ValueError – If the circuit needs no qubits, more qubits than the QPU has, or fewer
    qubits than its interaction graph involves. list [ list [ str ]] Inheritance previous BaseEnumerator next graph_builder By IQM Qubit Selector developers © Copyright 2022-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 2.0.0. Last updated on 2026-11-10.

title: iqm.qubit_selector.core.selector.score_layouts
description:
Score every candidate layout for circuit , best first, with the error split by source. Prefer this over select_layout() for deep circuits, where every candidate’s error rounds to
100% but total still ...
content:
Score every candidate layout for circuit , best first, with the error split by source. Prefer this over select_layout() for deep circuits, where every candidate’s error rounds to
100% but total still tells them apart. On a Star architecture the circuit’s MOVE gates are removed and the QPU is collapsed to
qubit-qubit couplings, so metrics must hold the matching fictional CZ fidelities, as get_metrics_data() returns them. Give the QPU either as client , from which the architecture and metrics are fetched on every
call, or as arch and metrics without a client. circuit ( Circuit ) – The circuit to place. arch ( DynamicQuantumArchitecture | None ) – Architecture of the target QPU. Leave out when client is given. metrics ( MetricsData | None ) – QPU metrics used for scoring. Leave out when client is given. client ( IQMClient | None ) – Client to fetch the architecture and metrics from. readout_mode ( ReadoutMode ) – Which readout metric to include, if any. remove_qubits_list ( list [ str ] | None ) – Physical qubits to keep out of every layout, e.g. known-bad ones. max_num_layouts ( int ) – Maximum number of candidate layouts to score. On a sparse coupling graph it
is also the VF2 state limit of each search; see VF2Enumerator for how to size it. All scored layouts, lowest total first. ValueError – If the QPU is not given as either client alone, or arch and metrics without a client. ValueError – If the circuit acts on more qubits than the QPU has left after remove_qubits_list . list [ LayoutScore ] previous selector next iqm.qubit_selector.core.selector.select_layout By IQM Qubit Selector developers © Copyright 2022-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 2.0.0. title: iqm.qubit_selector.core.metrics_data.fictional_two_qubit_fidelities
description: Return effective qubit-qubit CZ fidelities for a Star architecture. A Star QPU has no direct qubit-qubit CZ: CZ(q1, q2) runs as MOVE(q2, r) CZ(q1, r) MOVE(q2, r) through a shared computational resonat...
content:
Return effective qubit-qubit CZ fidelities for a Star architecture. A Star QPU has no direct qubit-qubit CZ: CZ(q1, q2) runs as MOVE(q2, r) CZ(q1, r) MOVE(q2, r) through a shared computational resonator r , so its
fidelity is taken as cz(q1, r) * move(q2, r) ** 2 ( [ 1 ] ; the same model as IQMTarget._create_fictional_cz_properties ). The pairs are those simplify_architecture() creates, so they match the collapsed
coupling graph. When a pair can be routed several ways (either qubit moved, or through several resonators), the
best fidelity is kept, since the transpiler is free to pick that route. Pairs missing a metric are
left out, so the cost model treats them as uncalibrated rather than perfect. cz_resonator ( Mapping [ str , float ] ) – Qubit-resonator CZ fidelities, keyed as in FullMetricsData.cz_resonator . move ( Mapping [ str , float ] ) – Single-MOVE fidelities, keyed as in FullMetricsData.move . arch ( DynamicQuantumArchitecture ) – The raw Star architecture, used for its CZ and MOVE loci. Two-qubit fidelities with both orderings of each pair, for MetricsData.two_qubit . dict [ str , float ] previous iqm.qubit_selector.core.metrics_data.ReadoutMetrics next iqm.qubit_selector.core.metrics_data.two_qubit_fidelities By IQM Qubit Selector developers © Copyright 2022-2026, IQM Finland Oy, Release 2.0.0.
